Setting
Classroom

Teacher Background
The earth has several major layers – a hot metallic core, a less hot liquid mantle,
and the solid lithosphere and crust on top (see background section of Journey
Through Earth for more information). The hot metallic core causes the mantle
immediately above to heat up. As the liquid rock in the mantle heats up, it rises
because a heated liquid (or gas) expands and becomes less dense than the cooler
liquid (or gas) nearby. When this hot liquid reaches the top of the mantle layer, it
gets pushed aside by more hot mantle rising below it, spreading out under the solid
lithosphere above like a cloud of steam hitting the ceiling of the kitchen. As it
spreads out, it cools. Cool liquids (and gases) shrink in volume and are more dense
than the warmer liquids (or gases) nearby. Therefore, the cooled mantle sinks to the
bottom of the mantle layer where it gets heated by the core and begins the cycle
anew.

This process through which heat energy is transferred through currents within a
liquid or gas is called convection. The cyclical nature of the process in an enclosed
system like the mantle of the Earth results in convection cells – local regions of
liquid or gas that form a relatively stable cycle (heating, rising, moving aside,
cooling, and sinking in roughly the same location over and over again).

Convection takes place in many other systems. A pot of water boiling on the stove is
a good example of convection. Watch spaghetti boiling in a large pot and you will
see the noodles rise near the middle of the pot above the flames, spread out over
the surface, and fall again near the edges where it is cool. In the Earth’s
atmosphere, convection results in regional weather patterns and thermals (rising
columns of heated air). Eagles and hang gliders both take advantage of thermals to
stay aloft. In the Earth’s oceans, the warm ocean water near the equator tends to
follow currents towards the poles while cold polar ocean water follow currents back
again to the equator.

A key concept is that hot fluid and gas rises and cold fluid and gas sinks. To
demonstrate this principle, you can create a hot air balloon in the classroom using a
dry cleaner bag and a hand-held hair dryer.

searchText:
www.amnh.org




               Activity: A Plate Tectonic Puzzle

               Introduction
               The Earth’s crust is not a solid shell. It is made up of thick, interconnecting pieces
               called tectonic plates that fit together like a puzzle. They move atop the underly-
               ing mantle, a really thick layer of hot flowing rock.

               By examining evidence such as similar rock layers in various places, fossilized desert
               belts, the distribution of fossils, and the physical shapes of continents, scientists
               have concluded that the Earth’s continents were once all connected to form a
               “supercontinent” called Pangaea that was surrounded by an enormous ocean. In
               this activity, students will use the different kinds of evidence to reconstruct how
               the Earth may have looked approximately 220 million years ago.

               Objectives
               Students will:
               • use logic and the evidence to reconstruct the position of large islands
                 and continents as they appeared 220 million years ago.
               • understand the theory of continental movement and plate tectonics.
               • describe how scientists use different kinds of evidence to form theories.

               Time Frame
               Two class periods (40 minutes each)

               Materials
               • Globe or world map
               • Answer page

               Per pair of students:
               • Reproducibles of instructions and continent cutouts pages
               • Scissors
               • Glue or tape
               • Sheet of paper
               • Ruler or compass




© 2007 American Museum of Natural History. All Rights Reserved.
                                                                                                        1
                                                                   www.amnh.org


                                                                                 Activity: A Plate Tectonic Puzzle
               Procedure
               Prior Knowledge
               1. Introduce students to the concept of continental movement and plate tectonics.
                  Call on volunteers to tell what they know about plate tectonics. Display a globe
                  or world map. Have students look carefully at the continents. Discuss with them
                  how Europe, Africa, South America, and North America might fit together as
                  puzzle pieces. Discuss what might explain this fit. Point out that millions of years
                  ago the continents were joined together in one supercontinent called Pangaea.
                  Using some of the same evidence that scientists use, they will reconstruct this
                  supercontinent.

               Exploration
               2. Have students work in pairs. Distribute the materials to each pair. Provide time
                  for them to review the instructions page.

               3. Explain that the landmasses they will be cutting out represent the continents
                  and some of the larger islands of the Earth the way scientists think they
                  appeared 220 million years ago. On a separate sheet of paper, have students
                  draw a large circle, about 8 inches in diameter, to represent the globe. Then
                  have them cut them out the islands and continents. Using the legend on the
                  instructions page, call on volunteers to identify what each symbol stands for.

               4. Tell students they are going to use the evidence (symbols) on the continents and
                  islands to reconstruct Pangaea, the supercontinent. Using the globe or world
                  map as a reference, discuss with students in what general area the continents
                  should be positioned. Ask them to identify what they should look for to deter-
                  mine which continental boundaries should be joined.

               5. Using the physical shape of continents, age of rock layers, fossilized desert belts,
                  and the distribution of fossils, have partners fit together the continents and
                  islands. Remind them that not all the boundaries may touch and that there
                  might be areas of water separating some of them. Once students are sure the
                  landmasses are in the correct position, have them tape or glue them onto the
                  world map. Have them label their maps along with the time period.

Figure 8.1.1

Finding the surface area
You can calculate or measure the total area of apple on the outside of this piece.
There are six faces.

The area of each face = 2 x 2 = 4 cm2.

The total surface on the apple cube = 2 x 2 x 6 = 24 cm2.


Finding the volume
The volume of a cube is found by the formula

volume = length x breadth x height

The total volume of the cube of apple = 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 cm3.
 Increasing the surface area
Now cut the apple cube into eight cubes with 1 cm sides. Do this by cutting the cube
in the middle of the length, the breadth and the height. Use Figure 8.1.2 to help you.

searchText: ﻿ Mineral are pure substances that occur naturally and there are about 3000 known minerals in the earth. Minerals can be found on their own and also mixed together in rocks. A mineral is the same substance all the way through. Many geologists know what the main minerals look like but often need to classify unusual minerals. Keys are used to identify minerals, including ores and minerals found in igneous rocks. COLOUR and LUSTRE • Colour refers to the main colour you can see. Many minerals have a range of colours. Sometimes impurities introduce new colours. • Lustre is the shininess of the surface. Is it metallic (like a shiny new coin) or is it non-metallic (dull)? HARDNESS • Hardness is how readily the mineral is scratched. Does your fingernail scratch the mineral? The Mohs scale measures the degree of hardness of different substances. On the Mohs scale, substances are rated from 1 (very soft) to 10 (very hard). STREAK and CLEAVAGE • Streak is the colour of the powdered mineral. You see this when you use the mineral to write on something hard, such as the back of a ceramic tile. • Cleavage is the ability to break along smooth planes, forming flat layers, sharp corners, boxes or other shapes. searchText: ﻿ Igneous rocks are formed when molten rock (magma) cools and solidifies either below (intrusive) or above (extrusive) the Earth’s surface. The rate at which the magma cools determines the rock’s properties. An igneous rock can take minutes or millions of years to form, depending on its rate of solidification and cooling of magma. Magma itself takes millions of years to be created as tectonic plates slide under each other and melt. Intrusive igneous rocks such as diorite, gabbro and granite have coarse grains. They have larger crystals than extrusive rocks because of a slower cooling and solidification rate below the surface. Extrusive igneous rocks such as basalt, obsidian and pumice have much smaller crystal formations than intrusive igneous rocks because of the faster cooling rates that occur on the surface. searchText: Making a Metamorphic Rock You are now going to make a metamorphic chocolate rock. You will place different stresses on chocolate pieces to form a metamorphic chocolate rock. The chocolate pieces represent grains in a rock or more easily visualized, individual grains like sandstone. As different stresses are placed on pieces students can witness or imagine how real rock reacts to the same stresses. Instructional Procedures: Place glass container on heat source with heat source off. Mix different kinds of chocolate pieces and M&M's and pour into glass container about 1 inch thick at bottom. Different colo urs allow students to choose a colo u r and wa tch as it changes instead of lo sing their 'grain' during the metamorphic process. Explain that the different pieces represent minerals in a rock or different gr ains in a sedimentary rock, i.e . quartz, salt, feldspar, amphibole, sand. Turn heat source on a low setting (do not let the mixture boil or melt). Warm the pieces until they become slightly soft. Explain to kids that metamorphic rocks are rocks that have been changed from one rock type (sedimentary, metamorphic, igneous ) into another rock type. The rock properties change like the chocolate pieces are changing before of them as they heat up. The minerals in real rock soften and are easily squished into different shapes when under pressure. Place plastic wrap around the object to be pushed into the jar. Now place pressure onto the chocolate pieces. This demonstration will take a few minutes to perform. That is fine, because time is the one factor affecting all metamorphic rock. Explain to students that the combined effects of heat and pressure over long periods of time are what change other rock into metamorphic rocks. Keep chocolate pieces on the heat source and under pressure until the pieces slowly squish together. Once the mass has become one "newly formed rock" remove from heat. After it cools cut up into pieces and give to kids to examine and eat. Discussion: As you perform the demonstration ask students to list the different stresses that form metamorphic rocks. On the same paper have students draw what is happening to the chocolate pieces. First, the pieces are normal. Second, placed on heat. Third, pressure applied, etc. Ask if one of the forces were removed would a metamorphic rock form? Try removing one of the forces (heat, pressure, or time). How much did the rock change from all stresses compared to only one? What changed from the first picture they drew to the last picture of the chocolate rock. Variation: Instead of using chocolate based pieces you may want to try jellybeans or some type of jelly concoctions. Replace the condensed milk with a Karo syrup and water mixture. The demonstration can be performed the same way.

title: Mantle convection moving plates
reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: Mantle convection moving plates: the golden syrup / hobnob teacher demonstration How convection currents in the mantle may be responsible for plate movement -the Golden Syrup and biscuit demonstration. Learning objectives: currents of solid but ductile mantle move beneath the lithosphere carrying the plates where plates collide one is taken down into the mantle and ‘destroyed’; where they move apart, new lithosphere is created. Timing: 15 minutes from the start of heating Preparation time: the syrup needs to be in the freezer for at least 1 hour in advance English National Curriculum links: 4.4.3n Health and safety: the syrup gets very hot Apparatus: large tin of Golden Syrup large beaker, 5 dm 3 packet of thin biscuits Bunsen burner, tripod and heatproof mat access to a freezer Pour the syrup into the beaker and leave in the freezer for 1 hour. Do not allow it to freeze, simply reduce the temperature to gain maximum viscosity. Break a biscuit in half carefully and place the two halves, touching, on the surface of the syrup. The biscuit halves need room to move apart, so ensure that the two halves are not too big (nibble pieces off the edges if necessary). Place the beaker and contents on a tripod without a gauze in place to ensure localised heating. Heat the beaker using a low blue flame directed at the centre of the beaker’s base. Slowly the central cone section of the syrup will change in colour as its temperature rises and its viscosity falls. Close observation will clearly show convection taking place in this region. After around 10 minutes (depending on the speed of heating and quantity of syrup used) the biscuit halves will have been driven apart by the convection currents. Convection currents in the mantle were thought, for many years, to be solely responsible for plate tectonic movements, with the movement taking rocks down at destructive margins and new rocks forming when plates spread. It is now thought likely that there are three possible driving mechanisms for plate tectonics: Movement of mantle convection currents as above The mass of the subducted plate (the sinking slab) at the subduction zone dragging the surface part of the plate across the surface At constructive margins , the new plate material sliding off the higher oceanic ridges .

searchText: ﻿ Metamorphic rocks are either igneous or sedimentary rocks that are changing. The word ‘metamorphic’ comes from the Greek words meta, meaning ‘after’, and morphe, meaning ‘change’, so it literally means ‘after change’. Metamorphic rock is rock that is changing its form. Sedimentary and igneous rock subjected to higher pressures and intense heat will start to change in density, crystal structure and other properties. This process of change takes millions of years and doesn’t stop. Gneiss is an example of metamorphic rock. Gneiss is formed from metamorphosed granites or sandy marine sediments. The rock cycle shows that this happens due to the heat and pressure of the surrounding rocks deep within the Earth. Metamorphic rocks are difficult to identify. They have properties of the original rock they are changing from, but also have new properties due to the changes it has undergone. title: Modelling Seafloor Spreading
subject: Science
searchText:
Unit
Plate Tectonics

Title
5. Seafloor Spreading

Summary
Students take what they know about earthquake, volcano and mid-ocean ridge
distributions (The Big One and Plate Patterns) and put it together with what they
know about convection in the Earth’s mantle (Journey Through Earth and
Convection in a Pan). They revisit what they know about how earthquakes are
created, by the sudden release of energy as plates collide or rub together (but not
so much when they split apart). They look for patterns in their world maps,
observing that mid-ocean ridges and dense earthquake/volcano zones tend to lie on
the opposite side of plates. With this information, they can infer the direction that
the plates are moving. Next students build a model illustrating seafloor spreading
and discuss the magnetic and seafloor age data that support this model. Finally,
students codify the different types of plate boundaries, describing the various
features and characteristics of each.

Objectives
Can find patterns on a map and use that information to infer the direction of plate
motion.
Can diagram and explain what causes earthquakes and volcanoes.
Can build and interpret a physical model of seafloor spreading.
Can describe some of the evidence supporting seafloor spreading.
Can describe the characteristics of the 3 major classes of plate boundaries as well
as differences between subducting convergent boundaries and continent-continent
convergent boundaries.

Vocabulary
Mantle
Lithosphere
Crust
Earthquake
Volcano
Mid-ocean ridge
Tectonic plate
Oceanic plate
Continental plate
Seafloor spreading
Convergent boundary
Divergent boundary
Transform boundary
Subduction
Island arc

Time
30-50 min hypothesize plate motions
20-25 min build seafloor spreading models and discuss evidence
 A MyScienceBox Lesson Plan by Irene Salter (http://www.mysciencebox.org). This work is licensed
 under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial License. To view a copy of this license, visit
 http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/2.5/ or send a letter to Creative Commons, 559 Nathan
 Abbott Way, Stanford, California 94305, USA.
 30-35 min study models and describe types of plate boundaries

Grouping
Inferring the direction of plate motion will occur in groups of 2 or 3. Making models
of seafloor spreading takes place individually.

Materials
   Cardstock paper
   Copy of Seafloor Spreading Model Pieces on cardstock for each student
   Colored pencils
   Stapler
   Scissors
   Students’ color coded World Earthquake Maps from Plate Patterns lesson
   Large labeled world map from Plate Patterns lesson or a copy of the “This
     Dynamic Planet” poster from the USGS, $14 + $5 handling
     http://www.minerals.si.edu/tdpmap/order.htm
   Optional: Pictures, animations or other information showing seafloor
     spreading, magnetic survey maps of the ocean floor, or age maps of the
     ocean floor (see sources section for resources).

Setting
Classroom

Teacher Background
Seafloor spreading is one of the most critical pieces of evidence in the development
and support of the theory of plate tectonics. It is through this process that new
oceanic crust is formed along the mid-ocean ridges as oceanic plates diverge and
separate. Magma wells up into the gap, hardens, and forms new crust. As the plates
continue to separate, these newly formed pieces of oceanic crust separate and
make room, gradually moving outward away from the mid-ocean ridges at the rate
of a few centimeters per year.

After several million years of this slow journey away from the mid-ocean ridges, the
oceanic crust collides with a different tectonic plate in a process known as
subduction. If the oceanic crust meets continental crust, the denser oceanic crust is
forced under the continental crust. If the oceanic crust meets oceanic crust, then
one or the other will be forced below the other. In these subduction zones,
earthquakes are common due to the build up and sudden release of energy at the
junction. Also, as the oceanic crust dives down below the other plate into the
mantle, the old plate melts, forming a pool of magma that is forced back up through
the crust above as volcanoes on the continent or a chain of volcanic islands on one
side of the subduction zone.

In some instances, some continental crust is riding along on the oceanic plate and
collides into another piece of continental crust. This is currently taking place in the
Himalayas and was part of the process that created California (see the background
section of Making California for more details). At these continent-continent
convergent boundaries, the two sections of continental crust ram into one another,
causing the crust above to buckle and fold into tall mountain ranges (the Himalayas
and the Sierra Nevadas).

Modelling Tectonic Plate Movement
 Aim: To model the Earth’s tectonic plate movement.


Equipment:
                                                          Safety Information
• Safety goggles
                                                          Hot syrup – risk of burns, may
• Large 1l beaker                                         spit when boiling.
• 300ml treacle                                           Wear goggles at all times. If burnt,
                                                          put area under running cold water for 10
• Biscuit (halved)
                                                          minutes and inform teacher immediately.
• Tripod
                                                          Glassware – risk of cuts if broken.
• Gauze
                                                          Apply pressure to wounds and inform teacher
• Bunsen burner                                           immediately.
• Heat proof mat                                          Bunsen – risk of burns.

                                                          Tie back hair, handle with caution.

                                                          If burnt, put area under running cold water for
                                                          10 minutes and inform teacher immediately.


Method:
Step 1: Set up the apparatus as shown in the diagram

Step 2: Pour the treacle into the beaker

Step 3: Lay the two halves of the biscuit onto the treacle, with
a small gap between them

Step 4: Light your Bunsen burner on a safety flame (hole closed)

Step 5: Move the Bunsen burner underneath the tripod
(remember: to safely move a Bunsen burner while it is lit, hold
it where the rubber tubing connects to the base)

Step 6: Gently heat the treacle with a blue flame until it begins
to bubble

Step 7: Observe the biscuits carefully, do not let the treacle boil
too much

Step 8: Remove the heat to control the bubbling of the treacle




                                                  Page 1 of 2
                                                                           Modelling Tectonic Plate Movement



                   In 1912, meteorologist Alfred Wegener describe his theory of continental drift, and
                   the idea that the different continents would have fit together like a jigsaw puzzle.
                   He couldn’t explain how though, and it was about 50 years later that the theory
                   of plate tectonics arose.



Questions:
 1. What does the treacle represent in this demonstration?

 2. What do the biscuit halves represent in this demonstration?

 3. How does the heated treacle cause the biscuits to move?

 4. Use the model to describe how earthquakes occur.




                                               Page 2 of 2
                                                                           Modelling Tectonic Plate Movement

Answers:
 1. What does the treacle represent in this demonstration?
    The molten magma layer of the earth

 2. What do the biscuit halves represent in this demonstration?
    The tectonic plates which make up the earth’s crust

 3. How does the heated treacle cause the biscuits to move?
    As the treacle is heated from underneath, the particles gain more energy and begin to move faster
    and further apart, making the area of treacle less dense. The less dense area of treacle floats
    upwards and into the underside of the biscuits. As more treacle rises up the top layer of treacle is
    forced to move sideways and with it carries the biscuit. The heat is being transferred
    by convection.

 4. Use the model to describe how earthquakes occur?
    As the tectonic plates pass one another they rub at their boundary and cause friction. When the
    forces become unbalanced then the plates will jerk past one another, causing an earthquake.

title: Notes summary for Plate Techtonics
subject: Science
searchText: Continental Drift and Alfred Wegner In 1915, Alfred Wegner proposed his Theory of Continental Drift. He proposed that the continents were once all joined together in a ‘supercontinent’ he called Pangaea . Over 180 million years ago this supercontinent began to "break up" due to continental drift. His evidence for the new theorywas The continents could be fit together (like a jigsaw puzzle). Worldwide distribution of fossils from the same time period. Rock layers in mountain chains on one continent match up with the rock layers in mountain chains on another continent. Rocks and fossils in many places don’t match the present climate or conditions. During Wegner’s lifetime his theory was not widely believed. Wegner could not explain what would cause such huge sections of the earth to move so slowly and for so long. In addition, most people simply accepted that the world was stable – generally because they could not see any change in their lifetime. Plate Tectonics During the 20th Century, further evidence arose supporting Wegner’s theory. The use of sonar in WWII led to the discovery of underwater trenches and volcanic seams under oceans The magnetic record of the ocean floor is a mirror image on either side of seams. Satellites have been used to measure the spreading of the ocean floor. This new evidence lead scientists developed the theory of Plate Tectonics. The theory suggested that the crust of the Earth is split up into seven large plates (see map below) and a few smaller ones, all of which are able to slowly move (less than 2.5 cm per year) around on the Earth's surface. They float on the semi-molten mantle rocks, and are moved around by convection currents within the very hot rock. 704491 879475 0 0 There are two types of tectonic plates - continental plates and oceanic plates. Continental plates contain continents and are lighter (less dense) than oceanic plates. Oceanic crust is much younger in geologic age than continental crust. Continental crust is on average thicker than oceanic crust. Why do plates move? The earth's tectonic plates are in constantly moving like giant 'rafts' on top of the semi-molten mantle below. However this movement is slow and rates vary from less than 2.5cm / yr to over 15cm/yr. The movement of the earth's crustal plates is believed to be due to convection currents which occur in the semi-molten mantle. These convection currents are created by heat from within the earth - much of which is generated by radioactive decay in the core. 3041650 -1530985 0 0 So how do convection currents cause plate movements? As semi-molten rock in the mantle is heated it becomes less dense than its surroundings and rises. As it reaches the crust above, it spreads out carrying the plates above with it. As the semi-molten rock then cools, it gradually sinks back down to be re-heated. (see diagram above) Plate Boundaries The point where two or more plates meet is known as a plate boundary. It is at these locations where earthquakes, volcanoes and fold mountain form. There are Three main types of plate boundary. These are Divergent, Convergent, and transform plate boundaries . . Plate Boundary Diagram Description Landforms Example Divergent plate boundaries Constructive plate boundaries occur when two plates move away from each other. Ocean ridge and volcanic islands North American and Eurasian Plate Convergent Subduction plate boundaries Oceanic vs Continental plates Destructive plate boundaries occur when an oceanic plate is forced under (or subducts) a continental plate. Fold Mountains and Oceanic trenches Pacific Plate and the Eurasian Plate Convergent Collision plate boundaries Continental vs ContinentalPlates Collision plate boundaries occur when two continental plates move towards each other . Fold Mountains Indo-Australian and the Eurasian Plate Transform plate boundaries Conservative plate boundaries occur when two plates slide past each other. Fault and slip lines North American Plate and the Pacific Plate Hotspots You should be aware that whilst most volcanoes / earthquakes occur along plate boundaries, there are exceptions. For example the volcanic Hawaiian islands which can be found in the middle of the Pacific Plate are formed due to a Hotspot. Hotspots are plumes of molten rock which rise underneath a thin or weak area in a plate causing localised melting and the creation of magma resulting in volcanic activity.

title: Plate Tectonics
subject: Science
searchText: Plate Tectonics Label the layers of the earth below: Plate tectonics is a geological theory that says the surface of Earth is broken into large plates. The size and position of the plates changes over time. The plates move in three ways: Convergence occurs when the plates move together and collide. This causes mountains to develop. Divergence occurs when the plates move away from each other. At that time, molten rock rises and cools and adds new material to the edge of the ocean crusts (ocean floor). Transform faults occur in the horizontal movement of plates against each other. This causes earthquakes. Now you are to make a simulation of plate tectonics. Follow the directions below to make a box that looks like the one below. Cut a long very thin strip in the top and cut holes in both sides of the box. Step 1. Take two sheets of blue paper to represent the oceanic plate. On both sheets place a triangular tube to represent the plate with an oceanic and continental crust. (Brown cardboard works well.) Put the unattached sides of the papers through the slit so that only about half of the paper is showing. When the paper is pulled down, this represents the convergence of the plates. When the paper is pushed up, this represents the divergence of the plates. Step 2. Move only the sheet with the cardboard attached so that the cardboard comes to the edge of the slit. This represents the ocean plate disappearing beneath the edge of the continent. This is called subduction . Step 3. On the plain sheet of blue paper, attach another triangle so that this also has a continental and an oceanic crust. Now pull both sheets of blue paper from the bottom. If you do this carefully, one of the triangles will go on top of the other showing the development of mountains when convergence occurs. Step 4. If the layers are moved toward the sides of the box, the students can see the action of fault lines moving in an earthquake. This is called a transform fault. Go to RLINK http://www.ucmp.berkeley.edu/geology/tectonics.html and see an animation of the plates moving into the position they currently hold. Write a paragraph to explain what you discovered when you followed the steps listed above. Be sure to use the correct terminology. Also make a diagram showing one of the steps and what happened when you did what you were asked to do. Draw diagram

Pompeii?

Where is Pompeii? It is in the Bay of Naples in Italy. Italy is in Europe.
Highlight number 18 on the map below. This is Italy.




Draw a big cross on the city of Naples. The area of coastline to the East of
   it is the Bay of Naples.
    On this map highlight Vesuvius and Pompeii.




The city of Pompeii was (is) in the Bay of Naples, part of the Mediterranean Sea. It
   was first inhabited about 2800 years ago(700BC). The place was very good for
   people to settle. The nearby sea provided an abundant harvest of fish. The soil
   of the area was rich and dark, producing good crops, especially when coupled
   with the warm climate. A river, the Sarno, provided plenty of fresh water for
   drinking. Much of the city's wealth could be traced to the rich soil of the area, so
   fertile that three crops of grain could be grown in a single year. Rows of vines
   supplied the grapes for the area's noted wine production. On the lower slopes of
   Vesuvius, groves of olive trees produced tons of olives for food and oil. Lush
   fields outside the city supported large flocks of sheep and a thriving wool
   industry.

      1.   Why would the soil have been so good?



   Pompeii grew up to be a very important town. It was a wealthy city with all the
   features of a successful Roman population. It had public baths, a theatre and
   bustling market.

IN the days before Vesuvius erupted the people living nearby had noticed some
    changes. Streams and wells had suddenly dried up, particularly those near Mt
    Vesuvius. Out in the Bay of Naples, the sea had mysteriously begun to boil in
    some places. Here and there even the ground had begun to rumble and quiver.
    Many animals—dogs, cats, mice and rats—had begun abandoning the city of
    Pompeii.

      2.   Why do you think the wells were drying up?



      3.   Why was the sea boiling in places?

                                      The Eruption
 In August of A.D. 79, the earthquake activity intensified. Then, on Aug. 24 the
world ended for Pompeii.

About noon that day, as thousands of Pompeians went about their daily activities
of farming, fishing, buying, selling, eating and drinking, they were startled and
shaken by a deafening roar.

The top of towering and vast Mt. Vesuvius vanished in a huge explosion. Dust,
red-hot coria, ash and flames were blasted kilometres into the sky.

A blanket of choking, gritty ash quickly began to cover the city. Panicked
Pompeians hurried to find family members and flee, seeking safety outside the
city. Others, terrified by the rain of burning ash, hurried inside, bolting doors and
shutters behind them.

Eventually dusk fell. By that time a metre of ash covered everything. Some
people lit torches and struggled through the ash, hoping to find safety at the port
or via the roads leading out of the city.

As night came, roofs began to collapse from the weight of the ash. Some,
realizing they would suffocate or be buried alive by the growing ashfall,
clambered out second-floor windows, gasping for breath in the ash-choked air.
Others in their desperation chopped holes through the roofs and walls of their
houses to escape. A few remained behind seeking shelter wherever they could.

At one residence, a dog chained in the yard climbed higher and higher as the
level of ash continued to rise. Finally, as his chain ran out and he could climb no
higher, the dog suffocated as the ash covered his nose and mouth.

Throughout the night the rain of ash continued to fall. Three times during the
night, avalanches of rocks, hot ash and poisonous gas surged down the mountain
but fell short of enveloping Pompeii. Even so, by the time the sky lightened
somewhat at dawn, seven feet of ash covered much of Pompeii.

Early that morning three more superheated avalanches, accompanied by a rain
of tons of very fine ash, swallowed the city. These scorching blasts, with their
poisonous gases and fumes, killed everyone that remained. There it would lay,
20 feet underground—a first-century city frozen in time until its chance discovery
and identification nearly 17 centuries later. It is the fact that the city was
preserved under the ash that we are able to find out so much about everyday life
in Pompeii.

Because so much of Pompeii was preserved under the ash are many
  things we can learn about life in Roman times from the ruins of Pompeii

searchText: ACTIVITY 24 NAME_____________________ 1. The Rock Cycle Read the information in the textbox below to get some background knowledge about how rocks just keep on changing. The rock cycle describes the geological processes that form rocks. Igneous rocks can change into sedimentary rock or into metamorphic rock. Sedimentary rock can change into metamorphic rock or into igneous rock. Metamorphic rock can change into igneous rock or sedimentary rock. • Let’s start with magma. • When magma cools it forms igneous rock. • On the Earth’s surface, wind and water can break the igneous rock into pieces. This process is called weathering and erosion. These pieces are called sediments. • The sediments can be compacted to make a layer. The layer can be buried under other layers of sediments. After a long time the sediments can be cemented together to make sedimentary rock. • Sedimentary rock can be weathered away to form sediments again. • When sedimentary and igneous rocks are heated they change into metamorphic rock. • Metamorphic rock can also be weathered away to make sediment. • Metamorphic, igneous and sedimentary rock can also be melted back into magma. • The rock cycle never stops. 2. Refer to the ‘Rock Cycle Flowchart’ attached to this sheet. • Working in pairs, carefully cut out the cards. • Next, organise the cards to represent the rock cycle. Keep rechecking the information box and talk about your decisions with your partner. • When you have checked with your teacher, paste them down on a coloured A4 sheet of paper or in your workbook. • Include the heading ‘Rock Cycle Flowchart’ on your A4 sheet or workbook. Adapted from ‘Science Rocks’ by Kathleen Gordon, p. 7-8, 14, 28. (Queensland Resources Council and the Department of Natural Resources and Mines. Minerals Education Victoria Tel: (03) 8614 1851 Fax: (03) 9629 8603 VELS Unit – Treasures from the Earth September 2007 ACTIVITY 24 NAME__________________ Rock Cycle Cards Adapted from “Science Rocks” by Kathleen Gordon, p 7-8, 14, 28 (Queensland Resources Council and the Department of Natural Resources and Mines) Minerals Education Victoria Tel: (03) 8614 1851 Fax: (03) 9629 8603 VELS Unit – Treasures from the Earth September 2007 ACTIVITY 24 Background notes for teachers The Rock Cycle The geological process that forms rocks is cyclical. Each type of sedimentary, igneous or metamorphic rock can be changed into each other type of rock. This is known as the rock cycle. The following explanation starts with igneous rocks. Igneous rocks start as magma. When magma - molten rock under the Earth’s surface – and lava – molten rock on the Earth’s surface – cools and hardens, it forms igneous rock. The igneous rock is broken down over time through the weathering process. These particles of broken rock, or soil, are washed away by water and accumulate in lakes or oceans and harden into rock again – this time as sedimentary rock. As the sedimentary rock is buried under more and more sediments, or comes into contact with magma, the pressure and heat can cause metamorphism to occur. This transforms the sedimentary rock into a metamorphic rock. If metamorphic rock is buried more deeply, temperatures and pressures continue to rise. If the temperature becomes hot enough the metamorphic rock melts and forms the molten rock called magma and so the cycle continues. Adapted from “Science Rocks” by Kathleen Gordon, p 7-8, 14, 28 (Queensland Resources Council and the Department of Natural Resources and Mines) Minerals Education Victoria Tel: (03) 8614 1851 Fax: (03) 9629 8603 VELS Unit – Treasures from the Earth September 2007 ACTIVITY 24 Background notes for teachers Our amazing Earth The Earth The crust of the Earth is made up of rocks and minerals from the tallest mountains to the floor of the deepest ocean. It makes up less than 1% of the Earth’s mass. The continental crust is up to 50km thick while the oceanic crust is, at most, 15 km thick. Most of the rocky crust is covered by either water, sand, soil or ice. The soil is a mixture of small, inorganic particles and organic material (plant and animal remains), which supports the growth of plants such as grass and trees. Most of the crust is made from only eight elements – oxygen, magnesium, aluminium, silicon, calcium, sodium, potassium and iron. These elements along with others are combined to from thousands of rocks and minerals that are very different. The mantle is the solid casing of the Earth and is about 2900km thick making up almost 70% of the Earth’s mass. It consists of silicon, oxygen, aluminium and iron. The core is mainly made up of iron and nickel and makes up about 30% of the Earth’s mass. The liquid outer core is approximately 2200km thick. The solid inner core is about 1220 km thick. Rocks A rock is made up of minerals that have been cemented together, squeezed and heated, or melted and cooled. Rocks are divided into three main groups: • igneous • sedimentary • metamorphic They are classified into these groups because of the way they were formed. Igneous rocks are formed from melted rock that has cooled and solidified. When rocks are buried deep within the Earth, they melt because of the high pressure and temperature. If this molten rock (called magma) cools slowly, usually at depths of thousands of metres, coarse-grained rocks form with large crystals ( for example, granite and gabbro). If the magma cools quickly, usually on the surface after a volcano erupts, the crystals are very small and fine-grained rocks are formed (for example, basalt, rhyolite and obsidian). Some examples of other igneous rocks are: pumice, tuff and andesite. Sedimentary rocks are formed from the cementing together of small pieces of rocks or shells. They are formed at the surface of the Earth, either in water or on land. They are usually made up of many layers of sediments, which include fragments of rocks, minerals and animal or plant material. Sandstone, limestone, shale, gypsum, conglomerate, coal, chert and flint are all sedimentary rocks. Sometimes igneous and sedimentary rocks are subjected to pressures so intense or heat so high they change. They become metamorphic rocks, which form while buried within the Earth’s crust. The process of metamorphism does not melt the rocks, but changes them into denser, more compact rocks. Slate, marble and gneiss are metamorphic rocks. They are transformed from shale, limestone and granite respectively. shale ⇒ slate limestone ⇒ marble granite ⇒ gneiss Adapted from “Science Rocks” by Kathleen Gordon, p 7-8, 14, 28 (Queensland Resources Council and the Department of Natural Resources and Mines) Minerals Education Victoria Tel: (03) 8614 1851 Fax: (03) 9629 8603 VELS Unit – Treasures from the Earth Mar 2007

searchText: Name ______________________ Hour ______ Date ____________ Rock Worksheet Directions: Read the information below carefully and answer the questions that follow on the back side of this paper. Answer the questions as completely as possible. Rocks and Minerals The ground we walk on, build on, and grow gardens on is made of rock. All the rocks in the world are made up of chemicals called minerals. Minerals are solid, inorganic (not living) substances found in and on the earth. Most are chemical compounds, which means that they are made of two or more elements. For example, the mineral sapphire is made up of aluminum and oxygen. A few minerals such as gold, silver and copper are made of a single element. Minerals are considered to be the building blocks of rocks. Rocks can be a combination of as many as six types of minerals. Through a microscope, a rock shows that it is made of crystals of different minerals, all growing together like a puzzle. Three types of rocks make up the Earth’s crust. Rocks are formed in three different ways to produce igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary rocks. Igneous rocks form when molten magma cools and solidifies. Metamorphic rocks form when a rock is chemically changed by heat or pressure to form a new rock type. Sedimentary rocks form when fragments of rocks and other debris are cemented together. Igneous Rocks When a candle burns, a runny wax is formed that trickles down its side and solidifies. Igneous rocks are formed in a similar way. The rocks solidify from a mass of molten rock, such as when a lava flow cools and hardens. Because of the heat needed to form igneous rocks, they are sometimes called “rocks of fire.” There are two main types of igneous rock: extrusive and intrusive. Extrusive types form when molten rock comes to the surface and cools quickly, as with lava. This produces a very fine-grained rock. Intrusive rocks are those that solidified underground, cooling slowly to produce coarse-grained rocks. Examples: Granite, basalt, obsidian. Sedimentary Rocks Sedimentary rocks are formed when sediment (bits of rock plus materials such as shells and sand) get packed together. They can take millions of years to form. You never know what you might find in a sedimentary rock since many rocks of this type are made up of lots of other rocks, or even animal remains, all stuck together. Sedimentary rocks are built up of particles laid down as layers or beds of sediment and are later buried , compressed, and cemented into a solid mass. Most rocks that you see on the ground are sedimentary. Examples: Sandstone, shale, limestone. Metamorphic Rocks Metamorphic rocks are igneous or sedimentary rocks that have been transformed by heat, pressure, or both. Metamorphic rocks are usually formed deep within the Earth, during a process such as mountain building. When you bake bread, you mix flour, yeast, and water together and bake in a hot oven. In a similar way, heat and pressure from the overlying rocks, may change the nature of the rocks below. This process is called metamorphosis, which means “change.” Examples: Schist, slate, marble. Did You Know? Most of the ocean floor is made of basalt. This igneous rock continues to flow from the Earth through an underwater mountain ranges known as “mid-ocean ridges”? Questions - Please write your answers in complete sentences! 1. What is the difference between rocks and minerals? 2. How many types of rocks make up the Earth’s crust? 3. What are the names of the 3 types of rocks? 4. How are igneous rocks formed? 5. What is another name for igneous rocks? 6. What is the difference between to two types of igneous rocks? 7. How are sedimentary rocks made? 8. How are metamorphic rocks made? 9. What does the word “metamorphosis” mean? 10. Which two layers of the Earth are made of rock? 11. What are the names of the other two layers of the Earth, and what are they made of? 12. People mined minerals from the ground to use as they were found, particularly gemstones, and later mined ores to extract metals such as Gold, Copper or Iron. In fact ages of human civilisation have been named after the mineral ores used — the Bronze Age and the Iron Age for example. A mineral is a naturally occurring solid that has a regular crystal structure and chemical make-up. Some minerals are made up of only one kind of atom. These minerals are called ‘native’ minerals and include gold and silver. Other minerals are made up of several or many different types of atoms. The mineral quartz (SiO,) is made up of molecules consisting of one atom of silicon (Si) and two atoms of oxygen (O). Quartz forms regular 18-sided crystals. Quartz is the most common mineral in the Earth’s crust. Gypsum Calcite Quartz There are over 3000 different minerals and many of these are common in rocks, however there are only about eight very common rock-forming minerals. Examples of common rock forming minerals include quartz, feldspar, mica, olivine and calcite. Some rocks are made up of several minerals (e.g. Granite) and some rocks are made of only one mineral (e.g. limestone). The appearance of rocks depends mainly on the type of minerals that make it up and the way the rock has been formed. Some rocks are made up of other broken down rocks that have been ‘cemented’ together and some are formed from interlocking crystals. The size of the mineral crystals or grains in rocks varies from very large (crystals about 5mm in granite) to microscopic (as in shale) making them very hard to see and identify. Mineral crystals are easiest to identify in rocks formed from slowly cooling molten rock deep under ground. searchText: Name: Date: Period: Modeling sea floor spreading Summary In this activity students will use actual data from historic oceanographic cruises to examine sea floor spreading. They will also model sea floor spreading at a spreading center such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Learning Objectives At the completion of this activity you should be able to : • Plot data on a diagram. • Draw conclusions from the data. • Make predictions about future events related to this data. Materials • Student Handout • Posterboard / cardstock • Paper • Scissors Background Using actual data from the Glomar Challenger cruises will allow you to see a real-world connection between classroom science and “real” science. Also, creating a model for sea flo or spreading will allow you to see a hands-on example of this phenomenon. Procedure Part 1 To create a working model of sea floor spreading, follow the model seen below (Figure 1) . The base is best if made from poster board or card stock. The width and length of the base are not critical, as long as they are at least 12 cm wide and 30 cm long. Cut 3 slits, each slightly more than 8 cm wide. One slit needs to be in the center, and the other two at either end of the base, at least 4 cm in from the ends. Label the slits A and B at either end. Cut out the plate strips and place them back to back (marked sides together with number 1 at the top) and tape the end as indicated (at the end nearest number 7. ) Shade alternating strips to represent the reversals of the earth’s magnetic field. Be sure that the shading on either side of the strip match the alternate side. Put the two strips up through the bottom slit and then off to the slits at either end of the base. (Figure 2.) Thread the two strips through the center slit of the base, keeping the taped edge at the bottom. Pull the “North American Plate” strip down through slit “A” and the “Eurasian Plate” strip through slit “B”. Push the strips up from below until you can see numbers 3, 4, and 5 on top of the base. searchText: ﻿ The formation of sedimentary rocks varies so there are a variety of sedimentary rocks. All of these rocks require a very long time for the processes of weathering, erosion, deposition, compaction and cementation to occur. These processes can take millions of years. Three types of sedimentary rocks are formed when weathered rock particles, organisms die or precipitated particles are compacted and cemented together. These three types of rocks are referred to as clastic sedimentary rock, organic sedimentary rock and chemical sedimentary rock, respectively. Clastic sedimentary rocks consist of smaller rocks cemented together. Examples include conglomerate and brecchia. Organic sedimentary rock is formed when organisms die and layers form that are eventually covered by clastic sedimentary rock and compressed. Examples include coal and limestone. Chemical sedimentary rocks form as a result of a chemical reaction that produces a precipitation. Banded iron formations (BIF) are chemical sedimentary rocks that contain iron oxide layers and are usually composed of the minerals magnetite and hematite. title: Structure of the Earth
subject: Science
searchText: ﻿GEOLOGY The Structure of the Earth a) Inside the Earth Scientists think that the Earth is composed of layers. The outermost layer is like a thin skin and it is called the crust. The crust is solid and it is composed of rocks and minerals. The crust is not an even layer; it is thickest where there are mountains ranges (and in general under the continents) and thinnest beneath the deep oceans. The average thickness of the crust is about 30 km; the distance to the centre of the Earth is about 6500 km. That is, the crust is very thin compared to the distance to the centre of the Earth. The temperature in the crust ranges from about 200C (at the surface) to about 5000C (at the bottom of the crust). That is, the deeper you go into the crust (and the Earth) the hotter is becomes. Beneath the crust is a much thicker layer called the mantle. The mantle is about 2900 km thick and the temperatures range from about 5000C to 20000C. These high temperatures are enough to melt rock, and so the mantle is made up of partially solid, partially liquid (molten) rock. Sometimes molten rock spills out onto the crust as lava. At the centre is the core which contains two main layers. The outer core is believe to be made of molten iron and nickel. It has a thickness of about 2270 km and a temperature of about 30000C. The inner core is thought to be made of solid iron and nickel. It has a radius of about 1300 km and a temperature of about 4000oC. b) Plate tectonics The theory of plate tectonics proposes that the outermost part of the earth, the crust, is divided into a number of rigid plates which move in relation to each other. There are six or seven major plates and a number of smaller ones. Both continents and ocean floors form the upper part of these plates. The Australian continent is on the Indian-Australian plate. The tectonic plates are thought to be floating on the upper potion of the mantle and their movement is thought to be due to convection currents (movement of the hot mantle material) caused by the tremendous heat within the earth. The boundaries of these plates were determined by mapping the positions of earthquake epicentres because earthquakes tend to occur where plates meet or move apart. Since the plates are moving with respect to each other, the edges or margins of the plates will be geologically unstable: i) where two plates are forced together i.e. they are colliding, one plate is often forced under the other. The plate that is forced underneath moves back into the mantle. Collision zones of plates, called subduction zones, are often associated with earthquakes, volcanoes, ocean trenches and fold mountains. This type of plate movement i.e. plate collision, is thought to have caused the formation of the Himalayas, in Asia, and the Andes mountains in South America. The ring of volcanoes around the Pacific ocean also is thought to be due to the Pacific plate is being pushed under other plates. ii) where plates are moving apart, new material from the mantle rises up to form new crust. Mid-ocean ridges (mountains), volcanoes and earthquakes are often associated with these areas. Two plates moving apart are thought to have caused the formation of the mid-Atlantic ridge, a mountain range under the Atlantic ocean. iii) where plates move past one another, faults, or breaks, occur in the rocks. This is called lateral movement of plates. Active volcanoes are absent in these areas, but severe earthquakes can occur as the two plates move in "jerky" movements past one another. This type of plate movement occurs along the western coast of North America, and it forms the San Andreas fault. As the plates move over the surface of the Earth, they carry the continents with them. It is thought that the continents were originally one land mass and over the billions of years they have slowly moved apart (and they are still moving!). c) Volcanoes Sometimes, due to pressure in the mantle layer, magma (molten rock) is forced through a weak part in the Earth's crust. When this happens, a volcano forms. The fluid magma which flows out of a volcano, over the surface, is called lava. "New" rock is formed when molten lava cools. Smoke, steam, ash and other gases also pour out of a volcano during an eruption. d) Mountain building The layers of rocks that make up the Earth’s crust are being continually pushed, twisted, split and folded by Earth movements. Mountains are often formed because of these tremendous forces exerted within and on the Earth’s crust: Folding of the crust can occur because of these forces. For example when two plates collide, fold mountains often form at the edge (or edges) of the plate. Most of the Earth’s mountain ranges have been formed this way. Another way in which rock layers may react to huge forces is by splitting or faulting. When a crack or a break forms in a layer of rocks, the rock on one side of the crack can move up, down or sideways, relative to the rock on the other side of the crack. This may result in one part of the Earth’s crust being higher compared to an adjacent part. Igneous Rocks Rocks which at one time were molten i.e. magma, are called igneous rocks. These rocks are composed of interlocking crystals. (Crystals are solids with a definite shape and straight, sharp edges) Igneous rocks can form from magma in two ways: i) when magma reaches the earth's surface, it becomes lava. Lava cools relatively quickly and produces igneous rock made up of small crystals. An example of rock formed this way is basalt. Basalt is normally a dark-coloured, hard rock. ii) at times, magma cools and solidifies below the Earth's surface . When this occurs, cooling is very slow, and the rock formed is composed of large crystals. An example of rock formed this way is granite. The magma which forms granite is too thick to be forced through weaknesses in the earth's crust, and it forms great domes underneath the surface. In time, the surrounding softer rocks are eroded, leaving the rounded domes of granite. Granite is a multicoloured rock composed of quite large interlocking crystals. Sedimentary Rocks a) Weathering Weathering is the process by which rocks are broken down into smaller pieces or changed to other substances when exposed to the atmosphere. This process is caused by contact of the exposed outermost parts of the rock with water, air and living things. Two types of weathering occur: i) Physical Weathering - this results in rock being broken down into smaller pieces (the composition of the rock is not changed). - physical weathering can be due to - temperature changes - action of frost or ice - abrasion by moving particles - action of plants and animals ii) Chemical Weathering - this results in the rocks being changed into different substances. - chemical weathering occurs when air and water come in contact with rock and a chemical reaction with the rock occurs - some of the chemicals in the environment that cause chemical weathering are: - carbonic acid, which is formed when carbon dioxide dissolves in water - humic acid, which is a weak acid formed from decaying plants in the soil. - oxygen and water b) Erosion Erosion is the process of removal of the weathered rock particles from the bedrock locality i.e. from the place where they were formed from the parent rock. The main agents of erosion are: i) water - moving water in the rivers, steams and in the ocean can transport rock particles from one place to another. The faster the movement of water, the larger the rock particles that can be moved. - water running over and through soil and rocks also causes erosion of small rock particles and soluble substances. ii) ice - a glacier is a very large river of ice and as it flows downhill it carves out a large valley by breaking off pieces of rock and carry them with it. iii) wind - the ability of wind to carry particles is less than that of water. However, wind can move much faster that water , and so can still carry quite large sand/rock particles. c) The formation of sedimentary rocks. The weathered materials carried by water, ice or wind in the process of erosion, will finally be "dropped" or deposited somewhere. This process is called deposition or sedimentation. The weathered material which is deposited during erosion is called sediment. Over time, different layers of sediment often form on top of one another. Layers of sediment can also be formed when a mixture of rocks and sand are deposited at the one time from the flowing water. The heaviest material will settle quickest i.e. it will form the bottom layer, then the next heaviest will settle etc. Thus layers, with the heaviest material at the bottom to the lightest as the top layer, will be formed. As sediment builds up, layer upon layer, it can be very slowly converted into rock, called a sedimentary rock. The process of forming many sedimentary rocks involves first compaction (pushing the particles in the sediment close together), and then secondly, the cementing of the particles together by chemicals. That is, in a sediment, the particles are just mixed together, but in a sedimentary rock, the particles are "cemented" together to form a solid piece of material. Some sedimentary rocks are formed from solids which have precipitated out of solution (salt), and other from remains of plants and animals that have been cemented together (limestone). Sometimes plants or animals e.g. shells, form part of a sediment. These dead plants and animals then become part of the sedimentary rock which forms. The remains or imprints of these plants and animals in the rock are referred to as fossils. d) Characteristics of sedimentary rocks i) Most sedimentary rocks have a layered structure. In a series of layered rock, normally the oldest (first deposited) rock is at the bottom, and the youngest (last to be deposited) is at the top. ii) Some sedimentary rocks show the remains of animals and plants trapped in the rock i.e. they contain fossils. iii) Many sedimentary rocks contain grains cemented together. iv) Sedimentary rocks are often much softer than igneous or metamorphic rocks. e) Some common sedimentary rocks Conglomerate - composed of large rounded pebbles (> 2mm in diameter) cemented together. Sandstone - composed of medium sized sand grains (< 2mm and visible to naked eye) Mudstone - composed of a mixture of silt and clay sized particles , cemented together Limestone - composed of calcium carbonate and is normally pale in colour - can be made of shell, coral or bone fragments cemented together - can be formed by the precipitation of calcium carbonate from aqueous solution Coal - black or brown solid composed mainly of carbon - formed from plant material that has been compressed under layers of sediment. Metamorphic Rocks When solid rock is subjected to heat and pressure in the earth's crust, it can change into a different rock. This new rock is called a metamorphic rock. Metamorphic rocks are often formed from rock which is formed or buried deep in the Earth's crust where there would be high temperatures and pressures. They are also formed in the crust in volcanic areas because the magma heats the surrounding rocks to sufficiently high temperatures to change them into metamorphic rocks. Metamorphic rocks are normally much harder than sedimentary rocks and they sometimes have visible grains. Examples of metamorphic rocks include: - marble - often white, has visible grains and is formed from limestone. - quartzite - very hard, has visible grains and is formed from sandstone. - gneiss - has visible grains and normally contains dark bands. It is formed from shale, which must first be changed into other metamorphic rocks before gneiss is finally formed. Marble and quartzite are normally formed in areas where the heat is supplied by volcanoes. However, gneiss is formed deep in the crust where high pressure and temperature conditions exist. title: Teacher sheet lesson one
subject: Science
searchText: Teacher sheet lesson one Introduction This unit will be organised around an edStudio presentation that will contain the majority of the student resources. All of the investigations will be listed in the find and prepare sections of the lesson plans. Each page of the edStudio will be a new lesson and the students can individually work through the activities and submit their produced work electronically back onto the pages via the digital drop boxes. The edStudio presented in this unit will need to be personalised for each individual class. You will need to make a copy of the edStudio and then alter the permissions and/or modify the content to suit specific classes. It is possible to teach the lessons without the edStudio. If you do not wish to use it, a full list of the resources used has been included in the lesson plans. Student instructions for activities, that appear as pop-up boxes in the studio, are included on each teacher sheet as student information. Introduction — The structure of the Earth (website) Student information: Welcome to the unit. Today we will be looking at a slideshow that revises what you learned about rocks in Year 8 and introduces the structure of the Earth. You will then be working in groups to build up a model of the Earth. Please follow the instructions on this page to work your way through lesson one. First watch the slideshow Structure of the Earth (http://media2. teachertube.com/files/articles/3933.ppt#256,1,Unit 17 STRUCTURE OF THE EARTH) Afterwards, your teacher will lead a discussion on what you have viewed. Task 1 — Introductory reading Student information: Open the website Structure of the Earth (http://scign.jpl.nasa.gov/learn/plate1.htm) and read the information about the layers of the Earth. Do not navigate away from this page. When you have finished reading, create a page of notes of the relevant summary points, then create a labelled scale drawing of the four layers of the Earth. You may complete this task in your science journal or you may create an electronic document and save it in a new folder for this unit. Teacher information: The Structure of the Earth website contains a few interconnecting pages. Ensure the students only summarise the information on the page that opens from the link. 1 of 5 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson1 Task 2 — Make a model of the Earth Student information: Now you have read about the structure of the Earth you will construct a model. Collect your materials then follow the supplied instructions. Make a recording of your group building the model and submit it to your teacher. If you are unsure of how to record, read through the section ‘How to prepare a presentation’ below. Once you have finished, view another group’s recordings and models. Teacher information: Student instructions are provided at the end of this document. For this activity the students will need the handouts ‘Make a model of the Earth’ and ‘How to prepare a presentation’. Task 3 — From clay balls to the centre of the Earth Student information: In task two you constructed a model of the Earth from a description based on accepted scientific theory. How do we know what the Earth is composed of if we can never see all the layers? Use the activity From clay balls to the structure of the Earth to gain some ideas about how scientists are using experiments to discover what the inside of the Earth is made of. Teacher information: Refer to the website From clay balls to the structure of the Earth (http://geophysics.esci. keele.ac.uk/earthlearningidea/PDF/74_Clay_balls.pdf). A student activity sheet of the same title is included at the end of this document. You will need to personalise this activity to suit your class. Culminating activity — Discussion questions Student information: Think about the two activities that you have completed and then read through the discussion questions below and write your answers in your science journal. Consider other students’ answers and reflect on whether you agree or disagree. Discussion questions: 1. What did you predict the centre of the two plasticine balls was composed of? 2. Do you need to cut open the balls to make this prediction? 3. Would you need to open the balls in order to draw a definitive conclusion? 4. What is the difference between a prediction and a conclusion? 5. Have scientists made predictions about the Earth’s composition or drawn conclusions? 6. Will scientists ever be able to draw conclusions about the composition of the Earth? It is important for this resource that misconceptions are not created by the students engaging with the activity. Explain to the students that the activities they complete on the clay balls are not mini-experiments that mirror current scientific investigation. They are, however, investigating that it is possible to form hypotheses based on experimental evidence, which is how scientists are currently developing a concept of the structure of the Earth. 2 of 5 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson1 Make a model of the Earth Materials: • Four colours of modelling clay • Plastic knife • Piece of paper for labels • Metric ruler • Four toothpicks Method: 1. You first need to be in groups of two or three and then collect your materials from the front of the room. Remember to organise the recording of your activity now. 2. Each group will be making one labelled model of a slice of the Earth. Use toothpicks and paper to make the labels. Below is an image of a finished product. Schoch, Catherine © The State of Queensland 3. This will be a scale model so the group will need to work out how thick each layer should be. You will be making a 1 cm:1000 km model. Look up the thickness of each layer in your notes from task one. You will need to include the inner core, outer core, mantle and continental crust as four separate layers (the oceanic crust will be impossibly thin on this model so use the continental crust thickness). Remember to record yourselves working out this information. 4. Once you have worked out the measurements for your model you may commence building it. Use a different colour of plasticine for each layer. You need to be careful that each layer is the correct thickness. One member of your team needs to narrate your procedure while you record building your model. 5. Once the model is completed you may make some little flags from toothpicks and paper. Label each layer with its name, size and composition. Don’t forget to keep recording. 6. Now hold up your model for the camera and give a short presentation on your finished model, including how and why you made construction decisions. 7. Your group is now finished this activity. Upload your recording to a computer and make some final editing adjustments before you submit the final presentation. 3 of 5 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson1 How to prepare a presentation You will be completing several experiments during the course of your study this year. As part of these lessons you will be required to record your participation in and reflection on each one. We will be recording in an electronic format and keeping digital copies of these records. So, how do I do that? Good question. You will be provided with some form of recording equipment at the beginning of the lesson. This may consist of a camera, a video recorder or a digital voice recorder. You will use these items to make a recording of the experiment as your group is completing the activity. Remember, you cannot go back and record an experiment once your group has completed it. Things to consider Your presentation on your experiment will still need to have the elements of a normal experiment ‘write up’. So you will need to state in your presentation the following elements: • The aim of the experiment — what is your group trying to discover? • Your group’s initial hypothesis — what does your group think you are going to observe? • How your group is intending to investigate this hypothesis — this is an initial discussion of your method. • Images of your equipment during and after set up — name the equipment and say why it is the most suited to the task (e.g. because we are only using small measures of materials we will use test tubes instead of beakers). • A commentary of your experiment method including any safety considerations your group has recognised. • A commentary and any images of your observations — what did your group see during the experiment? • Your concluding statements, and a discussion of these questions: –– Why did you see your observations? –– Are they what you expected to see? –– Did you have observations that may have been caused by errors in your method? • Your group’s reflection on the experiment and an analysis of your level of success or failure: –– How did your group manage the experiment? –– How many errors did you think you made? –– How did your results compare with your hypothesis? In a written presentation you would normally write out descriptions of these points, but for an electronic presentation your group will need to speak about these aloud as the group is working through the experiment. It may be a good idea to nominate someone to act as the ‘presenter’ for the recording. They will be responsible for the main commentary and for asking questions of the other group members. Once the experiment is finished and cleaned away you can download your presentation and give it some finishing touches. If you are taking photos and recording your voices, then a slideshow may be the best option for your format. If you have a video recording, then some general editing and additional audio via a voice recorder may be a good idea. 4 of 5 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson1 From clay balls to the structure of the Earth You made a scale model of the Earth for task two. How do we know that these predictions about the Earth’s composition are true? The Earth is very large and no one has been able to drill all the way to the core. This is impossible. For task three you will be looking at how scientists have come to formulate predictions on the composition of the Earth’s layers. Follow the steps below and conduct some tests on two objects to see if you can predict what the objects are composed of. Step one: Form into groups of two or three. Collect your materials from the front of the room. What are the two objects? Do they look the same? Do you think they are the same? Explain your answer. What do you think the inside of the objects look like? Note: You are not to cut the objects open during this activity. Make a list of the tests you could carry out on the two balls and then wait for the teacher to lead you in a discussion of your classmates’ ideas. Now take your two balls and complete some of the tests on them. Make a record of your observations for each investigation. 5 of 5 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson1

title: Teacher sheet lesson seven
subject: Science
searchText: Teacher sheet lesson seven Introduction In the previous lesson you learned about formation of new crust at diverging plate boundaries. In this lesson you will examine destruction of old crust at converging plates. Task 1 — Convergent plate boundaries Student information: Go to the website Subduction zones (http://www.platetectonics.com/book/page_12.asp) and read about convergent plate boundaries. Open a new Word document, create a labelled diagram of a subduction zone and include events and landforms that occur in this zone. Save this in the folder for this unit. a) Why do volcanoes form at convergent plate boundaries? b) Why do some places seem to have lots of earthquakes? Task 2 — Subducting plate Student information: How do we know that one plate is sliding under another? Construct a model using the information provided in ‘Model instructions’. The model is based on data from earthquakes. Record your group’s activity and submit to your teacher. View another group’s recording. Teacher information: For more information about the subducting plate model, follow this link. http://www.geosociety.org/educate/LessonPlans/RealEvidence-SubductingPlate.pdf Reflection questions and instructions for this activity are included below. 1 of 3 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson7 Model instructions The model you will be making today draws on actual earthquake data to provide evidence for the existence of a subducting plate. Earthquakes occur deep inside the Earth and the depth and size of all earthquakes is continuously being recorded. Research the answers to the following questions to review your understanding of earthquakes. 1. What is an earthquake? 2. Where do earthquakes usually occur? 3. What is the difference between the epicentre and the focus of an earthquake? Form into groups of four. Follow the instructions below to construct a model that shows the shape of the Nazca plate subducting under the South American plate. Remember you will need to make a recording of the activity and save it in the folder for this unit. First you need to collect the following materials from the front of the room. • Box • Scissors • 22 balls (or beads) of three colours • Copy of the map (whichever your teacher has provided) • Copy of the earthquake data table • Glue • 22 paper clips • Masking tape • String • 2 rulers 1. Use the information in the table to plot the earthquakes on the map provided. 2. Lay the box on the side and glue the map onto the top-facing side of the box. The bottom of the map should face the open end of the box. 3. At each epicentre on the map punch a small hole. It only needs to be big enough for the string to fit through. 4. Each of the balls (beads) will represent the focus of the earthquake. Each focus was recorded at its particular depth and these depths are contained within the table. For each epicentre of the map, find its focus. You will then need to attach a ball to a length of string that matches the depth of the focus. Make sure that you use an appropriate scale or you will not see the pattern in your finished model. Start with the deepest earthquake so you know they will all fit. 5. Work through all 22 epicentres on the map and hang each ball at the depth of each focus. 6. When you are finished with your model, answer the following questions either in a Word document or verbally as part of your recorded presentation. 2 of 3 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson7 Questions 1. What information does an epicentre provide about an earthquake? 2. What is the difference between the focus and the epicentre of an earthquake? 3. What is happening to the rocks at the focus of an earthquake, and what do we call this? 4. What do you notice about the depth of the focus of the earthquakes as you go further inland from the coast of South America? 5. According to your model, what appears to be happening to the two plates that meet along the west coast of South America? 6. Draw and label a diagram of the model showing what is happening to the plates along the west coast of South America as described in question 5. 7. Describe the type of plate boundary that is present along the west coast of South America. 8. Explain how your data supports your conclusions in question 5. 9. How can your model explain the deep trench that lies off the coast of South America? 10. Use a map of the world that shows the plate boundaries to find some other areas where this same type of plate boundary is occurring. 11. How is volcanism related to this type of boundary? 3 of 3 Sci_Y09_U4_ACT_TeacherSheetLesson7
