searchText: ﻿ Naming Compounds - (Chemical Formulae) Prefixes Mono _____________ Di _____________ Tri ___________ Tetra _____________ Pent _____________ Hex ___________ 7: _____________ 8: _____________ 9: ___________ 10: _____________ Naming covalent compounds of two non-metal elements 1. Covalent compounds are combinations of two or more non-metal elements. They are not ionic. 2. These compounds consist of molecules (eg, H2O, CO2, CO, SO3) in which atoms are sharing electrons so that each one has a full valence shell. 3. Some covalent compounds have “common names” that do not follow any particular set of rules. These must be learned - for example: Compound Common name Compound Common name H2O water CHCl3 chloroform CH4 methane HCl hydrogen chloride NH3 ammonia HBr hydrogen bromide H2O2 hydrogen peroxide HF hydrogen fluoride 4. For most other covalent compounds there are a number of rules to follow for naming them. 5. Naming rules (nomenclature) 1) The name of the first element in the formula is the same as the element itself. (eg; CO2 is carbon dioxide) 2) The name of the second element in the formula has its ending changed to IDE (eg; CO2 is carbon dioxide) 3) If there are more than one of the first element’s atoms, the prefixes di (2), tri (3), tetra (4), penta (5), hexa (6), hepta (7), octa (8), nona (9), deca (10) are used to show how many atoms there are. (eg; P4O10 is tetraphosphorus decoxide) 4) For the second element, the prefixes mono (1), di (2), tri (3), tetra (4), penta (5), hexa (6), hepta (7), octa (8), nona (9), deca (10) are used to show how many atoms there are. (eg; P4O10 is tetraphosphorus decoxide) Name these covalent compounds CO SO2 CO2 SO3 NO2 N2O3 N2O N2O5 Cl2O7 Br2O5 CH4 P2O3 P2O5 P4O6 NH3 SiF4 BF3 SF6 BrI5 OBr2 SiCl4 OF2 HCl H2O2 H2O SeCl2 NF3 PCl5 SiI4 IF7 B4O6 Write formulas for these covalent compounds Hydrogen sulfide Dinitrogen tetrachloride Sulfur pentabromide Selenium hexafluoride Nitrogen triiodide Tetraphosphorus hexasulfide Tetraphosphorus decasulfide Chlorine difluoride Oxygen dibromide Chlorine pentabromide Silicon tetrabromide Silicon tetrafluoride Disilicon hexachloride Disilicon hexabromide Methane Ammomia Sulfur tetrachloride Dinitrogen trisulfide Dibromine monoiodide Diselenium pentabromide Trisilicon octafluoride Tetrasilicon decachloride Diphosphorus tetrabromide Tellurium hexafluoride Tellurium trioxide Tellurium hexabromide Hexaphosphorus nonoxide Dicarbon trioxide Trisilicon diphosphide Boron monophosphide Astatine pentafluoride Naming Ionic compounds of one metal and one non-metal 1. Ionic compounds are formed between metals (left on the periodic table) and non-metals (right on the periodic table). 2. These compounds consist of a lattice of positive and negative ions. (eg, NaCl, AgNO3, Fe2O3) is which the metal has “donated” one or more eletrons to become positive, whilst the non-metal has accepted electrons to become negative. 3. Some ionic compounds have “common names” that do not follow any particular set of rules. These must be learned - for example: Compound Common name Compound Common name Fe2O3 rust NaCl Salt or table salt 4. For most other covalent compounds there are a number of rules to follow for naming them. 5. Naming rules (nomenclature) i) The Metal is named first and does not have its name changed, so it is written as seen in the periodic table. ii) The charge on the metal is indicated by roman numerals in brackets after its’ name. This is not necessary for metals that only exist in one state. (eg. Sodium is written as Na, because it only comes as Na+, whilst iron would have to be written as Fe(II) or Fe(III), as it exists as Fe2+ and Fe3+. iii) The non-metal ion has a suffix added which indicates its’ charge or form. searchText: ﻿The alkali metals, found in group 1 of the periodic table (formerly known as group IA), are very reactive metals that do not occur freely in nature. These metals have only one electron in their outer shell. Therefore, they are ready to lose that one electron in ionic bonding with other elements. As with all metals, the alkali metals are malleable, ductile, and are good conductors of heat and electricity. The alkali metals are softer than most other metals. Cesium and francium are the most reactive elements in this group. Alkali metals can explode if they are exposed to water. The Alkali Metals are: Lithium Sodium Potassium Rubidium Cesium Francium The 38 elements in groups 3 through 12 of the periodic table are called "transition metals". As with all metals, the transition elements are both ductile and malleable, and conduct electricity and heat. The interesting thing about transition metals is that their valence electrons, or the electrons they use to combine with other elements, are present in more than one shell. This is the reason why they often exhibit several common oxidation states. There are three noteworthy elements in the transition metals family. These elements are iron, cobalt, and nickel, and they are the only elements known to produce a magnetic field. The Transition Metals are: Scandium Titanium Vanadium Chromium Manganese Iron Cobalt Nickel Copper Zinc Yttrium Zirconium Niobium Molybdenum Technetium Ruthenium Rhodium Palladium Silver Cadmium Hafnium Tantalum Tungsten Rhenium Osmium Iridium Platinum Gold Mercury Rutherfordium Dubnium Seaborgium Bohrium Hassium Meitnerium Ununnilium Unununium Ununbium The 7 elements classified as "other metals" are located in groups 13, 14, and 15. While these elements are ductile and malleable, they are not the same as the transition elements. These elements, unlike the transition elements, do not exhibit variable oxidation states, and their valence electrons are only present in their outer shell. All of these elements are solid, have a relatively high density, and are opaque. They have oxidation numbers of +3, ±4, and -3. The "Other Metals" are: Aluminum Gallium Indium Tin Thallium Lead Bismuth Non-metals are the elements in groups 14-16 of the periodic table. Non-metals are not able to conduct electricity or heat very well. As opposed to metals, non-metallic elements are very brittle, and cannot be rolled into wires or pounded into sheets. The non-metals exist in two of the three states of matter at room temperature: gases (such as oxygen) and solids (such as carbon). The non-metals have no metallic luster, and do not reflect light. They have oxidation numbers of ±4, -3, and -2. The Non-Metal elements are: Hydrogen Carbon Nitrogen Oxygen Phosphorus Sulfur Selenium The halogens are five non-metallic elements found in group 17 of the periodic table. The term "halogen" means "salt-former" and compounds containing halogens are called "salts". All halogens have 7 electrons in their outer shells, giving them an oxidation number of -1. The halogens exist, at room temperature, in all three states of matter: Solid- Iodine, Astatine Liquid- Bromine Gas- Fluorine, Chlorine The Halogens are: Fluorine Chlorine Bromine Iodine Astatine The six noble gases are found in group 18 of the periodic table. These elements were considered to be inert gases until the 1960's, because their oxidation number of 0 prevents the noble gases from forming compounds readily. All noble gases have the maximum number of electrons possible in their outer shell (2 for Helium, 8 for all others), making them stable. Helium Neon Argon Krypton Xenon Radon

JSSS                                                                                       Student

Classification of substances as elements, compounds or
mixtures                                                                           OC3 OC4
You have used techniques such as filtration, evaporation and distillation to separate mixtures.
   1. What have all mixtures got in common?________________________________________
______________________________________________________________________________
______________________________________________________________________________
Substances that are not mixtures are called pure substances. Pure substances are either elements
or compounds.
      Elements are substances that cannot be broken down chemically into other, simpler
       substances.
      Each element has a symbol, for example, H = hydrogen.
      All known elements are listed in the periodic table of the elements.




                                             1
 JSSS                                                                                     Student


   2. What is the symbol for zinc?_________________________________________________
   3. What is the symbol for oxygen?_______________________________________________
   4. What is the symbol for copper?_______________________________________________
   5. What element does the symbol Fe represent?_____________________________________
   6. What element does the symbol N represent?_____________________________________
   7. What element does the symbol S represent?_____________________________________


Compounds are pure substances that can be chemically broken down into simpler substances
          Compounds are pure substances formed from two or more different elements
           combined in a fixed proportion by mass.
          When a compound is formed from its elements, the compound usually has different
           properties to those of the elements from which it is formed. For example, sodium
           chloride (common salt) is a white solid which is relatively unreactive chemically. The
           elements from which it is formed are sodium, a very reactive silvery metal, and
           chlorine, a very reactive pale green gas.
          Each compound has a chemical formula, for example, NaCl = sodium chloride.
          Compounds are not listed in the periodic table of the elements.


   8. Sodium chloride is a compound. If it is broken down chemically, what elements are
       formed?__________________________________________________________________
   9. Why is sodium chloride not listed in the periodic table of the elements?_______________

                                                   Periodic table - battleships

Teaching notes

This activity works just like the traditional game of battleships. It is played
in pairs and they need a copy of the periodic table.

Each student needs a grid to mark their own battleships on and one to
mark their turns on. They then add battleships to their grids (they should
all be simple rectangles and can be placed horizontally or vertically on the
grid).

They could add the symbols for the elements to each square that their
battleships cover.

They should take it in turns to choose a square by reading out the
coordinates and name of the element occupying that square in the
periodic table. If they get a hit they get another go. When one of their
battleships has been hit the student should tell their opponent what type
of vessel they have hit.

The first person to sink their opponents’ battleships wins, (or set a time
limit and the winner is the person with the most ‘hits’).

searchText: ﻿THE PERIODIC TABLE INTRODUCTION The periodic table was first published by Mendeleev in 1869. The modern form of the table is the one you are familiar with. The Periodic Table places the elements in order of Atomic Number, in Groups of similar chemical properties. You need to know the names and symbols of the first 20 elements and a few more. EXERCISES 1. Place the following elements on the periodic table: (Use a black pen) METALS : Li, Be, Na, Mg, Al, K, Ca, Fe, Cu, Zn, Pb, Ag, Sn, Ba, Au, NON METALS : C, N, O, F, H, He, P, S , Cl, Br, I, Ne, Ar, Kr, METALLOIDS : Si, B 2. On the chart, colour in the three areas of metals, nonmetals and metalloids in different colours. 3. Using a completed periodic table, place the atomic number (number of protons) for each element on your sheet. Put it at the bottom of your periodic table regardless of where it is on your completed table. 4. At the top of each box, write the name of your element in small writing. 5. Number the groups across from 1 to 18. Label Group 1 – Alkali metals, Group 2 – Alkaline Earth metals, Gp 17 – Halogens, Gp 18 – Noble gases, Gps 3-12 – Transition metals. QUESTIONS 1. Which elements have symbols that do not begin with the element’s name? Can you find the origin of these names? HINT: The symbols are derived from Latin. 2. Some groups have special names. From your table, list the elements from the following groups :- Noble gases, Halogens, Alkali Metals. 3. A dark staircase – shaped line separates the metals form the nonmetals. For the first 80 elements, find the number of metals and nonmetals. Calculate the percentage of metals in the first 80 elements. 4. How many symbols can you make using your full name? (Use the lab’s periodic table also). Try to name all the symbols you find.

The periodic table — atomic
structure
Student: ................................................................................................................... Class: ................................................

As the early scientists discovered more and more elements, it became more important that they agreed
on names for the elements. Each element was given a name and a symbol. During their experiments, the
scientists also found that some of the elements had things in common. Because of this they decided to
organise the elements into groups.
   The person who finally worked out a system for sorting the elements into groups was a Russian
scientist called Dmitri Mendeleev. His system is called the periodic table and a modern version is used
by scientists today. A small portion of the periodic table is shown below.
                                                                                   The atomic number of an element is the number of
                                                                                 protons present in each atom. For example, all
                                                                                 hydrogen atoms have only one proton inside the
                                                                                 nucleus, so the atomic number of hydrogen is 1.




                                                                                       A simplified diagram of a hydrogen atom



   Atoms are electrically neutral; that is, the number of protons in an atom is the same as the number of
electrons. The atomic mass of an atom is the sum of the number of protons and neutrons in
the atom.

review the structure of an atom in your textbook.

Thermal decomposition
Sometimes when chemicals are mixed they react to form a new substance and
sometimes a chemical will just need heat to break apart.
The word thermal means heat and another way of saying breaking down is
‘decompose’ – so thermal decomposition means to break down with heat.
One example of this happening is chalk. The chemical name for chalk is calcium
carbonate and when heated it breaks down into a chemical called calcium oxide and a
gas called carbon dioxide.

searchText: The Carbon Cycle – extracting information from a text Instructions  Read the short text below;  Complete the tasks underneath. “Living things are mostly made up from a handful of elements. Carbon is one of the most important of these. Carbon is found in the bodies of animals and in plants. Plants get the carbon from the atmosphere in the form of carbon dioxide. They take this in through their leaves. It is formed into sugars in the plant by the process of photosynthesis. Some of the sugars are used to provide the plant with energy in the process of respiration, which releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. They convert some of the sugars to other carbohydrates, which form the structure of the plant. When the plants die, the structural carbohydrates are broken down by decomposers in the process of decomposition. This releases the carbon in the form of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Some plants don’t decompose when they die. They get trapped in underground or underwater without the oxygen that decomposers need to break them down. This has caused some of the plants that did this hundreds of millions of years ago to form fossil fuels like coal. Fossil fuels are being dug up and are burnt in power stations as a fuel. This releases carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere in a process called combustion. The carbon may have been trapped underground for millions of years. This started on a large scale during the industrial revolution and continues to increase year after year. Some plants get eaten by animals. The carbon from the plant in the form of sugars and starches are mostly broken down inside the body of the animal. When the animal carries out respiration, some of the carbon is released back into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide. Some of the carbon is trapped in the body of the animal as part of its tissues. Some of the carbon passes straight through the animals because it isn’t digested. This is part of the animal’s dung. This is broken down by decomposers. When the animal dies, the carbon that is trapped in the body of the animal is released into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide when decomposers break the body of the animal down. Some of the carbon dioxide from the atmosphere can dissolve in water. Phytoplankton and other plants in the ocean can carry out photosynthesis, which traps the carbon inside them. These plants also respire, like plants on land. Some of these plants die and some might end up being eaten by animals. Some of the animals make shells from carbon and other elements. When the animal dies, the shell often takes a long time to break down and sometimes this get trapped, squashed and formed into carbonaceous rocks. Carbon dioxide is released from the water into the atmosphere. This happens more if water is warmer because the bubbles of gas don’t dissolve as well in warm liquids. Volcanic activity also releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere from rocks deep underground.” Tasks 1.                                                      Carbon cycle jigsaw
Teaching notes

This jigsaw helps students engage with the carbon cycle. Students
often struggle to link processes together in science and the carbon
cycle can be difficult in this regard, particularly for lower ability
students.

As an initial task, students are asked (either individually or in pairs)
to cut out and put together the pieces of the carbon cycle. This
gives them some familiarity with the key parts and processes
involved.

Students can then use the jigsaw they have created to do individual
research on the carbon cycle. There is a worksheet that follows on
from the jigsaw activity (resource 19849, ‘Carbon cycle questions’).

The diagram can either be printed on paper each time it is used, for
each student/pair to stick into their books, or it can be printed on
card for multiple uses.

Page 2 shows the completed image, which could be used for class
discussion.

A jigsaw for the nitrogen cycle is also available (resource 19846,
‘Nitrogen cycle jigsaw’), along with a set of questions (resource
19847, ‘Nitrogen cycle questions’) and a consolidation activity
focused on improving exam answers and based on peer-assessment
strategies (resource 19848, ‘Nutrient cycles peer assessment’).

There are also two fully interactive resources, one for each of the
nutrient cycles, available from the Teachit Science Biology whizzy
things page:

title: Carbon Cycle Notes
subject: Science
searchText:
The Carbon Cycle
All living things are made of carbon.
Carbon is also a part of the ocean, air, and even rocks.
The Earth is a dynamic place, carbon does not stay still.
In the atmosphere, carbon is attached to some oxygen in a gas called
carbon dioxide.
Plants use carbon dioxide and sunlight to make their own food and
grow.
The carbon becomes part of the plant.
Plants that die and are buried may turn into fossil fuels made of
carbon like coal and oil over millions of years.
When humans burn fossil fuels, most of the carbon quickly enters
the atmosphere as carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas and traps heat in the
atmosphere.
Without it and other greenhouse gases, Earth would be a frozen
world.
Humans have burned so much fuel that there is about 30% more
carbon dioxide in the air today than there was about 150 years ago,
and Earth is becoming a warmer place.
Ice cores show us that there is now more carbon dioxide in the
atmosphere than there has been in the last 420,000 years.

Antarctica
SCIENCE UNDERSTANDING                      VERBAL/LINGUISTIC


In 2009 it was reported by the U.S. Geological Survey that the ice sheets in
the southern part of the Antarctic Peninsula (Figure 1) were disappearing and
that the change in the amount of ice was significant. Since 1998
approximately 4000 square kilometres of ice has been lost from one area.
This area of ice lost is about one and a half times the size of the Australian
Capital Territory (ACT). This loss of ice is regarded as very strong evidence of
the effects of global warming on the planet.




Figure 1
This map identifies the main areas of Antarctica.


However, in the same year it was reported by the Australian Antarctic Division
that the ice is expanding in eastern Antarctica (see Figure 1) and parts of
eastern Antarctica are becoming cooler. Ice core drilling in the ice off
Australia's Davis Station in East Antarctica revealed that in 2008 the ice had a
maximum thickness of 1.89 metres. The ice had not been this deep for 10




             Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                   ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1 Page 1
 years. Since the 1950s, when continuous record began, the average
thickness of the ice at Davis has been 1.67 metres.

Data collected do not provide any evidence of large scale melting of ice over
most of Antarctica. The loss of ice in the west over the last 30 years has been
more than offset by increases in the Ross Sea Region which is just one part
of eastern Antarctica.

Over the past 30 years the area of sea ice around Antarctica has expanded.
The changes in Antarctic sea ice are thought to be an outcome of
modifications in the path followed by the Antarctic Circumpolar Current (see
Figure 2). Warm moist air is directed towards Antarctic causing the ice to melt
in the west and increased snow fall in the east.




Figure 2
When the Antarctic Circumpolar Current moves closer to Antarctica it carries warm moist air
towards the continent.




Effect on plants and animals
Flowering plants


             Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                   ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1 Page 2
 Antarctica is home to only two species of flowering plant and both these grow
on the Peninsula. The range (area over which they are found) and abundance
(number of plants in an area) have both increased in the last few decades.

Krill

Krill are tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that are a very important food source for
animals in the Antarctic. Krill numbers in Antarctica have declined by as much
as 80% since the 1970s. Krill feed on algae that live just under the surface of
sea ice. Where the amount of sea ice is decreasing, so too does suitable
habitat for krill.

Krill feed the fish of Antarctica and are the main food source for baleen
whales. In the years 1925 to 1975 baleen whales were hunted and their
numbers decimated. Without krill it will be difficult for baleen whale numbers
to recover to pre-hunting levels.

Penguins

With the shrinking sea ice in western Antarctica, the Adélie penguins
(Pygoscelis adeliae) have declined in numbers over the last 20 to 25 years. In
other parts of Antarctica the colonies are stable or increasing in numbers.
Adélie penguins feed only on krill. The penguins nest on land and parent birds
go out to the sea ice to find food for their chicks. A reduction in the amount of
sea ice not only reduces the Adélie penguins’ food supply, it also increases
the distance the parent birds have to travel to find food.

Some penguins are benefiting from the changes taking place in Antarctica.
Gentoo penguins (Pygoscelis papua) (Figure 1a) are nesting on the Antarctic
Peninsula. Studies of the bones and other remains found in penguin colonies
indicate that Gentoo penguins did not nest in this area before 1950. These
penguins feed on fish and squid as well as krill.

Chinstrap penguins (Pygoscelis antarctica) (Figure 1b) are also benefiting
from the changes. Where Adélie penguins are abandoning their nesting sites
Chinstrap penguins are taking their place. There is no evidence of Chinstap
penguins on the Antarctic Peninsula until about 50 years ago when the
average temperatures started to rise. Chinstrap penguins eat a wider variety
of food than the Adélie penguins and they also prefer open water.

Figure 3
Gentoo (a) and Chinstrap (b) penguins both benefit from the warmer conditions in Antarctica.

searchText: Global Systems An ecosystem , short for 'ecological system', includes all the living organisms ex isting together in a particular area. These plants and animals within an area interact with each other and with the non-living elements of the area, such as climate, water, soil and so on. An ecosystem can be very small, such as a puddle or an area under a large rock, or it can be vast, such as an ocean. A sustainable ecosystem is one that is diverse and supports all of the living things in that ecosystem. Biosphere is all of the ecosystems in the world added together. In this part of the term we will look at some of the different systems that work together in world and see how some of them are changing. Key words Word Meaning Ecosystem Sustainable ecosystem Biosphere Producers Plants that make food for an ecosystem by photosynthesis. Primary consumers (herbivores) Animals that eat plants . Secondary consumers (carnivores) Animals that eat primary consumer animals. Tertiary consumers (carnivores) Animals that each primary and secondary consumer animals.

Secrets in the ice
Scientists may not have discovered a time machine yet, but they do have
a way of looking back over 300 000 years by looking at ice cores.
Scientists drill into the ice of Antarctica and collect samples from deep
down. Ice cores provide information about the Earth and the atmosphere
over hundreds of thousands of years.
    For thousands of years, snow has fallen in Antarctica. The snow
turns to ice, which builds up over time. Dust, gases and other
substances from the air become trapped in the ice. The trapped
substances provide information about what was in the air at the time the
snow fell.
    By studying dust in the ice cores, scientists can work out when
certain volcanoes have erupted. They have linked radioactive
substances in the ice to nuclear disasters in various parts of the world.
The dust and radioactive substances were probably carried to Antarctica
by the wind.

Recycling carbon
Carbon atoms are found in the air, soil, rocks, oil and gas below the Earth’s surface, and all living
things. The number of carbon atoms on Earth always remains the same. When living things use carbon
atoms, the atoms don’t just disappear; they are recycled. The diagram below shows the recycling of
carbon. It also shows how humans have added to the amount of carbon dioxide in the air. We must take
care not to interfere with the natural recycling process.

title: Nitrogen Cycle
subject: Science
searchText: Nitrogen Cycle An important process in ecosystems is the recycling of nitrogen through its living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) components. The living components, or biota, of the ecosystem participate in the nitrogen cycle in a number of ways. If you look closely at the diagram, you will notice that we show the various ways in which nitrogen cycles through nature. Colour the arrows red (except K ) (1 mark) Approximately 78% of the air is composed of diatomic nitrogen. Nitrogen is essential to life because it is a key component of amino acids and nucleic acids. Even ATP, the basic energy currency of living things, contains nitrogen. Colour the air blue . (1 mark) Neither plants nor animals can obtain nitrogen directly from the atmosphere (A). Instead, they must depend on a process called nitrogen fixation (B). Key players in nitrogen fixation are legumes (C) and the symbiotic bacteria that are associated with their root nodules. Legumes include clover, peas, alfalfa and soy-beans. The bacteria associated with their root nodules are nitrogen-fixing bacteria (D). These bacteria convert nitrogen in the soil to ammonia (NH 3 ), which can be taken up by some plants. The bacteria and the plants are in a symbiotic relationship. Cyanobacteria are also nitrogen-fixing bacteria: they are prominent in aquatic ecosystems. Colour parts C and D in green. (1 mark) Nitrogen is fix ed into the soil through the actions of bacteria and, as we mentioned above, through bacteria that’s associated with root nodules of legumes. Both of these methods of fixing nitrogen lead to its incorporation into ammonia (NH 3 ) in the process known as ammonification (E). The soil is a major reservoir for ammonia and other nitrogen-containing compounds. After nitrogen ha s been fixed, other bacteria convert it into nitrate, in a process called nitrification (F). In the first step of nitrification, Nitrosomonas (G) convert ammonia to nitrite (NO 2 ), and in the second step, nitrite is converted to nitrate (NO 3 ), by Nitrobacter (H). The nitrate (NO 3 ) is then consumed by plants (I) as the diagram shows. Colour the nitrogen- fixing bacteria and the nitrogen containing compounds orange. (1 mark) However, not all plants consume nitrate: as we mention ed before, some plants are able to use the ammonia from the soil. In both cases, nitrogen enters the primary producers in the biotic community. The plants may then be consumed by animals (J). Herbivores are the primary consumers, and the nitrogen of the plants is used for the synthesis of key organic compounds such as amino acids, proteins and nucleic acids. Colour a herbivore purple. (1 mark) The final aspect of the nitrogen cycle is the process of denitrification (K). This process is performed by a variety of microscopic bacteria, fungi and other organisms. Nitrates in the soil are broken down by these organisms and nitrogen is released into the atmosphere (A). This completes the nitrogen cycle. Colour the K arrow black . (1 mark) Questions: 1. title: Polar bears and global warming
subject: Science
searchText: ﻿Chapter 6 Sustainability extra worksheet 3: Polar bears and global warming Science Understanding Science as a Human Endeavour, Verbal/Linguistic Logical/Mathematical Polar bears are found in Greenland, the former Soviet Union, Canada and Alaska. They inhabit the shorelines of the Arctic continents and islands where ice forms each winter. It is from these platforms of ice that polar bears hunt for the seals and young walruses that are their main source of food. Figure 1 The range of polar bears – shown in green. The polar bear is classified as a vulnerable species with 8 of the 19 polar bear subpopulations in decline. Vulnerable species are species that are experiencing a rapid population decline and are in danger of becoming extinct if the drop in numbers continues. Large scale hunting of polar bears by European, Russian and American hunters and trappers from the 1600s right through to the mid-1970s caused international concern about the future of the polar bear. The polar bear population was estimated at 5000 to 10 000 bears in the 1950s and 1960s. In 1973 an international agreement to strictly regulate commercial hunting came into effect. In 2007 the bear population was estimated at 20 000 to 25 000. Effects of global warming The International Union for Conservation of Nature now lists global warming as the most significant threat to polar bear populations. Malnutrition (inadequate diet) and starving to death are two possible effects of global warming on polar bears: • Sea ice is melting earlier in the year. Since polar bears hunt off the sea ice their feeding season is shorter. This means that the bears may not build up sufficient fat reserves to enable them to survive through summer and early autumn when food is in short supply. • With less sea ice the bears must swim further to capture their food. This increases the rate at which their fat reserves are used up. • Poor nutrition leads to fewer cubs being born, lower birth weight and an increased death rate for the cubs. Global warming may also affect the ability of pregnant female bears to build suitable dens in which to give birth to their cubs and tend their cubs for the first weeks of their lives. Matter of dispute Not all researchers have reached the same conclusions about the status of polar bear populations. In a report presented to the United States Senate in 2007, some scientists challenged the computer modelling of the effect of global warming on polar bear populations. Points raised include: 1 Of the 13 populations of polar bears in Canada, 11 are stable or increasing in numbers. 2 In the last 10 000 years, polar bears survived several periods where there was a much warmer climate than there is today. 3 There are a lot more polar bears now than there were 30 years ago. For example, in the Davis Strait area there is a population of 2100 now compared to 850 in the mid-1980s. Counter arguments put forward by other scientists who do believe that polar bear populations are under threat include: 1 The numbers of bears are increasing because of the controls on hunting both of the polar bear and controls on the hunting of the bears’ food supply – the harp seal. 2 In the area of Western Hudson Bay in north-eastern Canada the population of bears has shrunk by 22% over the last ten years – from 1194 animals in 1987 to 935 in 2004. 3 The population of bears may be increasing in two areas of Canada, but two others are definitely in decline. For the other 15 areas, proposals about the status of the populations cannot be made using the statistics available. Therefore the status for the polar bear population as a whole is unknown. Table 1 on the following page was presented to a meeting of the Polar Bear Specialist Group (PBSG) in Copenhagen (Norway) in 2009. It was updated in March 2010. Table 1 Polar bear population numbers and status in each of the 19 areas of its range. Population Number (year of estimate) Number (year of estimate) Current trend Comments Arctic Basin Unknown Insufficient data Baffin Bay 2074 (1997) 1546 (2004) Declining Barents Sea 2650 (2004) Insufficient data Chukchi Sea Unknown Declining Estimate of current trend based on reduction of sea ice and the possibility of illegal harvesting. Davis Strait 2142 (2007) Declining Increased over last 30 years. Current birth and death rates suggest a population decline. East Greenland Unknown Insufficient data Foxe Basin 2197 (1994) 2300 (2004) Insufficient data New survey is ongoing. Gulf of Boothia 1592 (2000) Stable Kane Basin 164 (1998) Declining Current harvesting of bears is unsustainable. Kara Sea Unknown Insufficient data Lancaster Sound 2541 (1998) Declining Population thought to be declining because of selective harvest of male polar bears. Northern Beaufort Sea 1202 (2006) Stable Norwegian Bay 190 (1998) Declining Low harvest. Low productivity. Thought to be declining. LESSON 8 E&C                        FLASH LIGHTS




        AIM OF THE LESSON


During this lesson students will:
       Apply their understanding of simple circuits, batteries, copper wire and globes to
        construct a torch.
       Use conductors and switches to construct a torch.


        EQUIPMENT


Per Class
       blu-tac
       masking tape


Per Group
       2 D batteries (1.5 volts)
       two lengths (15cms) of insulated copper wire with about 1cm of insulation
        removed at each end
       one small globe (have some spares)
       cardboard cylinders (recycled such as from paper towel or rolled up card)
       aluminium pie dishes (small)
       alfoil
       paper clips or split pins


Preparation
       Collect a variety of light sources e.g. pen light, torch, candle, sparkler, bedside
        lamp, kerosene lantern, mosquito lantern, spotlight, flare or emergency beacon
        (preferably one powered by battery, one by mains power and one chemical).

Safety
    Care must be taken if using sparklers and other light sources.
        BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR TEACHERS


Light Sources
     Chemicals: candles, flares, sparklers, kerosene lamps, mosquito lanterns.
     Battery: torches, pen light, toys that light up, caving head lamps, spotlights.
     Mains Power: bedside lamps, house lights.


History of Flash lights
      Searching in a dark closet before 1896, one had to use a candle or kerosene
       lantern. Accidents occurred and fires followed. A safer alternative was needed.
      In 1896, the first flashlight was invented.
      Portable electric lights were called "flash lights" since they would not give a long
       steady stream of light. The bulbs were inefficient and the batteries were weak,
       allowing the user to flash the light on for only a few seconds.
      Very early lights did not have an on/off switch, just a ring that would push against
       a band of metal. When batteries and bulbs became more efficient, the switch
       was improved.


Example of a Torch
           LESSON OUTLINE



  1. Introduction (Engaging Students)
      Show students a variety of light sources e.g. pen light, torch, candle, sparkler,
       bedside lamp, lantern or spotlight.


                                                     They all produce light.
 How are all of these items similar?

2. Activities and Strategies
      Discuss the aim, equipment and method. Students can make the torch in a variety
       of ways. Encourage creativity.
      Students design and construct a simple torch using
            2 batteries
            1 globe (test these first)
            A cardboard cylinder (as the battery case and torch shaft)
            An aluminium pie dish (as the reflector)
            A combination of two split pins and a paper clip as a switch
            Copper wire


      10 minutes: discussion in groups of what they will do and drawing their design.
      40 minutes: build the torch.
      Suggestions for the torch once students have attempted their own.
           All wiring and the switch should be on the outside of the cardboard
              cylinder
           Break the circuit using two split pins bridged by a swivelling paper clip.
           Ensure the circuit is complete, no breaks other than the switch.
              Pack the back of the torch with a ball of aluminium foil.
             Cut a small hole in the pie dish to enable it to touch the battery.
             The wire where it joins the globe and the base of the globe must not touch
                the pie dish so these need to wrapped in masking taps or blue tack to
                keep them separated.
             The wire joins the globe between the pie dish and the cylinder.

Wet cells, Dry cells and Batteries

The electrochemical cell.

A simple device that converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy.
A battery is one or more electrochemical cells together. Alessandro Volta
invented the first battery (or "voltaic pile") in 1800.

Wet Cell

A wet cell has a couple of parts




The electrodes. These are plates of _________ or ________. One plate breaks
down and gives away electrons. The other plate collects these __________.

The plate that gives away electrons us called the Anode.

The plate that collects electrons is called the Cathode

movement of electrons gives a current.

anode gives away its electrons it breaks down. Once the anode has
completely broken down the wet cell will stop working.

Dry Cell

A dry cell has the same basic parts as a wet cell, but has characteristics that
make it more useful. The electrolyte is a _________, not a liquid. As a result it
does not splash around and spill if the cell is moved. The zinc electrode has
been made into part of the outer casing of the battery. The other electrode
is often made of graphite.




Why is the dry cell so useful?
 Photovoltaic Cells

Another word for photovoltaic cell is ________ cell. These convert solar
energy directly into _________ energy. The solar energy knocks ______________
off of the silicon crystals inside. As the electrons move away they form an
electric current.

The current can be used straight away or it can be used to charge a battery
for later use.



Primary and Secondary Batteries

Primary batteries (disposable batteries). These are designed to be used only
once and then thrown away. This is a problem as the batteries must be
replaced regularly. Also the wastes in these batteries are toxic, so safe
disposal is not always easy.


Secondary batteries (rechargeable batteries or storage cells). These are
designed to be recharged and used many times.

Circuits you can try are on an attached sheet. Each component (buzzer, motor, etc.) on the board will work when DIRECT CURRENT (from a battery or D.C. power supply) is connected to them. They are not designed to work with alternating current (A.C.), which is the type of current we receive through the mains power supply. Each component has a certain amount of Resistance to electric current. It is helpful to be aware of the approximate resistance of each component, especially when you want to predict what will happen before you connect up a circuit. The resistances liven are the MEASURED RESISTANCES, when a 6 volt battery was connected to them. An explanation of resistance is given in the section on "Electricity - the main concepts" (a) Globes - There are two types, the only difference being their resistance. (i) one marked 6v 2w - resistance 27 ohms. (ii) the other marked 3.8 V 0.3 A - resistance 18 ohms. Globe (ii) glows more brightly than globe (i) when each is separately connected to a 6 volt supply. (Try it). The electric current flows into the base of the globe, through the filament and out of the metal side of the globe. The current can also flow in the reverse direction. The reason for the glass casing is to protect the filament from being knocked or touched when it gets white hot. and to keep oxygen away from the filament. If the filament was exposed to oxygen when it was hot it hot, it would instantly burn out. (b) continuity tester - This has many uses. When the two probes are connected together (that is, there is no resistance between them) the light emitting diode (L.E.D.) lights up. Therefore, if the L.E.D. lights up brightly when the probes are being used, the ~two points being touched by the probes are connected electrically. Other uses are listed in the ex]experiment section. The continuity tester works best when connected to a nine volt D.C. supply. (c) variable resistor - (Also known as a Potentiometer, or POT for short). The resistance between the centre socket and the ~o outer sockets can be changed from 10 ohms up to 10k ohms (10,000 ). The resistance between the two outer sockets is always 10k ohms. There is a protective 10 ohm resistor on the central socket of the pot on the demonstration board. If there was no resistor, the pot could BURN OUT Ok~ if a power supply is connected only across the pot. This is a danger with the students' pot, as there is no resistor attached to the central terminal. Students should always ensure that the pot is in series with another component such as a globe. (d) motor - The resistance of the motor is around 18 ohms when running with a 6 volt battery supply. The motor will change direction of spin if the leads in the two motor sockets are swapped. The optimum voltage supply to run the motor is only 3 volts, but it can run comfortably at 9 volts, provided it is not left running for a long period of time. It will spin at 6 900 revolutions per minute at these voltages, if not restricted. Provided in the kit is one means of restriction - an icypole stick, with a hole to fit onto the motor shaft. See later experiments with the motor for details. (e) buzzer - The resistance of the buzzer is around 600 ohms. There are two other sockets connected to the POSITIVE TERMINAL of the buzzer, each with an additional l50 ohm resistance. These resistors decrease the current going into the buzzer, and hence make in softer. If the students are using the demonstration board, you may PREFER to have them use only the "soft" volume socket. You can do the same with the students boards (as outlined in the later experiments). The buzzer needs at least S volts power supply with the positive of the supply connected to the positive of the buzzer. the following information provides suggestions for extended experimental options in the physics using the Electricity Demonstration Board. In other words. let them solve the problem. A.CHARACTERISTICS OF SOLAR PANELS. There are various aspects of the solar panels that can be investigated. (a) Plotting the light intensity on the panels against the current and voltage output. The output of the panels can be placed in series with a milliammeter and 100 ohm resistor, with a voltme[er in parallel ~ith the 100 ohm resistor. A light intensity meter used b>photographers can be used to measure the light intensity at the panel surface usin~ a 150 ~,~tt ii~ht globe as the source. (b) Using the set up as in (a), determine the percentage efficiency of the solar panels. For a particular distance of the panels from the ligh~ source (say x cm), the surface area of a sphere of radius x can be calculated (say area Y cmz). Assuming the light globe actually emits 150 joules per second as light, and that the light is evenly distributed over the imaginery surface of the sphere or radius x, it is easy to calculate the amount of light energy per second reaching the solar collectors. Using_' the P = IV for the output of the solar panels, you can determine the percentage efficiency of the panels. This efficiency can be determined for various distances from the globe. ~c) A variation on (b) could be to use colour filters to see if the panels are sensitive to particular colours. Ad.~ustment of distance may be necessary to keep the overall light intensity on the panels constant. There are a range of extensions to this topic, including visiting showroom of the latest solar technology, and writing up on their research. Students could also construct their o~ solar water heater, and determine the efficienc~~ of energ~ transfer. T]~_ ELEtmfRIC ~FoTOR The measureable parameters relevant to the motor are (a) its ms~ximum speed of rotation, (b) the best operating voltage, and the current dra~ by the motor at this voltage (the power consumed for various voltages can be determined); (c) the output power of the motor, and hence its relative efficiency' for a Oarticular load on the motor: (di the ms~ximum torque of the motor. Some of these parameters are more difficult to measure than the others, particularly (c) and (d). SUGGESTIONS (a) Use a stroboscope to determine the frequency of rotation for various inpu~ voltages immx. 9 volts, for short time only). Plot f vs input voltage. ib) From the graph of (a), determine the minimum voltage for ms~ximum f. (c) Put a piece of pencil with its lead removed on the end of the shaft so that it can act as a pulley. A long cotton thread with a light weight can be attached to the pulley. If the motor is then raised to a height of at least 2 metres, the students can then attempt to determine the power output (rate of change of potential energy of the weight) versus the input power to the motor. Because of the speed of the motor, students may wish to gear the speed of rotation do~, or file most of the pencil shaft down - the motor can make a light weight move ~.~]ERY rapidly. The challenge is to get the motor operating_ at its optimum efficiency! ld) By having a long ic.vpole stick firmly attached to the shaft lyou may want to file a The school will probably have other motors that students can compare. Students may not be aware of how many motors are in the average house. There maybe anything up to forty motors in one home, including in toys (trains and slot cars), appliances with moving parts - vacuum, dishwasher, washing machine, video, tape recorder and player, record player, exhaust fans, hair dryer, blow heaters, cooling fans, electronic type~Titers and printers, food processors. mix-masters, electric can openers, tumble driers, refrigerators and freezers (you hear the motor going on or off occasionally), electric tools in the workshop - drills, grinders, electric planes and touters, electric saws, etc. Try and estimate how many motors you have in your home. 7. ENERGY CHANGES - THE ~I4iN CONCEPTS There are a number of energy transformations that can be sho~m using the demonstration board. (a) If you have a circuit with a battery and a light globe {as with a torch), the energy changes that take place are - chemical energy (stored in the battery), electrical energy (transferred through the wires by means of electric current) and finally light and heat energy (given off by the light globe). Current – picture it!
Task

   1. Read carefully through the text.
   2. Put the images in the order that they appear in the text.
   3. Glue the images in the spaces provided on the worksheet and quote a small
       part of the text that you are linking the image to – this cannot be more than
       eight words! Next, say why you are matching the image to that piece of text.



        When you think about the word ‘current’ what is the first thing that
        comes to mind? Perhaps the current in a river or something present-
        day?

        The current of a river is the flow of water. As the current flows from high
        ground to low ground it can carry things with it, like leaves, twigs and
        even boats. Current can only flow from high ground to low ground.

        Current in an electrical circuit is very similar, it also flows and carries
        electrical charge. The electrical current that flows in one direction is
        called direct current. Just like a river, it cannot flow backwards and
        forwards, it can only flow from one side of the battery to the other.

        As long as the current flows through the wires and cell any components
        in the circuit, like lightbulbs or buzzers will work. However, it is very
        important that there are no breaks in the electrical circuit because if
        there were, the electrical charge would not be able to flow back to the
        cell.

        We can think of the cell as being responsible for ‘pushing’ the current
        around the circuit. A bigger push from the cell will mean that more
        current can flow.

        To measure the current we use a piece of equipment called an
        ammeter, and it is placed in the circuit so that it can measure the
        current that flows through it. An ammeter measures current in units
        called ‘amps’ or ‘amperes’. Amps are given the unit symbol, A, for
        example, 10 A is 10 amps. Remember that the ammeter must be part of
        the circuit and not on the outside of it.

        the current in a series circuit, it will always be the same.

searchText: ﻿Batteries and Cells A cell is a device which converts chemical energy into electrical energy. It is used in an electrical circuit to drive motors, lights etc. A battery is a combination of cells. The cells are connected in either series or parallel to provide higher voltage or longer life. When connecting cells in series, connect them positive to negative. Electrical circuits An electrical circuit allows electrons to flow from the source, through conductors and return to the source. When they flow through an appliance energy is transferred to the appliance and it works. ie a light glows or a motor runs. The electrons will not flow unless the circuit is complete. Circuits can be represented by circuit diagrams. Symbols represent the various parts of the circuit.

Electric Shock Comprehension
                                          Answers

1        The coma position involves the victim lying on their side with the leg closest to
         the ground fully extended and the other leg bent at the knee. The arms are
         stretched in front of the victim.

2        A current of 50 mA needs to flow for about 4 000 m s. This is about 4 seconds.

3        Th three factors are: voltage, the path taken and the skin resistance of the victim.

4        The first thing you should do is remove the source of the electricity from the
         victim. Use an insulator to separate the victim from the source.

5        The body of the car will probably be a conductor. If the wires are in contact with
         the car , the car will be “live” and will conduct a current to all of its surface.

6        You should reassure the victim, treat burns and send for medical assistance.

7        You should position the person in the coma position, open the mouth and clear
         any obstruction.

8        If the current flows across the chest it will effect the heart and may cause the heart
         to fibrillate.

title: Electrical Safety Teachers Guide
subject: Science
searchText:
Electrical Safety World
                                  Teacher’s Guide

Electrical Safety World uses information, experiments, games, and activities to teach
students the principles and practices of electrical safety. The site is geared for a range of
interests and reading levels and can be used by students in elementary and middle school.
(Non-readers will be able to play the games with adult assistance.)

This Teacher’s Guide contains three sections:

      Site overview.
      Questions and activities to review key safety principles.
      Experiments, guidance and set-up.

I. SITE OVERVIEW
 The informational areas of the site explain the basic science of electricity and electrical
safety principles with text, pictures, and experiments. The games simulate common
indoor and outdoor electrical safety situations, giving students a chance to put safety
principles into practice. The activities ask students to apply electrical safety know-how in
their own lives.

Here’s what each area contains:

      The Travels of Electricity (INFORMATIONAL)
       What electricity is, where it comes from, and how it travels. Covers the electric
       distribution system, conductors, and insulators. Contains experiments about
       circuits and conductors/insulators.

      How Electricity Can Hurt You (INFORMATIONAL)
       How electricity behaves and how it can hurt people. Covers grounding, electricity
       and water, appliance safety, and the effects of electric shock. Contains
       experiments about electricity and water, and short circuits.

      In Case of Emergency! (INFORMATIONAL)
       Teaches students how to respond to electrical fires, electric shock, downed power
       lines, power lines on a vehicle, and power outages.

      Tree and Power Line Safety (INFORMATIONAL)
       Explains the hazards of trees near power lines, and how students can climb, plant,
       and trim trees to avoid power line contact.

      Find the Hidden Dangers (GAME)
       A game to test students’ understanding of how to play it safe around electricity
       outdoors. Within busy street scenes, students must identify electrical hazards
       involving power lines and electrical equipment.

      Make the Safe Choice (GAME)
       A game to test students’ awareness about electrical safety inside the home. The
       game presents electrical hazards that are relevant to students’ lives and asks
       students to identify the safest response.

      Shock Blocker (GAME)
       Students play against the computer to prevent water from creating a path for
       electricity to flow from a power line, electrical outlet, or lightning bolt.

      Tell Me More About Electricity (INFORMATIONAL)
       This section is not safety-related but instead provides additional information for
       students interested in other aspects of electricity. Covers electricity basics,
       electricity generation, pioneers of electrical discovery, electric vehicles, and
       energy efficiency/conservation.
    Home Safety Audit (ACTIVITY)
    A checklist students can use with parents to inspect their home for electrical
    hazards.

   Tell Your Story (ACTIVITY)
    Profiles a real-life shock victim who is an Olympic kayaker. Asks students to
    interview someone who has had an electric shock, to tell their own electric shock
    story, or to report on one from a newspaper article. Focus is on sharing how the
    incident occurred and how it could have been prevented.

   Safety Certificate
    This is a checklist of site locations students can use to map their progress, plus an
    electrical safety pledge. We recommend students print the certificate before
    starting the site and have a parent or other adult sign it after they have visited the
    main areas.

   Glossary
    Definitions of electricity-related words found on the site. These definitions may
    be accessed by clicking on the words wherever they appear highlighted on the site
    (usually their first reference within a section.)

   Links to Related Sites
    Hot links to related sites about the science of electricity, electrical inventions, and
    electrical safety.
 II. QUESTIONS AND ACTIVITIES

These questions and activities review the key safety principles from Electrical Safety
World. Here are a few ideas for how to use them with your class:

      Use as discussion points for verbally reviewing basic electrical safety information
       with the whole group.
      Use as a pre- and post-test to assess student understanding of electrical safety
       principles before and after visiting Electrical Safety World. (To use as a written
       test for older students, cut and paste the questions into your word processing
       program, delete the answers, and print out one sheet for each student.)
      Put students into small groups and assign each group several questions; ask them
       to use the website to find the answers. (Answers to questions 1-12 can be found in
       The Travels of Electricity; questions 13-19 are based on How Electricity Can Hurt
       You.)
      After all students have completed all sections of the website, organize the class
       like a game show: “contestants” can continue to answer questions until they get
       one incorrect, at which point a new contestant takes their place.

Electrical Safety Questions

1. What is electricity a form of? (Energy.)

2. What does electricity travel on to get from the power plant to people’s houses?
(Overhead and underground power lines.)

3. What other equipment is involved in getting electricity to where it can be used by
people? (Some or all of the following are correct: substations, pole-mounted and pad-
mounted transformers, service drops, meter boxes, electrical wiring, appliance cords.)

4. How fast does electricity travel? (At the speed of light, 186,000 miles per second.)

5. Could you move faster than electricity? (No!)

6. List some good conductors of electricity. (Metal, water)

7. Is the human body a good conductor of electricity? Why/why not? (Yes, because it is
mostly water.)

8. What will happen if electricity travels through you? (You will be shocked and could be
badly hurt or even killed.)

9. List some good insulators. (Special rubber, glass.)

10. Why are insulators important? (They keep electricity from leaving wires.)
 11. What would happen if a power line were to fall from the power pole to the ground?
(It would energize the area around it with a lot of electricity and people touching the line
or coming near it would be hurt or killed.)

12. If you overload an outlet by plugging in too many things, what can happen? (Cord
insulation can overheat and melt, causing a shock and fire hazard.)

13. Why are people good conductors of electricity? (Our bodies are mostly water, and
water conducts electricity.)

14. Do you have to be touching the ground directly to conduct electricity? (No, you could
be touching something that is touching the ground, like a ladder.)

15. Why should you never touch anything electrical while you have wet hands or while
standing in water? (Water conducts electricity and you could be shocked.)

16. What is the purpose of rubber or plastic insulation around appliance cords? (It keeps
the electricity in the wires and prevents you from getting a shock.)

17. If a person is shocked, what can happen? (Muscle spasms, weakness, rapid pulse,
severe burns, unconsciousness, or death.)

18. Why can birds sit on power lines without being shocked? (The birds do not touch the
ground or anything in contact with the ground.)

19. Why could a kite caught in a power line be dangerous to try to retrieve? (If you touch
the kite while you are in contact with the ground or anything touching the ground, like a
ladder, electricity will travel from the power lines down the kite and into you, and you
will be shocked.)

Activities for Going Further

      Prepare a one-minute presentation or play for your class on the basics of how
       electricity travels from the power plant to appliances in people’s homes.

      Prepare a poster showing electricity going through a person on its way to the
       ground. The source of the electricity could be a power line or an appliance cord.

      Think of three ways you can convince your friends to be safe around electricity.
       Share them with the class.

      Create a radio commercial about outdoor or indoor electrical safety.

      Write an essay describing electrical hazards found in an imaginary house.
 III. EXPERIMENTS

Complete a Circuit

Materials:
Students will need the materials listed (1 D-cell battery, 1 1.2-volt lightbulb, 1 E-10
lightbulb base, two 12-inch pieces of insulated solid strand 18-22 gauge copper wire with
one inch of insulation removed at each end, masking tape). Bulbs, bases, and wire can be
purchased at stores like Radio Shack. Make sure the lightbulbs and bases match.


Safety First:
    Students should be supervised by an adult while doing this experiment.
    A teacher or another adult should be responsible for stripping insulation from
       wires.
    Explain to students that electricity can be dangerous if it is not handled correctly,
       and emphasize they should never experiment with the electricity that comes from
       a wall outlet. It’s much more powerful than the electricity made by small batteries
       and could seriously injure or even kill someone.

Objective:
Students will build a circuit and equate it to the path of electricity that comes from power
plants.

Getting It Across:
   1. Have students read the information and follow the steps on the page.
   2. Make sure they are able to identify the circuit electricity travels from the battery
       to the lightbulb and back, and the circuit electricity travels from power plants to
       homes and back. They should be able to equate the wires in the experiment with
       power lines and electrical wiring in the electric distribution system.

Questions and Answers:

      What part of the distribution system is like the wires in the experiment? (Power
       lines and electrical wiring.) What happens if you only tape one of the wires to the
       battery? Why? (The bulb does not light. The circuit is not complete unless both
       wires are taped to the battery, allowing electricity to flow in a circle.)
 Experiment with Conductors and Insulators

Materials:
Students will need 1 D-cell battery, 1 1.2-volt lightbulb, 1 matching lightbulb base, one
12-inch piece and two 4-inch pieces of insulated solid strand 18-22 gauge copper wire
with one inch of insulation removed at each end, and masking tape. Bulbs, bases, and
wire can be purchased at stores like Radio Shack. Make sure the lightbulbs and bases
match. Students will also need a variety of things they think might conduct electricity,
such as toothpicks, rubber bands, paper clips, plastic, fruit, etc.

Safety First:
    Students should be supervised by an adult while doing this experiment.
    A teacher or another adult should be responsible for stripping insulation from
       wires.
    Explain to students that electricity can be dangerous if it is not handled correctly,
       and emphasize they should never experiment with the electricity that comes from
       a wall outlet. It’s much more powerful than the electricity made by small batteries
       and could seriously injure or even kill someone.

Experiment Tips:
    Teachers should strip the wires ahead of time and make sure the batteries are
      fresh. Though the illustration does not show it, use tape to stick the wires to the
      ends of the battery.
    Students are likely to know that metals are good conductors, but they may be
      unaware that things with a lot of liquids in them also conduct well. Some things to
      have on hand include lemons, pickles, and potatoes. When testing these, make
      sure students stick wires into the wet part of the item.
    The key in the conduction of electricity is the movement of electrons. Metals are
      elements that freely share electrons. In liquids, dissolved ions can carry a charge
      as well. That is why water helps in the conduction of electricity. Salty water,
      loaded with sodium and chloride ions, helps even more.

Objective:
Students will learn the difference between conductors and insulators.

Getting it Across:
   1. Have students bring in things they think might conduct electricity.
   2. Have teams read the information and follow the steps on the page.
   3. Students should first test their circuit by connecting it without any trial material.

Questions and Answers:
    Ask teams to share their predictions and results. Were the results the same? If not,
       why not? (Answers will vary. Be sure the experimental setup was not at fault.)
    What conclusions can students draw about conductors and insulators? (Answers
       will vary. Students might generalize that metals are good conductors or plastic is a
       good insulator.)
 Electricity and Water

Materials:
Students will need the circuits they made for the “Conductors and Insulators” experiment,
plus a glass pint or quart jar, 2 nails, 2 alligator clips, salt, and water.

Safety First:
    Students should be supervised by an adult while doing this experiment.
    A teacher or another adult should be responsible for stripping insulation from
       wires.
    Explain to students that anything can conduct electricity when wet. Remind
       students that they can mix water and electricity safely in this experiment because
       the voltage is so minimal (1.5 V per D-cell battery).

Objective:
Students will demonstrate that water is a conductor of electricity.

Getting it Across:
Be sure students add plenty of salt to the water. Then have them predict, experiment, and
note their observations. Share results.

Questions and Answers:
   1. Ask students why they think the salt is needed. (Students will need to add a lot of
       salt to their water in order for electric current to flow. The voltage of the battery is
       so low that additional particles must be added to make the water MORE
       conductive. It is the impurities in water that make it a good conductor. Pure water
       will not conduct electricity. However, pure water is only found in the laboratory.
       That’s why there is so much emphasis on the conductivity of water as regards
       electrical safety.)
 Ben Franklin Was Lucky!

Materials:
Students will need the circuits they made for the “Complete a Circuit” experiment,
modified as shown in the illustration (strip a 1-inch section of insulation off the middle of
each wire). Students will also need a 6-inch piece of thicker wire with one inch of
insulation removed at each end.

Safety First:
    Students should be supervised by an adult while doing this experiment.
    A teacher or another adult should be responsible for stripping insulation from
       wires.
    Remind students that they are able to work with these batteries and wires because
       the voltage is minimal (1.5 V per D-cell battery). They should never experiment
       with the electricity that comes from a wall outlet. It’s much more powerful than
       the electricity made by small batteries and could seriously injure or even kill
       someone.

Objective:
Students will be able to describe a short circuit and compare it to the story about Ben
Franklin.

Getting it Across:
1. Have students read the information and follow the steps on the page.
2. Be sure students understand that they should immediately disconnect the thick wire
   and the battery after they observe what happens. The wires will get hot. This is a clue
   to why Franklin got shocked.

Questions and Answers:
 Students’ predictions and results will vary.
 Why is this called a “short circuit”? (Because the electricity travels a shorter route
   than the intended circuit. Electricity is not able to complete its intended path because
   the circuit is grounded somewhere.)
 Why did Ben Franklin get shocked? (His arms functioned like the thick wire in the
   experiment. Electricity traveled through his body instead of through the circuit, and
   he got shocked.)

What Makes the Electrons Flow? If you could see the atomic world inside a copper wire, you’d see that the atoms of copper can lose electrons so easily that there are billions of “loose electrons” hanging around between the atoms. These electrons are not going anywhere, but can easily jump from atom to atom. Copper atom Loose electron Every battery or other power source has an electric field. The field of a battery is produced by chemical reactions. The “mains” power is produced by magnetic effects in a generator at a power station. When the wire becomes part of a circuit, the electric field instantly reaches through the wire and exerts a force on every electric charge. The charged particles within the copper atoms cannot move, but the “loose” electrons immediately gain energy from the field and begin flowing in the wire. This flow of electrons is the electric current. The amount of “push” that the electric field can give the electrons is called “voltage”. searchText: Electricity and Safety Electricity can be dangerous for a number of reasons. It can cause fires. Remember , if current runs through a wire with high resistance it produces heat. This is good in a toaster, but not so good in some other situations. If resistance it too high in a wire it can over heat and cause a fire. This sometimes happens because too much current is put through a wire or a short circuit has occurred. What is a short circuit? Sometimes electricity takes a short cut through the wrong wire or through some other object that conducts electricity, such as a metal knife. We call this a short circuit. A short circuit is usually made accidentally. It bypasses part of a circuit. This can happen when two bare wires in a circuit touch each other. The part of the circuit bypassed by the short circuit stops working , and a large amount of current could start to flow through the short cut . This can generate a lot of heat in the wires and cause a fire Electricity can give you and electric shock . This is where current flows through a person. The heart and nerves of the bod y are controlled by electrochem ical impulses, so a large current can disrupt these and cause injury. An electric shock can also cause burns on the skin and internal tissues. Being Safe. Make sure wires are insulated. That is they have a plastic coating on them. If a wire has frayed insulation, have it repaired. Do not use electricity near water. Do not overload any one power outlet. Fuses and Circuit Breakers . Every electrical device in your home that is connected to a power supply is protected by a fuse somewhere along the circuit connecting it to electrical supply. The biggest fuses in your house are located in the fuse or circuit breaker panel . This is mounted on the wall where electrical power lines come inside your house and split into the c ircuits that run through your home . Without fuses, power surges from electric generators or short circuits within your house could burn out appliances, circuit boards and wiring. Any of these could lead to fires or further damage to the electrical systems within the building. Fuses all contain a filament or strip made of metals. This filament melts and break s when a certain current or "load" has been exceeded. It mel ts and breaks the circuit. This stops the current and prevents a fire. A new fuse must be used to re-establish the circuit. Depending on the circuit, different fuses will burn out(melt) at a specific current. Most household ci rcuits carry 10, 15 or 20-amp. Fuse wires are one-time use. Once they burn out, they have to be replaced. Circuit Breakers are like light switches. They do the same job as fuses but do not “burn out” when the current gets too high. When they overheat they switch off and lock. This "lock" (actually its more of a spring) causes the switch to shut off. You can flip the breaker to reset it, but generally if it’s too hot, it won’t stay on until it has cooled to a safe operating temperature. Make sure plugs and appliances have an earth wire. W hen a short circuit in the appliance occurs the earth wire allows the electricity to be safely conducted to the earth. This is better than the electric current running through you to the Earth. If in doubt use a qualified electrician .

searchText:
Electricity – pairs game

Introduction

A simple game designed to increase students’ confidence in the symbols of circuitry. Most
students have played ‘pairs’ at some time or other, so the rules are generally known to all.


Instructions

Divide the class into groups of between two and four players. Photocopy one set of the
sheets (as well as a sheet of answers) for each group. It is best to photocopy them onto
card or stiff paper that is thick enough so the typing cannot be seen through it!

Cut the sheets into individual cards. Remove any pairings not relevant to your group.

The aim of the game is to make pairs. A pair consists of symbol or graph with its
appropriate name. The answer sheet is given to each group to help them check the
pairings are correct.


Rules of the game

The cards are shuffled and spread out randomly face down on the bench.

The first player turns over two cards. If they are a pair, the player removes them and has
another go. If they are not a pair they are turned face down again. When the first player
has finished their go, play moves to the next player.

The winner is the one with the most pairs at the end.


Variations

One player can be nominated in each group whose sole responsibility is to check the
answers.

Groups of students can be formed according to their ability and different groupings of
cards given to them. The less able may find that sheets one and two are enough to start
with.

Also, with a bit of manipulation the names can be photocopied onto one colour of card and
the symbol or graph onto another. Therefore, when a student picks up a pair of cards they
are picking up two different colours. The game is faster this way.
