searchText: ﻿ Electricity is a form of energy where the energy supply comes from rapidly moving electrons. You may remember from year 8 that there are two main forms of electrical energy; • Static electricity • Current electricity Try this exercise to reacquaint you with static electricity 1. STATIC ELECTRICITY: SOURCES OF ELECTRICAL ENERGY A convenient source of electrical energy in the laboratory is the cell. The electrons the cell releases come from chemical reactions that occur within it. That is, cells are electron sources, and they can 'pump' electrons around an electrical circuit. A battery is made up of two or more cells linked together. 2. CIRCUITS a) Simple Circuits A circuit is a completed loop of conducting material joining the terminals of a cell or a battery. In the drawing of circuits, the following symbols are used: A circuit is drawn using straight ruled lines and in a rectangular shape even though in reality it may look quite different. Draw examples of circuits in the space below. i) a cell, a switch, a globe ,an ammeter, a resistor joined by conducting wires. ii) 2 cells, 2 globes, a bell and a resistor joined by conducting wires b) Electric Current An electric current is a flow of charged particles, pumped by a cell, around a circuit. In metals, the electric current is a flow of electrons. For a current to flow, the circuit must be complete. The size of current flowing around a circuit can be determined by examining the brightness of a globe in the circuit (the brighter the globe, the greater the current). A switch is a device for breaking a circuit. I can be drawn open or closed. Questions 1. In which of the following will an electric current flow? 2. Consider the following circuit: Which globes will glow when the following switches are on? i) Switch A ii) Switch A and Switch C iii) Switch B and Switch C iv) Switch A and Switch B 3. Now you draw a circuit in which there are 3 globes and 2 switches and 2 cells. When 1 switch is closed only 1 globe glows and when the other switch is closed the 2 other globes glow. ACTIVITY 1: Simple Circuits Materials: 1 electricity kit Examine all the components of the kit carefully and make sure you understand what each is. Method: 1. Build each of the following circuits and determine whether the globe is off, dim or bright. Draw each of the circuits and write your answer under each circuit diagram.. 2. Using 2 cells, 1 switch, 2 globes and conducting wires, build as many different circuits as you can, in which the light globes glows when the switch is on. Draw each of these circuits in the space below.. 3. Complete the tables by either connecting Put a  for lamp ON up each circuit, or by "tracing" the electron and a X for lamp OFF flow around the circuit. PROBLEM SHEET 1 – Simple Circuits 6. Complete the tables for the switches in the following circuits: 3. RESISTANCE Resistance in a circuit is any device that restricts or inhibits the current through it. 1. If a device e.g. a piece of wire, has a high resistance then the flow of electricity through it is greatly reduced. 2. If a device has a low resistance then the flow of electricity through it will be only slightly reduced. 3. The greater the resistance of a device, the smaller the current that will flow through the circuit. 4. When an electric current flows through resistance in a circuit, some of the electrical energy is transformed to heat energy i.e. heat is produced when electricity flows through resistance. 5. The greater the resistance, the greater the amount of heat produced. 6. Different conductors can have different resistance properties. For example, copper has a low resistance but nichrome and tungsten have high resistance. Light globes contain a piece of high resistance wire, which produces much heat (and thus light) when an electric current is passed through it. Thus, a light globe can be regarded as a device with high resistance. Example 1. Which of the following circuits has the greater resistance? 2. Which of the following circuits has the lower resistance? ACTIVITY 2: Resistance Method: 1. Set up the following circuit 1. How bright is the globe ? ______________________________________________________ 2. Replace the copper wire with a piece of nichrome wire (of the same length as the copper wire). How bright is the globe now ? ___________________________________________ 3. Compare the brightness of the globe with that obtained for the copper wire. _______________________________________________________________________________ 4. Which wire has the greater resistance, copper wire or nichrome wire? ______________________ 5. Now replace the nichrome wire with a small piece of 'steel wool' wire. Describe what happens to the globe now. ___________________________________________________________ 6. Explain what happened with the ‘steel wool wire’ . ____________________________________ ________________________________________________________________________________ 7. Electrical energy is more easily transformed to heat energy using ______________ resistance wire. Application of Resistance 4. SHORT CIRCUITS A 'short circuit' is an alternative conducting pathway of lower resistance, which by-passes a particular resistance, globe or other appliance in a circuit. It is not necessarily the shortest path however. E.g. in the following circuit, the light globe will not light up because of the 'short circuit' between points A and B (i.e. it is 'easier' for the electrons to travel through wire AB rather than through the light globe.) ACTIVITY 3: Short Circuits Method: 1. Set up the following circuit 2. Sides A and B are made of two wires each, joined together by twisting the ends 3. Place another conducting wire between A and B. This is the short circuit. 4. Predict what you think will happen. ________________________________________________ Test your prediction. 5. What happens to the globe when the wire between A and B is connected ? ______________________________________________________________________________ 6. Explain what happened to the globe. ______________________________________________ ________________________________________________________________________________ 5. FUSES Fuse wire is a relatively high resistance conductor with a low melting point. A fuse wire will melt if too large a current is passed through it. When it melts the circuit is broken and current can no longer flow. A fuse is a protective or safety device, included in a circuit, which melts when a short-circuit or overload results in too high a current passing through the circuit. In circuit diagrams, a fuse has the symbol Example In which of the following circuits would you expect the fuse to blow if a wire was placed between A and B? ACTIVITY 4: Fuses Method: 1. Identify the following statements as true or false a) An electric current can flow more easily through a wire of high resistance than through a wire of low resistance. b) Wire with high resistance restricts the flow of electricity through it. c) If a wire has a low resistance, it will probably heat up considerably when a current is passed through it. d) A 'short circuit' is a circuit which is very small. e) A 'short circuit' can occur if in a particular circuit an alternative pathway of low resistance is produced. f) Fuse wire is made from wire which has low resistance and low melting point. g) Fuse wire is made from wire which has high resistance and high melting point. h) Nichrome wire has a higher resistance than copper wire. i) The wire used to make the filament in a light globe has high resistance and low melting point. 2. Making an Electromagnet
 Aim: To build an electromagnet

Equipment:
• Insulated copper wire                               Safety Information
                                                      Take care when handling and cutting
• Wire strippers
                                                      wire to avoid cuts.
• Battery (9V)

• Iron nail (approx. 50mm)

• Crocodile clips - optional

• Paperclips

Method:
Step 1: Wrap the copper wire around the iron nail, leaving
about 10cm lengths at each end. Try not to wrap it overly
tightly around the nail - you should be able to remove the
nail from the coil after wrapping.

Step 2: Carefully strip the insulation from the ends of the
wire to expose the copper inside and to make a connection.
(Or connect with crocodile clips, if available).

Step 3: Connect the exposed ends, one to each terminal of
the battery.

Step 4: Test your electromagnet by observing whether it
attracts the paperclips.



  Exploring further
  You could investigate how the number of coils in your wire affects the strength of the electromagnet.

  You could investigate how the number of batteries connected affects the strength of the electromagnet.

  You could investigate how the metal core inside the coil affects the strength of the electromagnet.

   Secret writing has been employed about as long as writing has existed.
    Cryptology has long been employed by governments, military, businesses and
    organisations to protect their messages. Today, encryption is used to protect

   Morse code is made up of dots and dashes that are translated into long and short

LESSON 5 E&C                        CONDUCTORS




        AIM OF THE LESSON


During this lesson students will:
      Classify materials as conductors or insulators.
      Describe the role insulators and conductor in everyday appliances.


        EQUIPMENT


Per Class
      a selection of insulators and conductors:
            insulators (wooden pop sticks, plastic spoons, glass jars, paper, rubber,
              ceramic tiles, cotton, foam cups, kitchen sponge)
             conductors (alfoil, iron nails, steel wool, coins, copper, aluminium cans,
              drawing pins, paper clips)

Per Group
      2 D Batteries (1.5 volt)
      3 lengths (15cms) of insulated copper wire with about 1cm of insulation removed
       at each end
      2 globes
      cardboard (1 piece about 10x10cm)
      paper clips
      a few insulators and conductors as listed above
      masking tape


Preparation
     Collect a range of materials to test; students could bring one each from home.

Safety
    Mains electricity must not be used.

        BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR TEACHERS
 Circuits
      A circuit is a path in which electricity flows.
      Electrons are tiny particles that are found in atoms.
      Electric current is the movement of electrons, which creates the flow of
       electricity.
      The power supply pushes electrons through a circuit. This power supply can
       come in many different forms (for example, a battery is a power supply).
      You can think of the power supply as a pump that creates pressure to force
       water to flow in a hose.
      In a series circuit the batteries and light bulbs are connected in a line. There is
       only one path for the electrons to flow along. Therefore, the current through each
       of the circuit elements is the same.
      This is why when one Christmas tree light blows, the rest do not light up.
      Electricity can be transferred to heat, light, sound and motion energy.


Conductors and Insulators
      A conductor allows electricity to flow through it. Examples include metals such as
       wire made of aluminium, steel or copper.
      An insulator does not allow electricity to flow through it. Examples include non
       metals such as plastic, wood and foam.


Additional Information
      A parallel circuit is one in which electric current travels along more than one path
       (as in the home), because there is more than one path for the electricity to
       follow. Some parts of the circuit can be on while others are off.
      Voltage can be thought of as electrical pressure, which pushes the electrons
       through the circuit. Electric pressure is measured in volts.
      The most basic electrical devices in the home e.g. a kettle, are made from
       simple pieces of wire which resists the flow of electricity. The wire will become
       warm, perhaps red hot when electricity flows through it.
      The household voltage in Australia is 240 Volts.
      Wiring in houses is designed to have very low resistance so they don’t become
       warm with electricity flowing through them.
           LESSON OUTLINE



1. Introduction (Engaging Students)
      Direct students into groups.
      The students to design a simple circuit using two batteries, a globe and copper
       wire.
      The circuits should be built and taped onto a sheet of cardboard or their desk to
       hold the components in place.
      The group with their globe shining first is the winner.
      The teacher introduces the concept of materials that conduct electricity
       (conductor) and those that do not (insulators).


 What do we call materials that let                      Conductors.

 conductors.

 What do we call materials that do                       Insulators.
 not let electricity pass through
 them?
 Name some examples of insulators.
                                                         Foam, plastic, wood.

 How could we test materials to see                      the materials one at a time and
 if they are conductors or insulators?                   see if the globe still glows.




2. Activities and Strategies
      Write down the aim, equipment and method for the activity.
      Revise what is meant by a prediction and ask students to predict whether the
       globe will shine with each material (therefore a conductor) or not (therefore an
       insulator).
      Groups to break the circuit using two drawing pins a few centimetres apart.
      Groups test the different materials to see if they are conductors or insulators and
      record their observations.


3. Focus Questions (Explain and Elaborate)

searchText:
Cow’s Eye Dissection
Purpose: To identify and examine the various parts of a cow’s eye.

Materials: gloves     scissors   scalpel     forceps   cutting mat    newspaper
cow’s eye

Procedure:
Part A: External features of the eye
1. There is some fat around the eye. What colour it the fat?

2. What is the purpose of the fat around the eye?

3. What is the job of the muscles on the outside of the eye?

4. Cut the fat and muscles off the eyeball so that you can see the sclera.

5. What colour is the sclera? ________        iris? ________   pupil? ________

6. The cornea is the tough, clear covering over the iris and pupil. It is
   normally clear and colourless; however in your cow’s eye it may be cloudy.
   Why do you think it may have become cloudy?


7. The optic nerve carries information from the retina to the brain. Identify the
   optic nerve on the back of the eye. Describe what it looks like.


Part B: Internal features of the eye
1. Carefully use the scalpel to make a small cut near the centre of the eye.
   With the scissors, cut around the entire eye so that you have two equal
   hemispheres.

2. What colour is the sclera?

3. What did you notice about the texture of the sclera? Why is this important?


4. The jelly inside the eye is the vitreous humour. Gloop your vitreous
   humour onto the parts identification worksheet.

5. What is the job of the vitreous humour?


6. Pick up the back of the sclera, which contains the optic nerve. The retina is
   a thin layer on the inside of the sclera. Gently peel off the retina with the
   forceps and place it on the parts identification sheet.

7. What is the purpose of the retina?

8. You may have found it difficult to remove the retina because it was attached
   to the optic nerve. This area is called the __________ __________.
 9. They black, shiny layer under the retina is the choroid coat. It contains
   blood vessels that provide nutrients for the eye. Why is the choroid coat
   dark?


10. Use the forceps to carefully peel the choroid coat from the sclera and
   place it on the parts identification sheet.

11. You have now removed everything from the back half of the sclera.
   Place it on the parts identification sheet.

12. Pick up the front half of the sclera that contains the cornea, iris and lens.
   Remove the lens with the forceps.

13. When you remove the lens, you should notice a watery fluid between the
   lens and the cornea. This is the aqueous humour. What is its function?


14.   Look at the lens. Is it concave or convex?

15.   Gently squeeze the lens. Why is it important that the lens is flexible?

16.   Place the lens on the newspaper. What do you notice about the writing?

17.   Place the lens on the parts identification sheet.

18. Use your fingers to carefully remove the iris. When you look at the iris
   closely, you should be able to see thin lines. These are the muscles that
   cause the iris to contract or dilate. Draw the iris in the space below.




19.   What is the purpose of the iris?


20.   What is the hole in the iris called?

21.   Is the iris transparent, translucent or opaque?

22.   Place the iris on the parts identification sheet.

23.   Cut the cornea out of the sclera. What is the purpose of the cornea?

24. With your scalpel, cut through part of the cornea. You should feel and
   hear it crunch. The cornea is made of multiple layers to make it thick and
   strong. Why must the cornea be tough, especially in grazing animals such
   as the cow?


25.   Place the cornea on the parts identifications sheet.

LESSON 4 E&C                     SWITCHED ON




           AIM OF THE LESSON


During this lesson students will:
          Explore the concept of flow of electricity in simple circuit and how this can be
           controlled using switches.
          State that adding more batteries make globes shine brighter.


           EQUIPMENT


Per Class
          masking tape
          a bag of lollies e.g. M&Ms

Per Group
          2 D batteries (1.5 volts) per group
          3 lengths (15cms) of insulated copper wire with about 1cm of insulation removed
           at each end
          1 small globe (have spares)
          pop sticks for supporting batteries
          blu-tac
          alfoil
          4 drawing pins
          4 large paper clips
          2 split pins
          1 sponge cut in half (optional for extension)

Preparation
          Extension: cut sponges in half and cut a small square from the middle of each
           using a Stanley trimmer. The squares should be a uniform size i.e. 3cm x 3cm.
Safety
           Mains electricity must not be used.
     BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR TEACHERS


   Electrons flow from the negative end of the battery.
   As each electron move through a conductor, it pushes on the one ahead of it,
    such that all the electrons move together as a group.




   The tube is full of marbles, just as a conductor is full of electrons. If a single
    marble is inserted into this full tube on the left-hand side, another marble will
    immediately try to exit the tube on the right.
   Light globes consist of a glass bulb, which has a filament in between the two
    wires which go into and out of it. The filament is made from a very thin wire,
    which has a high resistance to electricity.
   This resistance causes the filament to heat up and glow when electricity
    passes through it.
   The electric current travels along the wire, enters the filament, heats up the
    filament, creates light and exits the globe through the other wire.
   The light that is seen from the light globe is the glow of the filament.
   Voltage e.g. 1.5 volts is a measure of how much energy each electron is given
    by the battery.
   A pressure switch is shown below that is suggested in the extension activity.
       LESSON OUTLINE



1. Introduction (Engaging Students)
 Take students outside.
 Have all students stand in a circle arms distance apart. They are the carriers of
   electricity (electrons). They release their arms once in position.
 Nominate two students to be the battery, they form an arch with their arms held
   high for students to walk though.
 Nominate a student to stand next to the battery and hold a bowl of M&Ms or
   similar at the edge of the circle.
 Nominate two students to be the light, they form an arch with arms together out at
   waist height. Students need to bend down to pass through.
   The students are given an M&M as they pass the battery as energy. They then use
   some of this energy to get under the arch of the light and they must keep some of the
   M&M in their mouth to make it back to the battery to be given more energy. The
   students must walk around the circle and always stay an arms width apart.
  This represents the flow of electricity in a simple circuit.

 pass through the globe.                                and heat.

 What did the lollies represent?
                                                        battery. Chemical energy that you

     Write down the aim, equipment and method for the activity.
     Students to set up a circuit using two batteries, one globe and three wires until

     Tape the working circuit onto the desk or a sheet of card. (optional but makes it

title: EXP-How Sound Travels
subject: Science
searchText:
How Sound Travels


Objectives:

1. To demonstrate that sound moves through different states of matter.

2. To observe that sound moves better through a solid than it does through a
  liquid or a gas.

Materials needed:

Demo: bell, tuning fork, cork, balloon, two spoons, musical triangle, slide
   whistle, two wood blocks, windup clock, 12" ruler, large jar filled
   with water, paper bag, metal can and lid, plastic container with lid,
   metal bar, music box motor.

Each group needs: meter stick, windup clock, self-sealing plastic bag filled
    with water, a block of wood (the same thickness as the plastic bag of
    water), two plastic cups with one end of a string through the hole in
    the bottom of one cup and the other end of the string through the hole
    in the bottom of the other cup. Knot the ends of the string to stop it
    from pulling out of the holes (home-made telephone), a third plastic cup
    with a string attached to the bottom of the cup, a metal rod.

Strategy:

Have the children identify different sounds made behind a screen (or desk) by
using various materials: ringing a bell, hitting a tuning fork on a cork,
blowing up a balloon and releasing air by stretching the neck of the balloon as
the air escapes, tapping two spoons together, striking the musical triangle,
blowing a slide whistle, hitting two wooden blocks together and ringing an
alarm clock. Record the children's answers on the board. Show the materials
used and check against the predictions made.

Hold a ruler over the edge of a desk and vibrate it asking such questions as:
What is happening? What is your evidence? What is always happening to an
object when it is making a sound?

Strike a tuning fork on a cork and quickly lower it into a glass of water.
Ask the questions stated above. Does sound travel through other things?

Activities:

Demo: Does sound travel through paper? through plastic? through metal?
   1. Put a ringing alarm clock in a paper bag.
   2. Close the bag. Can you hear the clock ringing now?
   3. Repeat steps 1 and 2 using a plastic container and a metal can.

    Does sound travel through water?
    1. Fill a glass jar nearly full of water.
    2. Have one student cover one ear with her/his hand. Put the other
      ear against the glass jar.
    3. Ask another student to hit two spoons together under water.
      Do you hear a sound?

Sound travels through different kinds of matter. Sound travels through gases,
liquids and solids.

Group: What kind of matter does sound travel best in--air, water, wood or
    metal?
  A. 1. Hold a plastic bag of water against one of your ears. Cover
       your other ear with your hand. Have someone hold a ticking
       clock against the bag of water. Listen.
    2. Keep the clock in the same place. Remove the bag of water. Listen.
    3. Place a block of wood between your ear and the clock. Listen.
       Do you hear the clock best through the air, the water or the wood?
   B. 1. Place the clock 20 cm away from your ear and listen to the ticking.
    2. Have your partner hold the clock at the 20-cm mark on the meter
       stick. Place your ear at the end of the meter stick and listen.
    3. Have your partner hold a metal rod to your ear and place the clock
       against the rod 20 cm away from your ear. Listen. Does sound move
       differently through some solids than it does through others?

  C. 1. Take the plastic cups (telephone) and hold your cup to your ear
       while your friend talks slowly and clearly into the other cup. Keep
       the string tight. How does it work? What is vibrating? How do the
       vibrations of your friend's voice reach your ear?
    2. Can a third person talk and listen if another cup with a string is
       attached? Take the separate cup with the string and attach it to
       the first line. Keep all strings tight while one friend talks into
       one cup and the other two friends listen. Can you hear the message
       of the third party? How many lines could you attach? Does each
       addition weaken the vibrations?

Draw three squares on the board and in each square draw molecules spaced
accordingly to illustrate the three states of matter: gas (molecules far
apart), liquid (molecules closer together) and solid (molecules closest
together). Have students identify the different states of matter for each
square.

Finally, take the small music box motor, hold it in your hand and allow the
music to play. Ask the students if they hear the music. Now place the music
box motor on top of your desk or on a large surface area and listen to the
melody. Is there any difference? Can the students hear the music now? Why?

searchText:
Investigating sounds
Aim

To investigate a number of different ways in which sounds are produced.
Equipment

Activity A
_ tuning forks of different frequencies
_ large rubber bung
_ ping-pong ball hanging on a thread
_ clamp stand

Activity B
_ board with six nails and elastic bands stretched between them

What to do
Carry out the experiments below, and for each one answer these three questions.
1 What is producing the sound?
2 How can the sound be made louder or softer?
3 How can the sound be made higher pitched or lower pitched?

A The tuning fork

Hold the tuning fork by the stem and hit one prong firmly against the rubber bung. Look
closely at the fork. What is happening while it is making the sound?
Sound the tuning fork again and touch one prong against the hanging ping-pong ball.
What happens to the ball?
Hit the rubber bung softly with the fork, so it just makes a sound, and then touch the
ping-pong ball again. Is there any difference between hitting the tuning fork firmly and
softly?
Sound a different sized tuning fork. Is the note higher or lower than with the first tuning
fork?




B The rubber band
Wearing goggles, pluck one of the rubber bands sideways and look closely at the band
while it is making the sound. What does it do?
 Pluck the other rubber bands. What difference do you notice in the sound? Can you see
a pattern? (The longer the band, the . . . )
Try plucking the same rubber band softly and then firmly. Is there a difference in the
sound?

What to do
Carry out the experiments below, and for each one answer these three questions.
1 What is producing the sound?
2 How can the sound be made louder or softer?
3 How can the sound be made higher pitched or lower pitched?

C The ruler

Hold the ruler down on the bench so that your hand is about 3 cm in from the
edge of the bench and about 20 cm of ruler extends over the edge of the bench.
Push the end of the ruler down slightly and let go. Does the ruler make a sound?
How does it move to make the sound?
Try again, but push the ruler down a bit more this time. Does the sound get louder or
softer?
Try again, but move the ruler so the amount hanging over the end of the bench is
shorter. Does the sound get higher or lower?




D Drinking straw pipes

Flatten about 2 cm of the end of a drinking straw. Cut the tapered end so that it makes a
point, like this:




Put this cut end into your mouth and blow.

Does it make a sound? What do you feel?
Practise with the straw until you can remember the sound. Can you change the
loudness?
Cut off 2 cm of the rounded end of the straw to make it shorter. Blow into the pointed
end again. Has the sound changed? Is it higher or lower?

title: EXP-Loud Music Causes Hearing Loss
subject: Science
searchText:
Loud Music Causes Hearing Loss
It is not uncommon among concertgoers to leave a concert unable to
hear. In most cases their hearing returns shortly. Unfortunately,
permanent hearing loss from loud concerts is becoming increasingly
common. The situation can be even more serious for musicians,
because they suffer more frequent and prolonged exposure to loud
music than most people. It can also be more devastating for a
musician to lose his hearing, because his livelihood and passion often
leave with his hearing.

Sound levels at concerts can be in the range of 120 to 140 db, well
beyond the 100 db normally recognized as the threshold at which
short-duration exposure can cause hearing loss. The loss is caused by
damage to fragile tissue strands within the cochlea. These strands are
called hair cells and resemble tiny hairs. They move with the fluid in
the cochlea to stimulate the electrical impulses in the auditory nerve.
The hair cells become damaged in the presence of loud noise.

The mechanism of damage is much like the mechanism by which
constant walking on grass can damage it. A person walking on a lawn
occasionally doesn't damage the lawn, because the grass has a
chance to recover between tramplings. But if the grass is subjected to
frequent traffic, it soon loses its ability to spring back and becomes
permanently damaged. Damage to the hair cells occurs the same way.
The louder and more frequent the exposure to loud noise, the more
damage the hair cells sustain.

Fortunately, our ears often warn us when we have subjected them to
potentially damaging sound levels. Temporary hearing loss is one
indication; ringing in the ears is another. If you experience either of
these symptoms after exposure to loud sounds, it's an almost sure
indication of temporary damage that could become permanent with
repeated exposure.

For people who are unable or unwilling to remove themselves from
noisy situations, earplugs can help preserve hearing. Earplugs are
especially effective at reducing the intensity of high frequency sound,
which is what does the most damage to the hair cells. A 15 or 20 db
reduction in the intensity of high frequency sound can delay or prevent
hair cell damage.

searchText:
Juliette M. Walker - Crown Community Academy



Now Hear This!

Juliette M. Walker        Crown Community Academy
751 E. 84st. Apt#2e         2128 S. St.Louis
CHICAGO IL 60619            CHICAGO IL 60623
(773) 488-3157            (773) 534-1680

Objective(s):

In this project, students will be able to describe how sounds are heard by the
human ear by creating a model of the human inner ear. This activity may be
utilized by grades 3 - 8.


Materials Needed:

Students may be placed into cooperative learning groups of 3.
 1long paper roll (used gift wrap rolls are perfect)
 plastic wrap        medium sized disc of foil rubber bands
 2cardboard paper discs doublestick tape             pink tissue paper
 flashlights        1 large box scissors       cardboard fork shape
(1 set of each item is needed for each group)

Strategy:

1. Students will create an eardrum by stretching a piece of plastic wrap across
  the end of the paper roll fixing it in place with a rubber band.
2. Students will create a set of ossicles with two cardboard discs and a fork
  shape of thin cardboard. This will be held together with doublesided tape.
3. Students will then attach a disk of shiny foil to one end of the roll, and
  will attach the other to the plastic wrap "ear drum" on the tube. This will
  complete the middle ear.
4. Students will then make an outer ear from a cone of cardboard with a hole
  at its end and will place it on the inside of the tube. Students may design
  their cone with pink tissue paper, for a more realistic look.
5. Students will then place the middle of the model of the ear on a box,
  leaving the ends of the rolls hanging off of the front and back.
6. Students will then shine a light onto the mirror and will ask a partner to
  to talk into the ear and watch for vibrations.
7. Have the students to watch the window of the ear. Have them describe how it
  responds to shouting, whispering, whistling etc.

Performance Assessment:

Students will be evaluated based upon their models, and oral explanations as
to how their ear works.

Conclusions:

This project works because the sound waves from the students voice makes the
plastic wrap vibrate. These vibrations are transmitted into the cardboard
"ossicles" and can be seen by watching the foil disc for movements. This is
a simple model of how the ear works.

References:

This project was adapted from the Encyclopedia of Science Projects written by
Pam Robeson, and Mick Seller (Shooting Star Press, 1994) (Aladdin Books, ltd,
1994)

title: EXP-Making Waves
subject: Science
searchText:
Waves


Objectives:

Students will be able to define, label and demonstrate the following vocabulary words: wave, wave motion,
longitudinal wave, transverse wave, pulse, crest, energy trough, amplitude, frequency, reflection,
Rarefaction, refraction and compression. Students will be able to state the properties that a medium must
possess in order that waves may be transmitted through it. Students will be able to tell the essential
difference between a longitudinal and a transverse wave. Students will be able to know how to make a
longitudinal or compress ional pulse and a transverse pulse. Students will be able to determine the time it
takes a pulse to travel down the rope or a slinky. Students will be able to understand that a wave is a
means of transmitting energy.

Apparatus Needed:

Marbles, grooved ruler or stick, hose or rope, large pan of water, cork, small stone, ripple tank, medicine
dropper, overhead projector, coil spring, meterstick, watch, slinky, string or fishing line, smooth pole or
stiff wire, curtain rings, movies

Recommended:

1. Place five or six marbles in a groove so that they touch each other. Roll another marble against the end
of the line of marbles. The vibration of waves will be transmitted through the line and the marbles on the
end will roll away. Roll two, then three and so on. Observe what happens.
2. Move the hose or rope up and down to make transverse waves. Drop the stone into the water. Observe
what happens.

3. Fill the flat pan about half full of water. Place the pan on an
overhead projector or tabletop. Fill a medicine dropper with water.
Allow one drop of water to fall into the center of the pan. Allow
another drop to fall near the edge. Notice what happens in each.
Sketch the pattern of waves that are seen.

4. Move a rope up and down. Describe and explain what kind of waves is observed. Cut equal-lengths of
string at least one meter long. Tie a curtain ring to one end of each string. Attach the free end of a piece
of string to every fifth coil of the slinky. Slip the curtain rings onto the pole [or wire], and then suspend it
from the ceiling. Observe: send a longitudinal pulse down the spring by pinching together several coils of
the spring and then releasing them. What kind of pulse is this? [Longitudinal or compress ional] What
happens to the shape of the pulse as it travels down the wire?
 Quickly pull the free end of the slinky to one side and then return it to its original position. What kind of
pulse is this? What happens to the shape of the pulse as it travels down the string? Determine the time it
takes a pulse to travel down the string. Change the amplitude of the pulse and again determine the travel
time. How does changing the amplitude affect the speed of the wave?
Change the medium by stretching the spring to a different length. Determine the speed of a pulse in this
new medium. How does changing the medium affect the speed of a wave?

searchText:
Reflection in a Plane Mirror
Aim: To investigate the law of reflection

Equipment: Hodson light box                 Plane mirror
           Single Slit Slide                Ruler
           Power pack                       Protractor
           Sharp pencil

Diagram of Equipment Set-up




Procedure
   1. Place the single slit slide in the end of the Hodson light box closest to the light source.
   2. Connect the Hodson light box to the AC terminals of the power pack, set the voltage to
      12 V and plug the power pack into the wall.
   3. Place the mirror on the line below.
   4. Shine the light ray onto the mirror so that it hits the mirror at the black dot.
   5. Mark the path of the incident ray and reflected ray by placing three dots along each ray,
      then use a ruler to connect the dots.
   6. Mark the incident ray, i1, and the reflected ray, r1.
   7. Repeat this for 5 other angles, making sure the light ray hits the mirror at the cross and
      labelling the incident and reflected rays as you go. (i2, r2, i3, etc)

Results
 Processing of Results
   1. Draw a line perpendicular to the mirror, starting at the black dot. This is the normal.
   2. Measure the angle between the normal and incident ray 1 and record it in the table.
   3. Measure the angle between the normal and reflected ray 1 and record it in the table.
   4. Repeat for all rays of incidence and reflection.

                              Angle of Incidence     Angle of Reflection
                  Ray 1
                  Ray 2
                  Ray 3
                  Ray 4
                  Ray 5
                  Ray 6


Questions

   1. What is the Law of Reflection?




   2. Do your experimental results support the Law of Reflection? Give a reason for your
      decision.




   3. Describe ways in which you could improve the results of your experiment.




   4. Give two examples where you have observed the Law of Reflection in action.

LESSON 3 E&C SIMPLE CURCUITS




           AIM OF THE LESSON


During this lesson students will:
             Explain the importance of electricity in everyday life.
             Explore the concept of a circuit using a battery, copper wire and a globe.
             Describe that batteries have stored energy that is changed into electricity in
              circuits.


           EQUIPMENT


Per Class
            roll of copper wire
            masking tape

Per Group
            2 D batteries (1.5 volts)
            2 lengths (15cms) of insulated copper wire with about 1cm of insulation
             removed at each end
            1 small globe (have some spares)
            2 pop sticks for supporting batteries
            blu-tac


Preparation
            Cut the copper wire into 15 cm lengths and remove approximately one cm of
             insulation at each end (later activities require four lengths per group).
            Globe holders and battery holders are useful for these activities if available.

Safety
          Mains electricity must not be used.
     BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR TEACHERS


   In order for electricity to travel to where it is needed, there must be a complete
    circuit or path.
   A complete circuit is like a circle. No circuit will work if it has a break in it.

   A switch can be used to provide a break in a circuit.

   For an electrical appliance such as a light globe to work, it must be joined with
    conductors (such as copper wires) to make the circuit work.
   A complete circuit must have an energy source (a battery or power source) to
    make an electrical appliance work.
   An electrical circuit can be made stronger by adding more batteries. This will
    make the globe shine brighter in a circuit.
   A battery is a device that produces electricity from a chemical reaction.
   A battery has a negative and a positive end (electrodes).
   Electrons flow from the negative end of the battery.

LESSON 10 E&C                    BUILD A LIGHTHOUSE




         AIM OF THE LESSON


   During this lesson students will:
            Apply their understanding of simple circuits, batteries, copper wire and a
             globe to construct a lighthouse.
            Use conductors and switches to construct a lighthouse.
            Design a simple pressure switch for the lighthouse circuit.



         EQUIPMENT


   Per Class
        Blu-tac, Glue, sticky tape
        Scissors
        Elastic bands, pegs


   Per Group
        2 D batteries (1.5 volts)
        3 lengths (15cms) of insulated copper wire with about 1cm of insulation removed
         at each end
        1 small globe (have some spares)
        12 sheets of A4 paper (recycled)
        1 m of alfoil
        paper clips or split pins


Preparation
    Nil


Safety
    Nil
        BACKGROUND INFORMATION FOR TEACHERS


Lighthouse features

      A lighthouse is a building that was made to guide ships. The most important part
       of a lighthouse is the light that it casts at night. Sometimes lighthouses guide
       ships to a port or harbour. Other times they guide ships away from a hazard.
       Sometimes they do both.
      At night, lighthouses guide ships with their light. All ships have a book, called a
       Light List, which tells them the characteristics of lighthouses. If a mariner saw a
       white light flashing every seven-and-a -half seconds, he could look it up and find
       out which lighthouse it is.
      During the day, lighthouses guide ships with a day mark. A lighthouse's day
       mark is simply its size, shape and colour.




Lighthouses in Western Australia


   A few of the well known light houses in WA include:
    Rottnest Island
    Cape Naturaliste, Dunsborough
    Cape Leeuwin, Augusta
    Fremantle North Mole (red)
    Cape Leveque
    Fremantle South Mole (green)




Diagram of Lighthouse
    The two main challenges are:
        Making the tower 50cms and free standing. A tripod shape with three
           legs also works well. These legs can be made of rolled up paper.

        Making the circuit from the battery at the bottom of the lighthouse to the
           globe at the top.

searchText:
Sound is Vibration


Objectives:

This lesson is designed for grade levels 1 - 3.
1. To understand that sound is caused by vibration.
2. To understand that sound travels through solids, liquids and gases.
3. To understand that high pitched sounds are caused by more vibrations and low
  pitched sounds are caused by fewer vibrations.

Materials Needed:

plastic ruler(s), tuning forks of 2 or 3 different pitches, ping-pong ball
attached to a string with tape, boom-box-type radio, balloon filled with air,
paper plate, tiny pieces of torn paper, baggie filled with water, scissors,
several glass bottles of the same size, large container for water, styrofoam
cups, wire coat hangers, string (different types), wire cutters, pencils (with
wooden ball attached to the eraser end if possible), stopwatch, flower pots of
varying sizes attached to rope, long tubes of PVC pipe cut to different lengths
for different tones, xylophone, plastic straws, tape.

Strategy:

1. Ask children if anyone knows what a vibration is. Ask children to vibrate
their bodies. Write vibrate on board. Put a plastic ruler overhanging the edge
of a table; hit the ruler and watch it vibrate. Ask: "Can we see the vibration?
Can we hear the vibration? Can we feel it?" Show tuning fork; hit; listen;
touch vibrating tuning fork to ping pong ball attached to a string. Observe the
effect; ask same questions. Pass tuning forks around so children can experience
the sound and feel the vibration; note differences in pitch. Hold inflated
balloon in front of boom-box speaker with volume turned up loud. "Can you feel
the vibration? Where is it coming from?" Place small paper plate with tiny
pieces of paper on it on top of speaker. (Boombox must be turned so that
speakers are facing up.) Observe what happens to the papers. Explain that all
sounds are caused by something vibrating; sound is vibration, etc.

2. How do vibrations from tuning fork and ruler reach us as sound? The
vibrations cause waves to carry sound through the air. (You will perhaps need
to discuss waves, depending on age and experience of children.) "We know
sound
travels through air. Does it travel through a solid? Put your ear on the desk.
Tap the desk. What do you hear?" Try several such examples. "Does sound
travel through a liquid?" Get children to talk about experiences they have had
such as talking underwater in the bathtub or swimming pool. Can they hear
sound
under water? "Try putting a plastic baggie filled with water next to your ear.
Have another child speak loudly directly into the other side of the baggie. Can
we hear the sound through the water? Does sound travel through a solid, a
liquid, and a gas (air)? When was it the loudest?" (through the solid) "Why
do you think this may be true?" (The molecules in a solid are more tightly
packed, so the vibration can travel without being dispersed as it does in air.)

3. Show a child's xylophone or an autoharp. Strike a short bar, then a long bar
and ask children what they heard. Do the same for the lengths of PVC pipe.
(Hit the end of the pipes with the palm of your hand.) Make a kazoo out of a
plastic straw by flattening one end and cutting it into a triangular shape;
blow. As one person blows through the kazoo, another takes a scissors and snips
an inch or so off the end. Keep doing this and ask the students to notice
 what's happening to the sound as the straw gets shorter. Help them relate the
shortness of length to high pitch through a variety of such experiences.

4. Now allow the children to experiment and "play" with all the materials so
that they develop strong physical understanding of vibrations in all the ways
that have been presented. Have a set of 8 identical bottles and a container of
water and have them fill the bottles with varying amounts of water. See if they
can match the scale of the bottles to that of the xylophone. Give children the
opportunity to make a string phone or wire-hanger chime. (Tie a length of
string to each end of a wire coat hanger. Put the other end of each string in
your ears, tap the hanger against something like a desk. Listen for the ringing
through the string.)

Performance Assessment:

1. Children must: Arrange bottles with varying amounts of water in row
according to pitch. Explain the relationship between the amount of water and
the pitch. Tell what is vibrating. Blow across or just into the top of each
bottle and explain how the relationship between pitch and the amount of water in
the bottle changes. Hypothesize as to why this might be.

2. Make a stereo coat hanger as explained above. Tell how you might make one
with a higher pitch (shorter wire). Cut hanger with wire cutter to get
different lengths and different pitches.

3. Make a straw kazoo. Listen to its pitch. Have your partner cut off an inch
or two with a scissors while you are blowing. What happens to the sound? Cut
off another inch. What do you notice now?

4. Listen to the sound of each tuning fork. (Strike tuning fork on your shoe

title: Gamma ray
reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: Gamma ray 1 Gamma ray Gamma rays (γ-rays) are electromagnetic waves with the smallest wavelengths in the electromagnetic spectrum.[1] They were discovered in 1900 by Paul Villard, and named in 1903 by Ernest Rutherford. Gamma rays are like x-rays, but the waves are smaller. Both gamma rays and x-rays are photons with very high energies, and gamma have even more energy. They are also a type of ionizing radiation. Gamma rays can travel through thicker materials than x-rays can. Gamma rays are produced by some types of radioactive atoms. Cobalt-60 and potassium-40 are two isotopes that emit gamma rays. Cobalt-60 is created in accelerators and is used in hospitals. Potassium-40 occurs naturally. Small amounts of potassium-40 are in all plants and animals. Gamma rays from potassium-40 each have an energy of 1460 thousand electron volts (keV). Gamma rays and X-rays can also be distinguished by their origin: X-rays are emitted by electrons outside the nucleus, while gamma rays are emitted by the nucleus.[2] Gamma rays in medicine Gamma rays can also go through the skin to kill cells, such as cancerous cells. Doctors can use radiation therapy machines which produce gamma rays in hospitals to treat people with some types of cancer.[] Doctors also use gamma rays to find disease. In hospitals, doctors can give patients radioactive medicine which emits gamma rays. Doctors can find some types of disease by measuring gamma rays which come from a patient afterward. You can also use gamma rays to sterilise (clean) hospital material.[] References [1] The electromagnetic spectrum is made of many types of waves that are like light, but you can not see all of them. [2] Feynman, Richard; Robert Leighton, Matthew Sands 1963. The Feynman Lectures on Physics, vol 1. USA: Addison-Wesley. pp2–5 ISBN 0201021161. title: Health Effects of Noise
reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: ﻿Health Effects of Noise Noise Exposure Noise is perhaps the most common occupational and environmental hazard. As many as 30 million Australians are exposed to potentially harmful sound levels in their workplaces. Outside of work, many people pursue recreational activities that can produce harmful noise. Non-occupational sources of noise include chain saws and other power tools, amplified music, and recreational vehicles such as motorcycles. Some types of toys for children can produce sounds capable of causing permanent hearing damage. Common Sources of Noise Sound Loudness (dB) Gunshot (peak level) 140 to 170 Jet takeoff 140 Rock concert, chain saw 110 to 120 Diesel locomotive, stereo headphones 110 to 120 Motorcycle, lawnmower 90 Conversation 60 Quiet room 50 Whisper 30 to 40 Noise can be described in terms of intensity (perceived as loudness) and frequency (perceived as pitch). Both the intensity and the duration of noise exposure determine the potential for damage to the hair cells of the inner ear. Even sounds perceived as "comfortably" loud can be harmful. Sound intensity is measured as the sound pressure level in the decibel (dB) scale. Noise can cause permanent hearing loss at chronic exposures equal to an average of 85 dB or higher for an eight-hour period. The decibel scale is a logarithmic scale. A 3-dB increase represents a doubling of the sound intensity. Four hours of noise exposure at 88 dB(A) is considered to provide the same noise "dose" as eight hours at 85 dB and a single gunshot, which is approximately 140 to 170 dB, has the same sound energy as 40 hours of 90-dB noise. Health Effects When sounds are measured in decibels, the softest sounds we can hear are about 1 dB and extremely loud sounds are about 150 dB. Most people find sounds louder than 130 dB very painful. To reduce the risks of hearing damage, workers in noisy jobs are now required to wear protective ear muffs. The cabins of noisy machinery are insulated to reduce noise. Apart from deafness, another common hearing problem caused by too much noise exposure is tinnitus. This is when you hear a constant ringing sound in your ears.

reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: Infrared 1 Infrared Infrared (IR) radiation is a type of electromagnetic radiation (a wave with electricity) . The wave is longer than light which humans can see and shorter than microwaves. The word infrared means below red. It comes from the Latin word infra (meaning below) and the English word red. (Infrared light has a frequency below the frequency of red light.) Red light has the longest wavelength that human eyes can see. Picture of dog in mid-infrared Infrared waves cannot be seen by the eye. The infrared wave is between 750 nm and 1 mm. People sense infrared as heat. Most remote controls use infrared to send the control signals. Telecommunications Before Bluetooth was invented, some computers, personal digital assistants, and mobile phones were using the infrared technology to send files to other devices. Bluetooth replaced infrared in the early 2000's. Infrared is limited by the need to have both devices in a "line of sight" with each other.[1] Infrared lasers are used to provide the light for optical fiber communications systems. Infrared light with a wavelength around 1,330 nm (least dispersion) or 1,550 nm (best transmission) are the best choices for standard silica fibers. Spectroscopy Infrared vibrational spectroscopy (IR spectroscopy) can be used to identify molecules by listing their chemical bonds. An IR spectrometer is a machine that shines infrared light from a set range of frequencies on a sample. It measures which exact light frequencies are absorbed by the sample. Each chemical bond in a molecule vibrates at a frequency which is characteristic of that bond. A group of atoms in a molecule may have multiple modes of oscillation caused by the stretching and bending motions of the group as a whole. If an oscillation leads to a change in dipole in the molecule, then it will absorb a photon which has the same frequency. The vibrational frequencies of most molecules correspond to the frequencies of infrared light. Typically, the technique is used to study organic compounds using light radiation from 4000–400 cm−1, the mid-infrared. The spectrometer records all the frequencies of absorption in a sample. This can be used to gain information about the sample composition in terms of chemical groups present and also its purity (for example a wet sample will show a broad O-H absorption around 3200 cm−1). title: Joes Eye and questions
subject: Science
searchText:
Eye
For concentrated complexities, no other organ in Joe's body can equal me. No larger than a Ping-Pong ball, I have tens of millions of
electrical connections and can handle 1.5 million simultaneous messages. I gather 80 percent of all the knowledge Joe absorbs. He
thinks of me as a miniature television camera. I consider the comparison insulting. I am much more sensitive than the biggest, costliest
TV camera ever made. I am responsible for one of the greatest of all miracles - sight.

Today's world is giving me a hard time. I was not built for it. For Joe's prehistoric ancestors, the eye's main job was to see things at a
distance danger to be avoided, game to be killed. Only lately have I been called on for continuous close-up work.

Look at my anatomy and you will understand why I am having difficulty adjusting to today's demands. First, my front window - my
clear, 20 cent size cornea. It starts the seeing process by bending light rays into orderly patterns. Next, my pupil - an adjustable gateway
for light. In bright sun it is nearly closed; on a dark night it is wide open. Up to this point there is nothing about seeing that a cheap
camera could not handle.

My wonders really begin with my lens-a little envelope of fluid the size and shape of an oval vitamin pill. My lens is surrounded by a
ring of tiny, superbly strong, unbelievably hard-working muscles. When they tense, my lens fattens for near vision; when they relax, it
flattens for distant vision. This was a fine arrangement for Joe's caveman ancestors. Since they were mainly interested in things six or
more meters away, the muscles were relaxed most of the time. But Joe now lives in a close-up world-lots of reading, deskwork and
such. This keeps my ciliary muscles tensed a lot of the time. They grow tired.
In front of and behind my lens I have two fluid-filled chambers In front the fluid is like water; in back it is about the consistency of
egg white. The watery fluid keeps me firmly inflated. Both fluids must be absolutely clear to permit passage of light. Those "specks"
Joe sees when he looks at a bright light are cellular remnants left over from his days in the womb when I was under construction.
They will float aimlessly in his eye fluid as long as he lives.

When Joe looks at some object, the light passes through my lens, which brings it into correct focus on my retina, a kind of onionskin
wallpaper, which covers the rear two thirds of my interior. Except in Joe's brain, I do not think that
anywhere else in his body is so much packed into so small a space. Covering less than three-square centimeters, my retina
contains 137 million light-sensitive receptor cells 130 million shaped like rods for black-and-white vision, seven million shaped like
cones for color vision.

The rods are scattered all over my retina. Let a firefly pass at night and a complex chemistry gets under way. The faint light bleaches
rhodopsin, a purplish-red pigment in my rods. The bleaching process generates a tiny wisp of electricity--a few millionths of a volt, far
 too little to tickle a mosquito. This feeds into my straw-size optic nerve and is transmitted to Joe's brain at about 450 km. per hour. The
brain interprets the signals flooding in and hands down its verdict: a firefly. All of this intricate electrochemical activity has been
completed in about .002 second!

If my rods seem complex, my cones are far more so. They are concentrated in the fovea, a pinhead size, and yellowish depression at
the rear of my chamber. This is the center for acute vision - reading, any close work--and for color. A leading theory is that these
cones, too, have bleachable pigments, one each for red, green and blue. Like an artist mixing paints on a palette, Joe's brain blends
these colors to make scores of other hues. If anything should go wrong with this intricate electrochemical process, Joe would be -
color-blind--as one in eight men is to some degree. In dim light, activity of my cones diminishes, color sense vanishes and every thing
becomes gray, as my rods take over.

While Joe sees with me, he sees in his brain. A crushing blow at the back of his head, severe enough to destroy the optical center of his
brain, would produce permanent blindness. A lesser blow and he sees “stars” - a chaotic electrical disturbance. Joe gets clinching
evidence of the brain's role when he dreams. He "sees" pictures, even with my lids closed in total darkness. Had he been born blind, he
would dream in terms of other sensory stimuli: touch, sound, even smell.

Joe was not born with the eyes he has today. At birth he could see only light and shadow. In the first few months he was farsighted,
like his caveman ancestors. To study his rattle, he held it as far as possible from his face. At first, Joe's eyes were poorly coordinated;
I would wander in one direction, my partner in another. Our wandering worried Joe's mother. It
should not have. A few months after birth we were moving in exact unison. By the time Joe was six, his vision was excellent.
But my peak sight did not come until age eight.

When he was young, Joe used to read in dim light. His mother warned that he was "ruining" his eyes. Nonsense. The young see
better in dim light than adults; and viewing under even the most adverse circumstances does no harm.

I have a number of other unusual attributes. Tiny though they are, my muscles, milligram for milligram, are among the body's
strongest. In an average day, I move about 100,000 times - to bring objects into sharp focus. Joe would have to walk 80km to give
his leg muscles similar exercise.

My cleaning equipment is similarly striking. My lacrimal glands produce a steady stream of moisture--tears to flush away dust and
other foreign material. My eyelids, of course, act as windshield wipers. Joe blinks three to six times a minute- more when I am tired.
This keeps my cornea moist and clean. The tears also contain a potent microbe-killer called lysozyme, which guards me from infective
bacteria.
 I try to ward off fatigue by resting as much as possible. I get time oh when Joe blinks. And my partner and I spell each other for a
while I may carry 90 percent of the work load, while Joe's other eye loafs; then it goes to work and I rest.

Nature gave me superb protection, placing me in a bony cavern with protruding cheekbones and forehead to act as shock absorbers
for direct blows. She also gave me supersensitive nerves to activate the alarm if there should be a potentially damaging intruder such
as cinder.

Still, I do have my troubles. My focusing apparatus often fails to work perfectly. Eyeglasses can correct 95 percent of this trouble.
Disease is a more serious problem. One potential disorder is really a plumbing problem either too much fluid entering me or too little
draining away. Pressure builds up, reducing the blood supply to my optic nerve. This is
glaucoma.

In severe instances, glaucoma can cause permanent blindness in a few days. More often it is a leisurely performer, producing
symptoms so mild they are apt to go unnoticed. These symptoms: colored halos around bright lights, loss of side vision, difficulty in
adjusting to the dark, a blurring of vision. At his age, Joe has one chance in 40 of glaucoma damaging his sight or blinding him
completely. His doctor can check for glaucoma simply by pressing a little gadget called a tonometer against my eyeball. Joe should
have this test every year. The treatment for glaucoma? Drugs in drop
form, or surgery.

Astigmatism is another of my common ailments. In this one, my cornea is not a spherical surface and distorts vision like a bubble flaw
in a piece of glass. Eyeglasses correct this condition A detached retina is more serious. It occurs when my retinal wallpaper blisters or
peels, and usually announces itself with flashing lights, image distortion blurring spots. A surgeon can "tack" my wallpaper back in
place with 80 percent chance of success.

Both my cornea and my lens-normally totally transparent tissue--can cloud and lead to blindness. If it is the cornea, Joe can re gain
sight with a corneal transplant. If it is the lens, he will need a cataract operation, and either thick eyeglasses or contact lenses
afterward.

Fortunately, Joe has so far escaped all these things. Just the same, I am growing old--like Joe's other organs. The transparency of my
lens is lower, accommodation muscles are weaker, hardened arteries are diminishing blood supply to my retina. These processes will
continue, but Joe should not worry unduly. The odds are heavily in favor of my providing him with serviceable vision as long as he
lives.

                          3. What is the role of the retina?
                 4. What is the role of rods and cones in the eye?
                        5. Compare myopia with hyperopia.
                             6. What causes glaucoma?
                                 7. Why do we blink?

searchText: 2019 Version Light and Sound Junior Science What is light? Light is a form of energy that we can see and is given out by hot objects. It is made up of waves that travel outwards from a light source. Some of the waves reach our eyes, but most continue elsewhere. Waves can be transverse or longitudinal The two main types of wave form are transverse waves and longitudinal waves. All types of electromagnetic waves, including light, as well as water waves travel as transverse waves. Sound waves travel as longitudinal waves. Particle movement in transverse and longitudinal waves Longitudinal waves (sound) are a compressing and expanding wave that needs a medium to travel in. A medium could be gas, solid or liquid. Transverse waves (light) are a moving wave where each part of the wave travels up and down in repeating motion as the wave moves forward. These do not need a medium to travel through and can travel through empty space. Sound travels as a longitudinal wave Sound waves are mechanical waves requiring particles. (a medium to travel through) Air particles vibrate back and forward creating repeating patterns of high (compressed particles) and low (spaced apart particles) pressure. Sound travels in the form of longitudinal waves. One wave stretches from one compressed area of particles to the next. Waves of sound energy travel through air, water or solid. Waves generated from Earthquakes can be transverse or longitudinal The waves generated from an earthquake travel through the ground as both longitudinal and transverse waves. Primary (or P) waves are longitudinal waves and move the fastest. They are similar to sound waves and can travel at 5000 metres per second through solid rock. Longitudinal waves can also travel through liquid and gas, travelling at the speed of sound through air. Secondary (or S) waves are transverse waves and can only travel through solids. They travel at nearly half the speed of P waves. Waves transfer energy Waves are a means of transferring energy from one place to another without also transferring matter. Some waves need a medium (matter) to travel through in order to transport their energy from one location to another and are known as mechanical waves such as ocean waves, sound waves and earthquake waves. Other waves can travel through the vacuum of space where there is little or no atoms. These are know as electromagnetic waves. Examples of those waves include light waves, microwaves and radio waves. Electromagnetic radiation travels as waves Light and other types of electromagnetic radiation from the sun and even further away stars travel through space in a vacuum – Light does not need matter or a medium through which to travel. Each particular type of electromagnetic radiation, including each different colour of light, has a unique fixed length of wave, called the wavelength (λ), that it travels in. GZ Science Resources 8 Types of Electromagnetic radiation Some objects, such as the sun, release large amounts of energy. The energy can be emitted from the energy source in the form of electromagnetic radiation and travels in electromagnetic waves. Light, radio waves and x-rays are all forms of electromagnetic 9 radiation. GZ Science Resources Features of a wave Waves have troughs, the lowest point, and crests, the highest point. A wavelength is the distance between two closest crests. The amplitude of a wave is a measure of its height. The height is taken from a midpoint between a trough and a peak up to the top of a peak of a wave. A higher amplitude wave indicates a wave has more strength and that a light wave contains more photons, little packets of light energy. A nanometre is very small Small objects such as atoms, viruses and light waves need to be measured using very small units called a nanometre. A metre (m) can be divided into one thousand equal parts called millimetres (mm). If one millimetre is divided into a thousand equal parts then we have a micrometre (µm). If one micrometre is divided into a thousand parts then we have a nanometre (nm). A nanometre is one- billionth of a metre. Wavelengths can be measured in metres (m) or nanometres (nm). The type of electromagnetic radiation can be determined by its wavelength. 11 Frequency of a wave The frequency of a wave is calculated by the number of waves that pass by a fixed point in a given amount of time. The frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). Because all electromagnetic radiation travels at the same speed then more waves of shorter wavelength will pass by a point over the same time as waves of longer wavelength . wave speed = wavelength x frequency Waves always travel at the same speed. A scientific value that always remains the same is called a constant. The constant for the speed of light is c = 3x108 m/sec or 300,000 kilometres per second. Because we know the speed of light, if we know either the wavelength (λ) in metres or the frequency ( f ) in hertz then we can calculate the other. Wavelength = speed of light / frequency c Frequency = speed of light / wavelength λ f 13 Light energy is carried by photons The amount of energy in a wave depends upon the frequency of the wave. The energy of a photon can be calculated by multiplying the frequency by another constant called Planck’s constant (h). This constant is named after a famous German scientist called Max Planck who made many discoveries about light and how it also travels as particles called photons. A photon does not have mass like matter does, it only contains energy. Planck’s constant is 6.626 x 10-34 joules per second. This value is so small because a photon is so tiny but there are so many of them within a light wave. Structure and Function of the human ear Sound waves travel through the ear canal and cause the eardrum to vibrate. The small bones of the inner ear transfer this vibration to the inner ear cochlea. The cochlea is fluid filled and lined with many hair-like nerve cells. Different length nerve cells detect different wave frequencies and transmit this information to the brain using electrical impulses that move along the nerves. Audible range of humans and other animals Humans can hear between 20 – 20,000 Hertz, a measure of frequency. The frequency of a wave is calculated by the number of waves that pass by a fixed point in a given amount of time. In comparison to many other animals, humans have a very limited audible range. Bats and dolphins can hear and produce sound at an exceedingly high frequency – and use it to bounce back off objects as sonar to “see” without light. Low rumbling noises of elephants and moles are below our auditory range but can travel long distances. Pitch and Loudness of sound Sound can be described by “characteristics” called pitch and loudness. Pitch is related to frequency – the higher the frequency then the higher the pitch of the note (a single sound at a particular level). Loudness is related to amplitude – the higher the amplitude the louder the sound. Reflecting sound waves Sonar (originally an acronym for SOund Navigation And Ranging) is simply making use of an echo. When an animal or machine makes a noise, it sends sound waves into the environment around it. Those waves bounce off nearby objects, and some of them reflect back to the object that made the noise. Whales and specialized machines can use reflected waves to locate distant objects and sense their shape and movement. Total internal reflection When waves are going from a dense medium to a less dense medium they speed up at the boundary. This causes light rays to bend when they pass from glass to air at an angle other than 90º. This is refraction. Beyond a certain angle, called the critical angle, all the waves reflect back into the glass. We say that they are totally internally reflected. All light waves, which hit the surface beyond this critical angle, are effectively trapped. The critical angle for most glass is about 42 °. Fibre optics makes use of this so light rays can travel down a glass fibre that has curves in it. Light energy can travel as rays Light travels fast and in straight lines. At the speed of light, which is 300,000 kilometers per second, light from the sun takes about 8 minutes to travel 149 million kilometers to earth. Light can go around the earth 7 times in one second. Light travels perfectly straight, until something bends it. The straight paths of light are called light rays.. Gaze Light energy can be reflected, refracted or dispersed Light travels in a straight line until it strikes an object or a force. Light can be: 1. Reflected by a mirror 2. Refracted by a lens 3. Absorbed by the object Light interacts with matter by transmission (including refraction) which is travelling through it, absorption where it enters but doesn’t leave again, or scattering (including reflection) where it bounces off. To see an object, light from that object— emitted by or scattered from it— must enter the eye.                                  Light Energy
If you can read this, you are relying on light energy. Light energy and our eyesight are the
two things we need to be able to see; without one or the other there would be no sight.
Can you imagine what life would be like without light energy? Quite simply, there would
not be any life at all. Plants need light to live and if there were no plants, there would be no
animals, including people.


Sources of Light

Light energy is one of the forms of radiant energy that comes to us from
the Sun. This light energy is formed in nuclear reactions that occur within the Sun.
Other objects and substances can also give off their own light energy. These objects
are said to be luminous. The light carries energy away from luminous objects as
electromagnetic waves.

1.        Give examples of objects or substances that are luminous.




Many light sources emit light energy because they are hot. However, there are light sources which give out light without
getting hot. These include fluorescent tubes, the paint on the hand and numerals of clocks, fireflies and some deep sea
fish.

          not produce their own light.

How light travels

One scientific theory proposes that light energy travels in a wave motion. The light that we
can see has a wavelength of about th of a millimetre. Light energy travels at a speed of about
300 million metres per second.

                                        Earth, how long does it take light energy from the Sun
                                        to reach Earth?

example, light will travel in a straight line unless some other substance is placed in its path.

When light energy hits an object, several different things can happen. What happens depends on the substance making up
the object. Some substances allow light energy to pass through them. Other substances will not allow light energy to
pass through and either reflect (bounce off) or absorb the energy.

bounce off the object enable us to see it.

Absorption and reflection of light

Although sunlight appears to be white, it is not actually a single pure white colour. It is made up of seven different
colours that you can see, called the visible spectrum. The colours of the visible spectrum are red, orange, yellow, green,
indigo and violet. Each of these colours correspond to light of different wavelengths with red light having the longest
wavelength and violet light having the shortest wavelength.

Different materials absorb some of the colours in sunlight (white light) and reflect others. The colour we see in an object
depends on the colours that are reflected back to our eyes. For example, a yellow object absorbs all colours except
yellow, and it reflects yellow.

White objects appear white because they reflect all the colours of sunlight, but black objects appear black because they
absorb all the colours and reflect none.

When light energy meets a new substance, the light changes direction or bends. When light bends going from one
substance to another, we say that the light is refracted. The light bends when going from one substance to another
because it moves at different speeds through different materials. It travels slower through water and glass than it does
through air.

searchText: ﻿Heating Effect of an Electric Current High resistance in a conductor produces heat. Electrical energy is converted into heat energy Conductors which are long, have small diameters and have a high resistivity produce the most heat. Nichrome and tungsten metals have high resistances Appliances which convert electrical energy to heat are: electric heater (nichrome) light globe (tungsten) toaster (nichrome) electric kettle Magnetic Effect of an Electric Current A conductor carrying an electric current produces a magnetic field. When the conductor is wound on a soft iron core it is an electro magnet. The conductor only acts as a magnet as long as the current is flowing. Electro magnets have many varied uses: cranes, generators, motors

subject: Science
searchText: Microwave 1 Microwave A microwave is a kind of high-frequency radio wave. It is often used to cook food in a microwave oven. We can see waves travelling through water. There are many sorts of these waves, such as ripples, swell, tsunami, and even sound waves that we do not see, but we hear if our ears are under the water. Likewise, many different types of waves can travel through the air. We detect one type with our eyes as colours; we detect another type when it lands on our skin, as warmth; another type is called X-rays. Other types of these invisible waves are called microwaves. We cannot see them. They can quickly penetrate quite deep into materials that contain water, for example most food. The energy in these waves makes the water molecules vibrate faster, which means the water gets hotter. Although they can also heat some metals, there are materials, including many plastics, which they pass right through, without heating at all. Although many plastics used in bowls or cups will melt and get super-heated in microwave ovens. Mirrors and Lenses

Ray diagrams in a plane mirror
Ray diagrams are used to show an image of an object reflected in a mirror. Straight lines from the object are
drawn towards the mirror. Using the rule from the angle of incidence and reflection the lines are then reflected
back. Arrows are used on the lines to show the light rays’ direction.

The main rule for mirrors is that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.




                                                                           This means that the angle of the light ray
                                                                           between where it arrives and the
                                                                           perpendicular line called the normal, to
                                                                           where it hits on the surface of the mirror
                                                                           is the same angle it leaves and the same
                                                                           perpendicular (normal) line.




Convex and concave mirrors
Mirrors work because light is reflected from them. The three types of mirrors are:




The images in the plane mirrors are the same size, the right way up but laterally inverted (changed right to left)
and is a flat reflecting surface.

The images in the concave mirror are
   a) magnified and the right way up when you are near to the mirror
   b) smaller and upside down when you are further away from the mirror
The images in the convex mirror are reduced and the right way up

99 | P a g e    GZ Science Resources
 Ray diagrams in a concave mirror

                                                        With concave mirrors, light being reflected converges
                                                        (goes in an inward direction) towards the focal point
                                                        (x). From a distance, images appear upside down but
                                                        when brought nearer, image become larger in size
                                                        and appears right side up. A focal point is where
                                                        parallel rays meet.




Ray diagrams in a convex mirror

The image formed in a convex mirror is always
upright and smaller in size. The light rays
diverge (spread apart). The focal point is behind
the mirror where light rays do not actually pass
through.
