 Convex traffic safety mirrors are designed for road    Concave mirrors are commonly found in the head

 They are also used in car side mirrors to see a wide   the mirror

 Light can be Refracted by a lens
Refraction

A glass or plastic lens is transparent. This means that
light can be transmitted through the object without the
light being absorbed.

The medium of a plastic or glass lens has a different
optical density to air. Light rays entering the lens are
refracted to a different angle.

Refraction is when light travels between two optically
different (densities) mediums that bend light towards
or away from the normal.
Refraction in a glass block
                                       The ray of light bends or refracts inwards when it moves into the
                                       glass. This makes the angle of refraction smaller than the angle of
                                       incidence.

                                       When the ray emerges from the glass back into the air then it
                                       continues on a parallel path to the original ray.


                                       A medium is any space or substance which will allow light to travel
                                       through it called transmission. Examples of different media include
                                       air, water and glass. Each medium has different optical density. The
                                       optical density of a medium affects the speed at which light rays
                                       travel through. When a light ray passes from one medium into
                                       another (e.g. from air into water) it will change direction where two
                                       media meet. This ‘bending’ of light is called refraction and it always
                                       occurs when the two media have different optical densities.

subject: Science
searchText: Radio wave 1 Radio wave Radio waves make up part of the electromagnetic spectrum. These waves are packets of energy with differing wavelengths, similar to visible light waves, X-rays or Gamma rays, except longer. A radio wave, like other electromagnetic waves, is similar to an ocean wave or any other type of wave. Both types of wave have a hill and valley shape, repeating over and over. A wavelength is measured as the distance from the top of one crest to the top of its neighboring crest. While the wavelength of visible light is very very small, less than one micrometer and much less than the thickness of a human hair, radio waves can have a wavelength from a couple centimeters to several meters. Antennas designed to detect radio waves are usually similar in size to the wavelength they wish to detect. This is why many radio antennas (like those on cars) must be very long. If the antennas are not close to the size of the wavelength they do not usually do a good job of detecting the waves. Manmade radio waves have been used for a long time to send information, receive information, and to 'see' objects. Radar uses radio waves to 'see' distant objects by bouncing waves off an object and seeing how long it takes for the waves to return. Radar can even be used to find oil or see what chemicals are in soil. Radios also use these waves to send and receive information. Natural radio waves were first discovered in the 1930s by Karl Guthe Jansky, working for Bell Laboratories. Before his discovery, everyone thought only people could generate radio waves. Bell was detecting static on his radio channels, and had Jansky try to figure out where this static, or interference was coming from. Surprisingly, the interference was coming from space! This discovery eventually led astronomers to look at radio waves along with optical waves to find things in the sky. These radio astronomers use giant Radio telescopes, shaped like satellite dishes, to gather and analyze the waves. Uses Radio waves are used for many things today. They broadcast radio and television, communicate with satellites, let mobile phones communicate with each other, make radar systems, and allow computers to share information without wires. searchText:
Refraction
 Aim: To observe the relationship between angle of incidence and refraction


Equipment:
                                                         Safety Information
• Ray box
                                                         Filament bulb – risk of burns
• Single slit plate
                                                         Handle with extra care. Rinse any
• Lab pack (if needed)                                   burns under cold running water for
                                                         10 minutes and inform the teacher immediately.
• Protractor

• Pencil and ruler

• Paper




                Figure 1. Set-up



                                                                 Figure 2. Measurements


Method:
Step 1: Place the glass block flat in the middle of the paper and draw around it.

Step 2: Direct the light from the ray box onto one of the longer sides of the glass block, at a diagonal
angle.

Step 3: Trace over the ray as it leaves the ray box and enters the glass box (the incidence ray). You can
tidy up the line with the ruler afterwards.

Step 4: Trace over the ray as it leaves the glass block on the other side (the emergent ray). You can tidy
up the line with the ruler afterwards.


                                                 Page 1 of 2
                                                                                                 Refraction

Step 5: Remove the glass block and join the incidence and emergent rays with a straight line.

Step 6: Use the ruler and protractor to mark normal lines at the point where the incidence ray enters
the glass block, and the point where the emergent ray leaves the glass block.

Step 7: Measure the angle of incidence (A), angle of refraction (r) and angle of emergence (B). Record
these in the table.

Step 8: Repeat steps 1 to 7 for at least four different angles of incidence.


Results:


      Angle of Incidence                 Angle of Refraction                   Angle of Emergence




Questions:

1. Describe the relationship between the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction.

2. Describe the relationship between the angle of incidence and the angle of emergence.

3. What is the name of the type of wave by which light is transmitted?

4. Explain refraction in terms of density and wave speed.



                                                 Page 2 of 2
 Answers:
1. The angle of incidence is greater than the angle of refraction; A > r.

2. The angles of incidence and emergence are equal.

3. Transverse wave (electromagnetic spectrum wave).

4. The velocity of the light wave is decreased as it enters a denser medium (the glass block). As
   it enters at an angle, the ray is ‘bent’ (refracted). When the light ray emerges into the original
   medium again (air) it resumes the same velocity and angle as before it entered the glass block.

searchText:
Safety With Electricity
Below are two press articles which refer to electrical safety. Read the articles and answer
the questions which follow. You may need to refer to other sources for some of the
answers.


Schoolgirl Dies
An 11-year-old Sydney schoolgirl has died from injuries received in a pool accident which also killed her
best friend. A spokesman for Westmead Hospital said she died early yesterday morning. She never
recovered from receiving electric shocks in a swimming pool on 19 December. Her friend, also 11, died
later that same day. A live wire came into contact with the water in which the two girls were swimming
after the pool filter's electrical cable was accidentally cut.

The Age, 27 December 1988


Electrical Shocks More Likely in Summer
By DAVID THOMSON

People are twice as likely to suffer electrical shocks in summer as in the rest of the year, the SEC
has warned.
  A survey of the number of shocks reported in the 10 years to 1986 found that 65 per cent of
them occurred between October and March, the SEC's acting Victorian Chief Electrical
Inspector, Mr Ian Graham, said.
   He said the risk increased in summer because portable appliances were used outdoors and in
tents and caravans, people were barefooted or near water, especially pools, and people tried to do
their own electrical repairs and installations.
   Mr Graham said 500 electrical shocks had been reported to the SEC last year. There had been
another 100 cases in council supplied areas. About one-tenth of all shocks were the result of
dampness.
    He said there had been 17 fatalities from electrical appliances in 1987. There have been two
deaths from electrical contact with swimming pools since wiring regulations were revised in
1976 to isolate electrical equipment, including earthing and lighting, from pools.
   Mr Graham said checking existing electrical fittings was much more difficult than issuing
guidelines for new works.
   "We cannot check every single pool in Melbourne; we do not have the right to interfere."
    Mr Graham said pool owners should check permanently wired electrical fittings such as
pumps and underwater lights. Variations in water levels and heat caused power lines to sag,
which was dangerous where they crossed water.
    He said there had been a number of fatalities caused by hair dryers falling into baths. Mr
Graham said people should remember that it was illegal and unsafe for unlicensed tradesmen to
work on fixed wiring of houses, and that caution was needed with extension cords to tents and
caravans.

         avoided ?

2        List the reasons why it is more likely that more electric shocks are experienced in
         summer.

4        Why would dampness contribute to a large number of electrical shocks ?

Science in the news – living ear grown in lab

Teaching notes

This task can be used when covering cells, tissues and organs with GCSE students or high achieving
KS3 groups.
It is based on the article from The Week magazine called ‘Living ear grown in lab’. Further information
and web links can be found at http://www.nhs.uk/news/2013/08August/Pages/Artificial-ear-grown-in-
lab.aspx.
All links were available at the time of publishing.


Starter
As an interesting stimulus show the class the famous image of a human ear grown on a mouse's back
(http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/health/1949073.stm). You may also like to show them a video
(http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LHHe_q3DNas).
Ask the students to discuss in pairs why they think scientists have done this and feedback their ideas.
Explain that some people have lost ears through injury or because they were born without them (you
might like to show a suitable image at this point) and this kind of research is helping to work out ways
of building human tissue in the lab to help such people. It is called tissue engineering. The image
shown at the start shocked the world when it was released in 1997. Since then, tissue engineering is
making progress and the same team have recently announced improvements to the human ears they
are engineering.


Main
Students complete Task 1. If you have access to microscopes and slides with cartilage then students
could use them to take a look at some cartilage and draw what they observe.
Go through the answers with the students:

2. Cartilage is a tissue because it is made up of one type of cell (chondroblasts). The ear is an organ
   because it is made up of several different tissues all working together to perform a function.
3a. Cartilage in the outer ear contains mostly elastin in its extracellular matrix so it is flexible.
3b. The cartilage that makes up the rings around the trachea contain mostly collagen so it is strong
    enough to hold open the trachea so air can pass through.
4. Titanium was used because it is lightweight so the ear would be light enough to wear and also it is
   non-reactive. This is important so it does not react with the cells.
5a. The rat's immune system would have attacked the foreign cartilage cells and rejected the ear if it
    had a functioning immune system.
5b. If the ears are to be used in humans then the patient's immune system would have to be
     suppressed or the ear would be rejected. With a weak immune system the patient would be at
     risk from infections.
5c. To avoid this problem the replacement ear would have to be made using the patient's own
    cartilage cells.

Then ask students to work in small groups to complete Task 2. They should cut out the cards and use
the information to answer the question: 'How close are we to building replacement outer ears?'

Ask students from each group to read out their statement. Discuss with the class what steps the
researchers need to take next.



Plenary
Discuss with the students the need for scientists to develop techniques to build other replacement
body parts such as whole organs. Talk about why this is more complicated and why. For example,
organs are made up of many tissues working together, they require a blood supply and connection to
the nervous system.
Ask the students to consider the question: 'How close are we to building replacement organs?' Ask
them to stand in a line to form a continuum to show where they think we are in this endeavour.



Homework idea
Ask the students to do some research into other teams that are working in the field of tissue
engineering and summarise their work in their own words. For example, another recent news story
reported that a team have grown a miniature human brain (see http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/health-

1. How was the current in the series circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?
   The current remains the same / unchanged in a series circuit.

2. How was the current in the parallel circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?
   The current is shared between the number of branches / bulbs in the parallel circuit.

3. How was the voltage in the series circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?
   The voltage is shared between the bulbs in a series circuit.

4. How was the voltage in the parallel circuit affected by increasing the number of bulbs?
   The voltage remains the same for all bulbs in a parallel circuit.

5. Compare the effect of the number of bulbs on the current of series and parallel circuits.
   Changing the number of bulbs in a series circuit has no effect on the current, whereas in a
   parallel circuit the current is shared between the branches.

6. Compare the effect of the number of bulbs on the voltage of series and parallel circuits.
   Changing the number of bulbs in a parallel circuit has no effect on the voltage supplied to each
   bulb, whereas in a series circuit the voltage is shared between the bulbs.

searchText: ﻿SERIES AND PARALLEL CIRCUITS There are two basic arrangements of components in a circuit. Series Circuits The resistors are added end-to-end so that the whole current flows through each resistor in turn. • There is only one path for the current through the circuit. • If one component stops working, they all stop working. • Resistance increases with more components added. Parallel Circuits The resistors are on separate branches, and the current splits up to flow through each branch, depending on its resistance. • Current splits up - there are multiple pathways. • If one component is turned off, the others keep working. • Resistance decreases for more and more resistors connected in parallel.

searchText:
Sight, Sound and Colour

Structure and Function of the human ear



                                                               Sound waves travel through the ear canal and
                                                               cause the eardrum to vibrate. The small bones
                                                               of the inner ear transfer this vibration to the
                                                               inner ear cochlea.

                                                               The cochlea is fluid filled and lined with many
                                                               hair-like nerve cells. Different length nerve cells
                                                               detect different wave frequencies and transmit
                                                               this information to the brain using electrical
                                                               impulses that move along the nerves.

Audible range of humans and other animals

Humans can hear between 20 – 20,000 Hertz, a measure of frequency. The frequency of a wave is calculated by
the number of waves that pass by a fixed point in a given amount of time.

In comparison to many other animals, humans have a very limited audible range. Bats and dolphins can hear
and produce sound at an exceedingly high frequency – and use it to bounce back off objects as sonar to “see”
without light. Low rumbling noises of elephants and moles are below our auditory range but can travel long
distances.




Pitch and Loudness of sound

                                                           Sound can be described by “characteristics”
                                                           called pitch and loudness. Pitch is related to
                                                           frequency – the higher the frequency then
                                                           the higher the pitch of the note (a single
                                                           sound at a particular level). Loudness is
                                                           related to amplitude – the higher the
                                                           amplitude the louder the sound.



105 | P a g e     GZ Science Resources
 Reflecting sound waves

Sonar (originally an acronym for SOund Navigation And Ranging) is simply making use of an echo. When an
animal or machine makes a noise, it sends sound waves into the environment around it. Those waves bounce
off nearby objects, and some of them reflect to the object that made the noise. Whales and specialised machines
can use reflected waves to locate distant objects and sense their shape and movement.




Structure of the Human eye
                                                         The human eye is a “collecting” organ that allows light
                                                         to reach sensory nerves which then transmit electrical
                                                         signals to the brain. The convex lens focuses the images
                                                         seen onto the retina of the eye. Various sensory cells in
                                                         the retina called rods and cones detect both amount of
                                                         light and colour of light. The iris opens to let more light
                                                         into the eye when it is dimmer. The muscles around the
                                                         lens change the shape of the lens. The blind spot is the
                                                         point of entry of the optic nerve on the retina and has
                                                         no light receptors. The cornea is the tough transparent
                                                         layer at the front of the eye.

                                                         Messages from the retina travel through the optic nerve
                                                         to the brain. The brain further processes the images in
                                                         various parts of the brain responsible for language,
                                                         speech and thinking.


White light is made from colours mixed together
                                                 White light is a combination of all the other colours of light mixed
                                                 together. The main colours that make up white light can be seen
                                                 in a rainbow. They are red, orange, red, green, blue, indigo (a dark
                                                 inky blue) and violet. They can be remembered by the acronym
                                                 ROY G BIV.

                                                 The sun releases visible light of all wavelengths, when combined
                                                 becomes white light. When this white light hits the surface of a
                                                 red apple all the other colours of light except red are absorbed.
                                                 The red light is instead reflected, and when hitting our eyes, we
                                                 see the apple as red because that is the only wavelength
                                                 detected.
106 | P a g e    GZ Science Resources
 We see colours because of what wavelengths are reflected
A colour is a property processed by an object as
a result of the way it reflects, absorbs or emits
light of a specific wave length.

We see a tree as green because the leaves absorb
the red and blue light waves, and only the green
light is reflected into our eyes.




Prisms work by diffracting colours of different wavelengths
                                                    A prism is a triangular block used to disperse
                                                    white light. This causes light of different colours to
                                                    be refracted differently and to leave the prism at
                                                    different angles, creating an effect like a rainbow.
                                                    The degree of bending of the light's path varies
                                                    with the wavelength or colour of the light used,
                                                    called dispersion. This can be used to separate a
                                                    beam of white light into its spectrum of colours.


Primary and Secondary colours

 Combining light colours is said to be
 additive. Each wavelength of light
 adds to another.

 The three main colours of light are
 called primary. Two primary colours
 together make a secondary colour
 and all three primary colours
 together make up white light.

 NOTE: Paint absorbs light waves. The
 paint is called subtractive because
 with each addition of colour more of
 the wave lengths are absorbed. The
 three primary colours of paint are
 cyan, yellow and magenta. When
 these three are added together the
 resulting colour is black: all the
 different wavelengths of coloured
 light are absorbed.

Sound occurs when something vibrates. Something vibrates when it moves back and forth very

How does sound move?

If a tuning fork is struck, it vibrates. When the prongs of the fork move forward, energy is transferred from the prongs to
the air particles and the particles are pushed closer together to form a patch of compressed air. Once formed, this area of
compression moves through the air as the particles collide with other particles and pass their energy on. This causes a
travelling vibration which is called a sound wave.

When the vibrations reach the ear drum, it is made to vibrate in step with the tuning fork. The vibrating ear drum passes
its energy on to smaller parts in the ear which finally results in electrical signals being transferred to the brain. The sound
is then heard.




The layers of compressed air produced by a vibrating object behave rather like the coils of a "slinky" spring.

How fast sound energy is being transferred can be determined by measuring the number of
vibrations produced per second. This is called the frequency of the sound wave.
The frequency of a sound wave determines the pitch of the sound. Low notes have a small
frequency and high notes have large frequency.

Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), where 1 Hz = 1 vibration per second.

searchText: ﻿Sound Production in Musical Instruments [OCR from document pages] Sound Production in Musical Instruments What produces thi ind? rq How can th| chang Musical Instrument Families Musical instruments are classified by the way they make sounds. Sounds are the result of vibrations and in each type of instrument the vibrations come from a different source. String Instruments Vibrating strings provide the sound in stringed instruments. The player makes the strings vibrate in one of three ways: plucking, bowing or hitting. How the pitch is changed The length, thickness and tension of the string all affect its pitch. Longer, thicker or looser strings will vibrate more slowly than shorter, thinner or tighter strings. Faster vibrations will cause a note that is high in pitch and slow vibrations will cause notes that are low in pitch. The different pitches on stringed instruments are obtained by having many strings of different lengths or by changing the vibrating length of the string by stopping them at different points. Five examples of the type of instrument. String Instruments Wind Instruments Percussion Instruments Musical Instrument Families Musical instruments are classified by the way they make sounds. Sounds are the result of vibrations and in each type of instrument the vibrations come from a different source. Wind Instruments Sound produced by wind instruments comes from a vibrating column of air inside the instrument. There are two types of wind instruments, brass and woodwind. For brass instruments, the column of vibrating air is caused by the vibrating lips of the player. The vibrating column of air in woodwinds can be created in one of three ways: by blowing across an edge, like the flute, by blowing between a reed and a fixed surface, as in the clarinet or by blowing between two reeds, as in the oboe. How the pitch is changed Wind instrument pitch depends on the volume of air that is vibrating. A larger volume of air vibrates more slowly than a smaller volume causing a lower pitch. The player can change the pitch by opening and closing holes along the instruments length Musical Instrument Families Musical instruments are classified by the way they make sounds. Sounds are the result of vibrations and in each type of instrument the vibrations come from a different source. Percussion Instruments In percussion instruments the source of sound is a vibrating membrane or a vibrating piece of solid material. The percussionist normally causes the materials to vibrate by hitting them but many are played by shaking or rubbing. How the pitch is changed Due to the complex ways the sound source vibrates, most percussion instruments do not have a definite pitch. The pitch of these instruments depends on the amount of material that is vibrating. This means that the instruments must have a different vibrating body for each note. The pitch of percussion instruments with membranes also depends on the thickness and tension in the membrane.

subject: Science
searchText: Sources of Light We can see most objects because light bounces off of them into our eyes. However some objects are a source of light as they are luminous . This means they produce their own light eg the sun or a torch. Objects that do not produce their own light eg the moon or people, are non-luminous . They require light from another source to be seen. Non-luminous objects can be classified into 3 groups: Transparent – Light can trav el through it easily without any interference eg glass, air, water Translucent – Some light is transmitted but some is absorbed. Vision is interfered with eg frosted glass. Opaque – No light is transmitted eg people, wood and metal. When ever light is prevented from hitting a surface by an opaque object a shadow is formed.

title: Static Electricity
reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: ﻿ Lesson 2 e&c DANCING WITH STATIC­­­­­­­­­­­­­­ AIM OF THE LESSON During this lesson students will: • Describe how a transfer of energy from one material to another can create static electricity. • Name some examples of static electricity. EQUIPMENT Per Class • 1 foam cup filled with water • 1 compass or sharp object • 5 tea bags • a variety of materials eg nylon; wool; fur; silk; paper; cotton; rubber; chux; stockings; polyester; plastic; sponge ( a few of each is best) Per Group • 2 balloons • 1 plastic comb or plastic pen cover • 1 ball of wool (not acrylic) or piece of wool cloth • 1 empty soft drink can • 5 or 6 styrofoam balls/ packing foam/ beans out of bean bag or puffed wheat Preparation • Collection of materials to test (Students could bring in one each and could be a piece of clothing as they do not need to be cut). Safety ▪ Nil Background Information for teachers Electricity ◦ The word electricity comes from the Greek word for amber – electron. ◦ Electricity is a form of energy that is used in many ways in daily life. ◦ Electricity can be observed in the natural environment – eg lightning. ◦ All matter is made of small particles called atoms. ◦ Within atoms are tiny particles called electrons which are negatively charged. Static Electricity • When materials come in contact with each other electrons may be transferred from one material to the other. • This causes a build up of charge which is called static electricity. • If a substance picks up electrons it becomes negatively charged. • When materials have different charges they attract each other. When they have similar charges they repel. • When there is a very big difference between these charges, when the objects come in contact they produce a spark. • By rubbing certain objects together they become charged with electricity. • Wool cloth and human hair readily give up electrons. • Humid weather reduces the effectiveness of static electricity. • When students rub materials on their hair it is best if the hair is fine and dry with no gel or hair spray. Electric Shocks • If you rub your feet on a carpet, your entire body can become charged. • The excess electrons in your body need to go somewhere. Therefore, when you touch something that is not charged (like a large piece of metal) it absorbs the extra electrons suddenly. • The electrons flow quickly through the tip of your finger into the object you touch with a ZAP! • The flow of electrons might be great enough for you to see a tiny spark and hear a snapping sound. Balloons • A balloon rubbed with a wool cloth becomes negatively charged. • When this balloon is held above some foam balls, the neutrally charged balls become positively charged and leap upward to cling to the balloon. • After several minutes, some of the electrons may drain off the balloon onto the balls. This will cause the balls to become negatively charged and be repelled by the balloon. When this happens they may actually leap off the balloon and back to the table. • The repelled foam balls may then transfer their excess electrons to the table after a few minutes and once again leap toward the balloon. Activities • After the Styrofoam clings to the balloon, students who are patient and wait several minutes may see some of the Styrofoam leap forcibly away from the balloon back to the table. • Students who observe very closely will notice that the same grains of tea will alternately leap toward and away from the comb. Investigating Scientifically • Prediction: what you think may happen in an experiment based on your experiences. Lesson Outline 1. Introduction (Engaging Students) Demonstration • Fill a foam cup with water. • Ask a student to rub a plastic comb with a ball of wool or their hair for 10 secs but do not put the comb down. • Use a compass to put a tiny hole in the bottom of the foam cup to produce a very fine stream of water ( a tap is better if available). • As soon as the water starts to flow hold the charged comb next to the stream of water without touching it. The comb should cause the stream of water to bend towards it. The comb is attracting it like a magnet. Transfer of energy or electrons. Getting a shock when stepping out of a car. Combing hair causes unusual attractions. Turning the TV off sometimes causes a zap and shock. Lightning. Clothes out of the dryer cling together. 2. Activities and Strategies • Write down the aim, equipment and method for the activity as a class. • Discuss what is meant by a prediction. Students write a prediction for each activity. • Students conduct the activities on the handout. 3. Focus Questions (Explain and Elaborate) Opposite charges. Like charges. Electrons moving from one material to another. Static electricity is through the air. Other electricity travels in wires. 4. Reflection • In groups, students share one idea that summarises what they have learnt about static electricity. • These could then be shared with the class. • Students to write a conclusion. Extension Activities • Investigate a range of other materials found in the classroom to see if they attract or repel other materials e.g. plastic rulers, erasers, pencil cases. Record your results in a table. Links to other learning Areas • Write a poem about lightning. • Design a bookmark using lightning or static electricity as the focus. • Research about Benjamin Franklin who flew a kite in a lightning storm. • Write a story about a lightning storm. • Make up a crossword puzzle or word sleuth that includes the types of materials you have used in this lesson. • Find out if we see lightning or hear thunder first and why this is so. ACTIVITY 2 DANCING WITH STATIC Aim (What are we going to find out?) Equipment (What do I need to complete the task?) Method (How is the task to be done?) Results (What did I observe?) No Method Prediction (What I think will happen) Observations (What I saw) 1 Rub a balloon with a ball of wool and hold the balloon over a friend’s hair. 2 Rub two balloons with a ball of wool and then hold the balloons side by side. 3 Rub a balloon on your hair and hold it near some small torn up pieces of paper. 4 Rub a balloon on a ball of wool, see if you can get it to stick to the wall. 5 Rub a comb with a ball of wool and bring the balloon close to the foam balls. Wait to see what happens. 6 Rub a comb with a ball of wool and hold it above ¼ teaspoon of tea leaves on your desk. Wait to see what happens. 7 Rub a comb with a ball of wool and hold it next to an empty soft drink can which is on its side on a flat surface. • Rub a plastic comb or a plastic pen cover with a selection of materials. • After rubbing each material hold the comb near some foam balls. • Record the material you used and your observations. No Material Observation (attracted or repelled the foam balls) 1 2 3 Conclusion (What did I learn about static electricity?)

title: Static Electricity Over Head Version
subject: Science
searchText: ﻿STATIC ELECTRICITY Atomic Structure The structure of the atom has a cloud of electrons orbiting around a nucleus in energy shells. It is the outer electrons that are involved in the production of static electricity. Static Electricity Friction between two surfaces can rub electrons off one object and onto another. The object that gains electrons becomes negative - the other becomes positive. This produces static electricity. Static Electricity: stationary charges on an object. e.g. A plastic comb rubbed on a cotton cloth becomes positively charged by losing electrons. Interaction of Charges Charge Law: Similar charges repel each other while opposite charges attract each other. Examples of Static Electricity Lightning • Caused by the friction between the air and the clouds. • Convection currents within the cloud also cause ice particles to produce static charge. • Charge on the ground below the ground becomes oppositely charged. • Lightning is discharged to the ground or tallest structure with a large charge density. Pollution Control • Chimneys have special electrostatic traps to attract smoke particles. • This reduces the amount reaching the atmosphere. Getting "Zapped" • Moving cars build up a charge as they move through the air. • Passengers sometimes get "zapped" as they get out of the car and touch the metal part of the door. • The charged flows around the person to the Earth.

searchText:
Taboo – circuit symbols
Teaching notes

Taboo is a word guessing game. The objective is to have your team guess the
keyword on top of a card. This must be accomplished without using the word
itself or any of the additional ‘taboo’ (forbidden) words listed on the card.

 1. Students work in teams

 2. Each team needs a set of cards.

 3. The cards need to be shuffled and placed face down.

 4. An individual from the first team takes the card from the top of the pile,
    and then describes the symbol and keyword at the top of the card without
    using the words below. The rest of their team must guess which word is
    described. Participants are not allowed to say ‘sounds like’ or ‘rhymes
    with’ and no gestures or sounds. The rest of the team guess the keyword
    and/or draw the symbol.

 5. Should the individual use one of the taboo words, a member of the
    opposing team may challenge and the individual must move on to the
    next word.

 6. Each individual is allowed two minutes to describe as many words/symbols
    as possible to the players in their team before play passes to the next
    team.

 7. For each word which is correctly guessed, the playing team receives one
    point.

This activity is designed to extend the students’ vocabulary range by finding
other ways to describe the keyword. It allows a review of scientific vocabulary
in addition to reinforcing the students’ memory of each scientific term and
symbol.

In the lesson or homework prior to playing this game, the students could
research the keywords and symbols.

title: The Speed of Sound
subject: Science
searchText:
The Speed of Sound:

 Sound travels at different speeds depending on what it is traveling through.
Of the three mediums (gas, liquid, and solid) sound waves travel the slowest
through gases, faster through liquids, and fastest through solids.
Temperature also affects the speed of sound.
Medium=

Molecules=

Properties=

Collide=

Magnitude=

Rapidly=

Obstacles=

Effectively=

Ocean dwelling=

Majority=

Gases:
The speed of sound depends upon the properties of the medium it is passing
through. When we look at the properties of a gas, we see that only when
molecules collide with each other can a sound wave move. So, it makes
sense that the speed of sound has the same order of magnitude as the
average molecular speed between collisions. In a gas, it is important to know
the temperature. This is because at lower temperatures, molecules collide
more often, giving the sound wave more chances to move around rapidly. At
freezing (0º Celcius), sound travels through air at 331 meters per second
(about 740 mph). But, at 20ºC, room temperature, sound travels at 343
meters per second (767 mph).
Liquids:
Sound travels faster in liquids than in gases because molecules are more
tightly packed. In fresh water, sound waves travel at 1,482 meters per
 second (about 3,315 mph). That's well over 4 times faster than in air! Many
ocean-dwelling animals rely upon sound waves to communicate with other
animals and to locate food and obstacles. The reason that they are able to
effectively use this method of communication over long distances is that
sound travels so much faster in water.
Solids:
Sound travels fastest through solids. This is because molecules in a solid
medium are much closer together than those in a liquid or gas, allowing
sound waves to travel more quickly through it. In fact, sound waves travel
over 17 times faster through steel than through air. The exact speed of
sound in steel is 5,960 meters per second (13,332 mph)! But, this is only for
the majority of solids. The speed of sound in all solids are not faster than in
all liquids.


Sound travels faster in a liquid than in a gas
because the particles are ____________ together in a
liquid.
Sound travels faster in a solid than a liquid because
the particles are _________ together in a solid.

Topical science - healing light
Task
Read the following article and answer the questions.

       Imagine a vivid red light.
       Now think of a time when you were younger and hurt yourself; perhaps you fell
       over and grazed your knee, or scalded yourself whilst helping in the kitchen.
       Imagine simply shining a red light on the injury and the wound healing more
       quickly than usual! This really does work. Not in seconds or hours, that still only
       occurs in science fiction, but shining a certain type of red light onto a wound
       does speed up healing time.
       The light in question is deep red (close to the infra-red part of the
       electromagnetic spectrum). It has a wavelength of 670 nanometres and it
       causes the mitochondria in cells to release more energy (ATP).
       How does it do this?
       At first, scientists speculated that the red light affected the enzymes found in
       mitochondria by speeding up their activity.
       However, the most recent research reveals that it is water which is affected by
       the red light. Water seems to become less viscous (sticky) under this
       wavelength of light.
       The light causes each water molecule to move slightly further away from its
       neighbour, making water 'runnier'. Cells are full of water and it seems enzymes
       in mitochondria work more easily when they are surrounded by water which is
       more fluid.
       Scientists are investigating how this effect could be used to help heal skin
       wounds and burns. It may also be used to help treat some cases of infertility in
       males.

  1. What are mitochondria?
  2. What is the role of mitochondria in cells?
  3. Describe what you know about infra-red light.
  4. Would the deep red light described in the text be
     visible to our eyes? Can you explain your answer?
  5. Is this light safe to use in this way?
  6. What does 'viscous' mean?
  7. Think of six liquids you might find at home.
     List them in order of viscosity.
  8. Draw a diagram to show the effect of shining
     deep red light on water molecules.

title: Ultraviolet
reviewStatus: Text content checked; preview validation pending
subject: Science
searchText: Ultraviolet 1 Ultraviolet Ultraviolet is the part of the spectrum shown on the left side of the picture above as black—because humans cannot see light of such short wavelength (or high frequency). Many animals such as some insects, some reptiles, crocodiles, salamanders, and small birds can see things that reflect this light. The name 'ultraviolet' uses the ancient Latin prefix ultra-, which means 'behind', 'beyond', or 'far'. Ultraviolet is beyond the visible violet light in terms of frequency, wavelength, and energy. Its wavelengths are between about 10 nanometers (nm) about 400 nanometers. UV is a common abbreviation of ultraviolet, mainly used in technical contexts. Frequency and wavelength are closely related. The equation that shows this relationship is: ν = c/λ (nu, i.e. frequency = speed of light ÷ lamda, i.e., wavelength), so saying that something has a short wavelength is equivalent to saying that it has a high frequency. Ultraviolet radiation Ultraviolet light can damage or kill cells. Any electromagnetic radiation (light) that has a wavelength shorter than 450 nm may cause trouble. Therefore humans that live in places with more ultraviolet light have adapted by getting darker skins. Pigments absorb the ultraviolet radiation, so it does not get through the skin to kill or injure cells inside. Injury to the skin by ultraviolet is called "sunburn." The only difference between violet light and ultraviolet light is the wavelength (or the frequency). The only difference between ultraviolet light and x-rays is also the wavelength or frequency. Ultraviolet is beyond violet, x-rays are beyond ultraviolet, and cosmic rays are beyond x-rays. Cosmic radiation can also be called gamma rays, or gamma radiation. Technically, electromagnetic waves with a frequency of 789 terahertz or more are called ultraviolet. This corresponds with a wavelength from 380 nanometers down to approximately 5 nanometers. A single light quantum or photon of ultraviolet Indoor tanning device carries an energy around some 3.26 electron volt. The higher a photon's frequency, and so the shorter its wavelength, the more energy a photon carries. Ultraviolet 2 Although the air of the Earth is transparent to a broad range of ultraviolet, some ultraviolet sunlight is absorbed at a very high altitude by the ozone layer. Recent and ongoing destruction of ozone in high altitudes caused by human influence—mostly by industrial chemicals and air travel—has greatly increased the amount of ultraviolet light reaching the Earth's surface. This, in turn, has increased the risk of skin cancer to mankind, and this risk will only increase with time unless the ozone layer is better protected. Ultraviolet wavelengths less than 200 nanometers, X-rays, and gamma rays, are collectively called ionizing radiation since the energy in any such light quantum is high enough to 'kick' an electron out of an atom. This is why these kinds of radiation are dangerous to life. Ordinary glass does not let radiation through if its wavelength is less than 200 nanometers, so it acts as a shield against the more dangerous range of ultraviolet light, but some special sorts of glass do not shield as well, including many car windows. One use for ultraviolet radiation is tanning. Use of tanning devices can cause skin cancer because ultraviolet goes through the skin and causes destruction to cells causing sunburn. Because of the destructive power of ultraviolet light, it can be used to kill germs. Sunlight is a powerful disinfectant. Ultraviolet lamp An ultraviolet lamp is one that emits light mostly at a frequency higher than violet, called ultraviolet. These lamps are often used to kill microbes (germs). They can be very powerful, so the people who work around them when they are turned on may need to wear protective glasses and keep their skin covered to avoid injury. In the laboratory pictured, ultraviolet lights are turned on when the workers are gone so that anything on the table surface will be killed. Besides ultraviolet light, which makes up most of the light produced by these lamps, there is also a little violet and blue light. So people can easily tell when the ultraviolet lamps are turned on. searchText: ﻿VOLTAGE, CURRENT AND RESISTANCE Voltage / Potential Difference (V): provides the energy to drive electrons around a circuit. Measured in - volts (V) Current (I): a measure of the rate at which charge (electrons) flows in a circuit. Measured in - Amperes (A) Resistance (R): a measure of the difficulty electrons have in moving around a circuit. Measured in - Ohms () Voltage equals current times resistance V = IR The resistance of a wire is dependent on the following. • Type of material used. e.g. Copper has a lower resistance than nichrome wire. • Diameter of the wire. e.g. Thin wire has a greater resistance than thick wire. The filaments in globes are very thin to give them high resistance which makes the metal get very hot and glow. • Length of the wire. e.g. Long wire has more resistance. Rheostats (variable resistors) used to control fans and lights have the wire wound around a non-conductor to save space.

searchText: Waves and Rays What is light? Light is a form of energy that we can see and is given out by hot objects. It is made up of waves that travel outwards from a light source. Some of the waves reach our eyes, but most continue elsewhere. Waves can be transverse or longitudinal The two main types of waveform are transverse waves and longitudinal waves. All types of electromagnetic waves, including light, as well as water waves travel as transverse waves. Sound waves travel as longitudinal waves. Transverse waves (light) are a moving wave where each part of the wave travels up and down in repeating motion as the wave moves forward. These do not need a medium to travel through and can travel through empty space. Longitudinal waves (sound) are a compressing and expanding wave that needs a medium to travel in. A medium could be gas, solid or liquid. Sound travels as a longitudinal wave Sound waves are mechanical waves requiring particles. (a medium to travel through) Air particles vibrate back and forward creating repeating patterns of high (compressed particles) and low (spaced apart particles) pressure. One wave stretches from one compressed area of particles to the next. Waves of sound energy travel through air, water and solid substances. Waves transfer energy Waves are a means of transferring energy from one place to another without also transferring matter. Some waves need a medium (matter) to travel through in order to transport their energy from one location to another and are known as mechanical waves, such as ocean waves, sound waves and earthquake waves. Other waves can travel through the vacuum of space where there is little or no atoms. These are know as electromagnetic waves. Examples of those waves include light waves, microwaves and radio waves. 93 | P a g e GZ Science Resources Features of a wave Waves have troughs, the lowest point, and crests, the highest point. A wavelength is the distance between two closest crests. The amplitude of a wave is a measure of its height. The height is taken from a midpoint between a trough and a peak up to the top of a peak of a wave. Frequency of a wave The frequency of a wave is calculated by the number of waves that pass by a fixed point in a given amount of time. The frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). Because all electromagnetic radiation travels at the same speed then more waves of shorter wavelength will pass by a point over the same time as waves of longer wavelength. wave speed = wavelength x frequency Waves always travel at the same speed. A scientific value that always remains the same is called a constant. The constant for the speed of light is c = 3x108 m/sec or 300,000 kilometres per second. Because we know the speed of light, if we know either the wavelength (λ) in metres or the frequency (f ) in hertz then we can calculate the other. Wavelength = speed of light / frequency Frequency = speed of light / wavelength Light energy can travel as rays Light travels fast and in straight lines. At the speed of light, which is 300,000 kilometers per second, light from the sun takes about 8 minutes to travel 149 million kilometers to earth. Light can go around the earth 7 times in one second. Light travels straight, until something bends it. The straight paths of light are called light rays. 94 | P a g e GZ Science Resources Light energy can be reflected, refracted or dispersed Light travels in a straight line until it strikes an object or a force. Light can be: 1. Reflected by a mirror 2. Refracted by a lens 3. Absorbed by the object Light interacts with matter by transmission (including refraction) which is travelling through it, absorption where it enters but doesn’t leave again, or scattering (including reflection) where it bounces off. To see an object, light from that object— emitted by or scattered from it—must enter the eye. Transparent, Translucent and Opaque Shadows are created when light rays are stopped A shadow is a dark area that is formed due to light travelling in straight lines which opaque objects block. An object that stops direct light rays creates a shadow. The shape of the shadow resembles the shape of the object. The shadow created when the Moon blocks the light from the Sun to the Earth is called a solar eclipse. 95 | P a g e GZ Science Resources The length of the shadow depends on the angle of the light source The length of the shadow formed on the ground depends on the angle that the light rays hit the object blocking the light. If the light rays hit the object straight on, then this will create the smallest possible shadow. The greater the angle the light rays hit the longer the resulting shadow. The changing of length of shadow can be seen as the Sun moves across the sky. In the morning and afternoon, the shadows created are the longest as the Sun is at the greatest angle. The shortest shadows are formed at midday when the sun is directly over-head (in Summer). Sources of light and reflectors of light Light is a form of energy. The Sun is our most important source of light, which is produced along with heat energy, that is transformed from matter during a nuclear reaction. Other sources of light energy such as electrical lighting, fire and the glow from bioluminescent animals are produced during energy transformations as well. Light sources need energy to be transformed to produce light. These are also called illuminators. Objects that appear to produce light such as the Moon or shiny objects but do not use energy are reflectors of light. Light rays must originally come from a light source, such as the Sun’s light reflecting off the moon. 96 | P a g e GZ Science Resources Waves and Rays Review Questions 1. Identify the diagrams as either transverse or longitudinal waves 2. Complete the table below showing a list of examples of transverse and longitudinal waves Ripples on water sound light ‘Mexican’ wave pressure waves (P) in an earthquake vibrations in a guitar string radio waves squashing and releasing slinky 3. identify parts of the wave trough crest amplitude wavelength 97 | P a g e GZ Science Resources 4.  What is Energy? (Revision)                     Energy is what causes things to change.
 There are many different types of energy. Here are just a few:

 Kinetic (in moving objects) Change in position because object is moving.

Information sheet 1

White light

White light is a mixture of many different colours.

White light can be split into a spectrum using a prism, a triangular block of glass or
perspex. Light is refracted (changes direction) when it enters the prism, and each
colour is refracted by a different amount. Light leaving the prism is spread out into its
different colours, a process called dispersion.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2017                                              26290                                                                Page 2 of 6
                                                                              White light
Information sheet 2

White light

White light can be generated by a variety of sources both in space and by artificial
sources on Earth. For example, the Sun is a source of white light. Artificial sources
include fluorescent light bulbs and white LEDs which produce white light. White light is
a mixture of many different colours, each with a different frequency (number of waves
that pass a point in space in a time interval, usually one second).

White light can be split up into a spectrum of these colours using a prism, a triangular
block of glass or Perspex plastic. Light is refracted when it enters the prism, and each
colour is refracted by a different amount. This means that the light leaving the prism is
spread out into its different colours, a process called dispersion.

When white light passes through a prism, it is dispersed and the different colours of
the spectrum separate. Dispersion causes rainbows and the colours of the spectrum
include: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet (lowest to highest
frequency).
Dispersion happens because the different colours of light travel at different speeds in a
medium such as glass. The amount of bending increases as the change in speed
increases, therefore blue light bends more than red light.




                   White light




                                          Prism




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2017           26290                                Page 3 of 6
                                                                                White light
Information sheet 3

Splitting white light

White light can be split into a spectrum of many different colours using a prism. This is
a block of glass with a triangular cross-section. The light waves are refracted as they
enter and leave the prism. The shorter the wavelength of the light the more it is
refracted. As a result, red light is refracted the least and violet light is refracted the
most, causing the coloured light to spread out to form a spectrum.

When a ray of light goes from one material to another, it bends. The amount of
bending depends on the angle at which it strikes the surface, as well as on the
difference in the speed of light in the two materials. The bigger the speed difference,
the more it bends.

Prisms work because the speed of light changes as it moves from one medium to
another (air to glass). The speed at which it travels causes the light to be refracted
and bend. All light strikes the front of a prism at the same angle, but when it hits the
back of the prism, the different colours are travelling in different directions due to the
change in speed. The colours strike the back of the prism at different angles. They
come out of the prism at different angles which separates then into the colours of the
spectrum. This creates an effect similar to a rainbow.

searchText: X-ray 1 X-ray X-ray is part of the electromagnetic spectrum, with wavelength shorter and energy higher than ultraviolet radiation. The wavelength of X-ray covers a wide range. Radiation with shorter wavelength (higher energy) than X-ray is called Gamma ray. X-rays can go through many solid materials. They can be produced by hitting metal with fast-moving electrons. X-ray photography is used in medicine to see bones and cancer, and other things inside bodies. A Computed tomography scanner combines an X-ray machine and computer to construct a three dimensional (3D) picture. X-rays are photons, tiny packets of energy that interact with atoms in the body. The way they interact depends on the wavelength (energy level) of the x-rays. X-rays with low-level energies ("soft" x-rays) go An X-ray photograph of lungs. through the Photoelectric effect, mid-level energies go through Compton scattering, and high-level energies ("hard" X-rays) go through pair production. Medical x-rays can experience the Photoelectric effect and sometimes Compton scattering. Radiation therapy that treats cancer use Compton scattering and sometimes Pair production. There are small amounts of X-rays in the atmosphere. Like other ionizing radiation, X-rays can change living cells. This means that exposing the human body to high doses of x-rays for a long time should be avoided. Changing living cells can be dangerous. It can cause cancer and other diseases. It can also be good, as cancer cells can be killed that way. Like with any treatment, there are side-effects. X-rays cannot see soft tissue very well. To detect tumors, other imaging technologies are used; such as Magnetic resonance imaging. searchText: [OCR from document pages] 3.3 Understanding genetic basics Genetics is sometimes called the lottery of life. The genes that are passed from parents to offspring are a random selection of half of the genetic instructions that make up each parent. Together, the two sets of genes provide all of the information that an organism needs to grow and live. ? fof Full set of 46 Full set of 46 chromosomes chromosomes (2N) (2N) Both produce sex cells, called gametes, that contain half a set of chromosomes Ova cell (1) Sperm cell (N) contains 22 contains 22 autosomal autosomal chromosomes chromosomes and 1 sex and 1 sex chromosome (X) chromosome (X or Y) P (parental generation) meiosis =e generation) Female Male © Chapter 3 Biology skills ing genetic format teristics. It is the organism's An organism’s genes determine its che characteristics that are then used to classify it into a kingdom, such as Plants or Animals, and into a specific family and species. Genes are also responsible for characteristics that determine how an organism obtains food, its resistance to infection and its behaviour. Genetic information is passed from one generation to the next in the form of chromosomes. You receive half your chromosomes from your mother and half from your father. When the two halves combine, they make a full set. A full set is found in every body (somatic) cell. This is written as 2N (diploid). In the full set in somatic cells, every chromosome has a matching chromosome with the same size, shape, binding pattern and assortment of genes. Together, they are said to be a homologous pair. In humans, a full set is 23 pairs, or 46 individual chromosomes. Of these 23 pairs, there are 22 pairs of autosomal (body) chromosomes and two sex chromosomes; XX in females and XY in males. Gametes (sex cells—the ova and sperm) only contain one chromosome from each of the pairs. This is half a set. Sperm and eggs are said to be haploid (N). Which chromosome is inherited from each pair is completely random. This means different offspring of the same parents will each get a different combination. This is why children in the same family look a little like each other and a little like each parent, but are not identical to them. #%& Checkpoint 1 Copy and complete the table below with the missing number of chromosomes for each organism. The first has been completed for you. Organism | Chromosomesineach | Chromosomes in each somatic cell (2N) gamete (IN) Human 46 23 Aa Apple 34 Chicken g Dog 39 Mosquito | 6 z Gender determination Females have two X sex chromosomes, which means they only produce ova containing X chromosomes. Males have one X and one Y sex chromosome and so a sperm can contain either an X or a Y chromosome. Cell division that produces gametes (meiosis) will put one sex chromosome in each sperm or ovum. It is therefore the male gamete that determines the sex of the offspring. X (ovum) + X (sperm) = XX female X (ovum) +¥ (sperm) = XY male ; The illustration can also be shown in a Punnett square. Punnett squares are covered in more detail in Skill 3.4 on page 64. * Checkpoint 2 Propose a reason why the probability (chance) of producing a male is the same as producing a female Genes and alleles Im The chemical that stores the genetic code is called DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid). Its structure resembles a double helix. Each chromosome contains one very long and tightly coiled strand of DNA. Sections of DNA that contain complete instructions are known as genes. Genes are like ‘carriages’ along the DNA ‘train’. All human cells (except red blood cells and gametes) contain 46 chromosomes, which include approximately 42 000 genes. Each gene has a specific role in providing information and is only ‘turned on’ in the cells in which the gene is relevant. For example, the gene for eye colour will only be turned on in the iris of the eye, and not in skin cells A homologous pair of chromosomes carries the same genes, in the same places (loci), on each of the chromosomes. ‘There are different variations of every gene that have arisen from mutations. ‘The different variations are called alleles. These alleles may be the same on each pair of chromosomes, or different. For example, blue, brown, green and grey are all alleles of the gene for eye colour in humans. Each somatic cell has two corresponding alleles that code for the same trait. Sometimes, one allele is expressed (revealed) while the other allele is masked (hidden). The allele that is expressed is the dominant allele. The allele that is masked is the recessive allele Genotype is the term used to describe the particular combination of alleles that the individual has. Phenotype is the term used to describe the physical characteristics of an individual that result from the influence of the alleles that are expressed and also the effect of the environment. A carrier is an individual who has one dominant and one recessive allele for a characteristic in their genotype. They carry the recessive allele but it is not evident in their phenotype. The allele can still be passed (carried) on to the next generation. Alleles are represented by symbols, usually a letter of the alphabet that relates to the characteristic being investigated. For instance, the gene for flower colour may have an allele for red flowers. This is given the uppercase symbol R because it is a dominant allele. The recessive allele for white flowers is given the lowercase symbol r. depend on the time available. There are extension
activities on the last page which you may like to try.

Your class will be provided with the following apparatus:

This activity will allow you to explore the wide variety of beak types that can be seen within the bird

food sources within an environment.

BATTLE OF THE BEAKS

                       Biology Practical—Beak adaptation
                                   INSTRUCTIONS FOR TEACHERS

It is expected that the practical part of this task can be completed in 45–60 minutes. The activity is
intended for the whole class, but students should work individually within the group. Practical work may
be carried out in a classroom or laboratory. Discussion and further research will depend on the time
available. Extension activities could also be completed individually as homework exercises.

The following items are required for a class of 28 students.

APPARATUS

     7 pairs of scissors
     7 teaspoons
     7 pairs of tweezers
     7 clothes pegs
     28 plastic beakers or cups

MATERIALS

     large paperclips
     large rubber bands
     toothpicks
     macaroni (or other small pasta)
     marbles
     mini-marshmallows
     peas


Students will simulate bird feeding by using a beak to collect food and place it into a stomach. There are four
different beak types and a range of different food types to choose from.

This activity will allow students to explore the wide variety of beak shapes that can be seen within the bird
population, as well as developing an understanding of the way in which beak shape is related to the available
food sources within an environment.

If you wish to expand the learning experience for your students, you could provide them with some
background information and perhaps a hypothesis, then ask them to develop their own experimental
protocol to test their theories. This is a good way to help students get to grips with using the scientific
method as well as developing analytical skills.




                                                                                                                  1
                                         BATTLE OF THE BEAKS




                       In any habitat, food is limited and the types of foods available can
                       vary. Animals with variations allowing them to take advantage of
                       available foods will be more likely to survive. We call beneficial
                       inherited variations adaptations. Animals with the most helpful
                       adaptations will be the most likely to live long enough to pass their
                       genes on to the next generation.

                       Many birds have evolved specialised beak shapes that are well
                       suited to the available food sources in their environment. The
                       image to the left shows a variety of these specialised beaks, as
                       well as they food source they are most suited to. Students should
                       be encouraged to study the beak shapes and form their own
                       conclusions as to why each shape is best for each food. This can
                       also be used as a reminder of generalist versus specialist feeding
                       strategies.

                       Although this experiment only examines beak adaptations,
                       students should be urged to think about other variations which
                       may help animals adapt to their environment. These could include
                       feet, wings and colouration in birds, and a whole host of other
                       features in animals. Ask students to research animal adaptations
                       which are unusual—these could be physical or behavioural.
                       Suggest that they stay away from the common examples of polar
                       bears, cacti, penguins, camels etc.

                       During the experiment, encourage the students to discuss their
                       observations. Ask questions such as:
Wikimedia/L. Shyamal

                                    HUMAN FEET ARE STRANGE
INTRODUCTION
Humans, along with familiar species such as orangutans, gorillas, lemurs, baboons, and chimpanzees, are
primates. Among living primates, modern humans are most closely related to chimpanzees. The two species
shared a common ancestor that lived about 6–7 million years ago. One of the traits that distinguish humans
from all other primates, including chimpanzees, is the way we walk. Chimpanzees are primarily quadrupedal,
which means that they walk on four limbs. Chimpanzees move with their hands turned under so that their
knuckles make contact with the ground, which is why they are also described as knuckle-walkers. Humans, on
the other hand, are bipedal, meaning that we walk on two legs.
We walk with our feet close together and directly underneath our hips, enabling us to balance on one leg
while the other leg swings forward. Chimpanzees can walk on two legs only for short distances. Because their
feet are not directly under their hips, they sway side to side to help maintain balance when walking on two
legs.
Because humans are the only primate to walk on two legs, bipedality most likely evolved in the lineage that
led to humans. When did this human trait first evolve? The “Human Feet Are Strange” activity will help answer
that question. Part 1 focuses on observing modern human footprints and what we can infer from them. In Part
2, you will make observations and inferences from a portion of the Laetoli trackway, a trail of footprints that
were made in what is now East Africa about 3.6 million years ago! You will compare human feet and
chimpanzee feet to the footprints in the Laetoli trackway, to determine whether those footprints were more
human-like or chimp-like.

searchText:
Short Film
                      Great Transitions: The Origin of Humans                                               Educator Materials
                                                                                                                                           	
  
	
  
                                             HUMAN FEET ARE STRANGE
OVERVIEW
The activity “Human Feet Are Strange” was developed to supplement the film Great Transitions: The Origin of
Humans (http://www.hhmi.org/biointeractive/great-transitions-origin-humans). In the film, starting at time
mark 9:40 minutes, paleoanthropologist Dr. Tim White describes the Laetoli trackway, a set of preserved
hominid footprints in Eastern Africa discovered in 1976. Fossils of the hominid species Australopithecus
afarensis have been found near the Laetoli footprints. Since A. afarensis was the only hominid species known
to be living in the area at the time, it is assumed that the footprints at Laetoli were made by A. afarensis.
Dr. White also says that, “human feet, we’re all used to them, but they’re really strange.” What does he mean
by that statement, and what is the significance of the Laetoli footprints? Students will explore these questions
in this activity.
Students first study footprints made by themselves or their classmates. The prints are made by covering the
soles of the feet with water-soluble paints and then walking on a 3 foot × 10 foot sheet of paper (“classroom
trackway”). They are then asked to analyze the shape of their feet and the position of their toes, arches, and
stride. Next, students make observations and draw inferences from an illustration of the 3.6-million-year-old
trail of Laetoli footprints (“Laetoli trackway”), compare their own footprints with those of the Laetoli trail, and
evaluate the evidence in support of the conclusion that the Laetoli footprints were made by a fully bipedal
human ancestor. This activity ends with a summary activity, which students can complete as homework.
KEY CONCEPTS AND LEARNING OBJECTIVES
•        The fossil record provides a history of life on Earth and includes not only the fossilized bones of dead
         organisms but also trace fossils, such as footprints.
•        Bipedalism, or walking primarily upright on two legs, is one of the traits that distinguish modern humans
         from all other modern primates.
• The observation of living organisms can provide insights into traits and behaviors of extinct species.
Students will be able to
•        learn the difference between observations and inferences and
•        draw inferences based on observations and other types of evidence.
CURRICULUM CONNECTIONS
       Curriculum                                                       Standards
       NGSS (April 2013)                      HS-LS4-1
       AP Biology (2012–2013)                 1.A.4
       IB Biology (2016)                      5.1
KEY TERMS
Australopithecus

  bipedalism,	
  great	
  apes,	
  hominid,	
  hominin,	
  Laetoli,	
  Lucy	
  
TIME REQUIREMENT
This lesson was designed to be completed within two 50-minute class periods but may take longer depending
on the amount of class discussion. Parts 1 and 2 of this activity can be completed during one 50-minute class
period. Part 3, the summary activity, may be completed on a second day or as homework. The 20-minute film

www.BioInteractive.org                                                                   Published September 2015; Revised October 2016

Great Transitions: The Origin of Humans may be viewed in class on another day or assigned as homework.

To reduce the amount of time for the activity, some teachers have volunteers make the trackway (Part 1)
before the scheduled class time.
SUGGESTED AUDIENCE
This activity is appropriate for all levels of high school biology, including AP and IB.
PRIOR KNOWLEDGE
Students should be familiar with the tree of life and that modern humans belong in the primate group, with
modern chimpanzees as the closest living relatives. Further, students should have a basic understanding of
evolution, including the unifying theory that species descend, with modification, from other species and that
the fossil record is a way of knowing about past events.
MATERIALS
Materials are for a class of 24 students.
Part 1
•      One handout per student, excluding the summary activity (Part 3), which you will hand out separately
•      One 3 foot × 10 foot strip of white paper for the trackway
•      Four or five plastic, 33-gallon trash bags to place

searchText:
Chapter 2                                     Geological time
EXTRA WORKSHEET 1: Carbon-14 dating


Carbon-14 dating is also known as radiocarbon dating. Carbon-14 dating is
really important for finding the age of organic materials from living things that
lived in the last 40 000 to 50 000 years. Organic materials are compounds
containing carbon that are produced by living organisms. These compounds
include carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and vitamins.



Formation of carbon-14
Carbon-14 is formed high in the atmosphere by cosmic rays (radiation from
the Sun) changing nitrogen atoms in to carbon-14 atoms. The carbon-14
atoms combine with oxygen and form radioactive carbon dioxide. The
proportion of carbon dioxide molecules which are radioactive is tiny. There is
only 1 radioactive carbon atom in 1 000 000 000 000 carbon atoms
(1 million million).



Carbon-14 in plants and animals
The radioactive carbon dioxide is absorbed by plants in photosynthesis and
made into sugar. Some of the sugar is then converted into many different
organic compounds such as proteins, lipids and vitamins in the plant. When
the plant is eaten by animals, the radioactive carbon atoms become part of
the animal’s body tissues. When organisms die they stop absorbing
carbon-14.




             Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                  ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1         Page 1
 Radioactive decay of carbon-14
Carbon-14 atoms decay into nitrogen atoms. In comparison to other types of
radioactive decay, the decay of carbon-14 is very fast. The half-life of carbon-
14 is 5730 years. Only half of the original radioactive carbon will be left after
this time. The decay curve for carbon-14 is shown in Figure 1. The vertical
axis shows the percentage of carbon-14 remaining. Carbon-14 decays so fast
that radiocarbon dating is not accurate beyond about 50 000 years. Any older
than that and carbon-14 dating is not accurate because so little radioactivity is
left that is the amount is hard to measure.

searchText:
Connect 4 – genetics and inheritance

Teaching notes
This could be a starter, plenary or revision activity.
It can be carried out using scraps of paper, exercise books, with laminated
cards, or on an interactive whiteboard. There is a Magnet interactive resource
that can be used with the activity.
Working in pairs, students look at the words and phrases, trying to choose four
which are connected in some way. They agree on one or two sentences which
include the four words and explain the connection between those words. They
can then put up their hands; the class is stopped and everyone listens to the
connection. If the explanation is agreed to be valid, those four words are
scrubbed from the list and everyone has to start again with the remaining
words and phrases.
It is up to you to decide whether to continue with the game if a combination of
words does not match one of the suggested answers. You could praise
students for their ingenuity but urge the class to continue to search for a group
of four which matches the suggested answers; this way you will not be left with
a group of mismatched words at the end. (However, your class might enjoy
rising to the challenge of linking, for example, recessive, meiosis, clone and
Franklin!)

Suggested answers

   haemophilia                              cystic fibrosis      colour blindness
                          anaemia
   vegetative

  reproduction

  Levenne and
