title: The Peppered Moth
subject: Science
searchText: ﻿The Peppered Moth: An Example of natural selection In England there is a type of moth called the peppered moth. It is a light creamy coloured moth with darker patches. It lives on trees and was camouflaged by the lichen growing on the tree trunks. In 1848, the first black peppered moth was seen in the Manchester area of England. At that time, the industrial revolution was happening and Manchester was a big industrial town. The sulphur dioxide that was produced from the burning of coal killed all the lichen on the trees so the trees appeared darker. The creamy coloured peppered moth was no longer camouflaged but the black moth was well hidden on the dark tree trunks. By 1895, 95% of the peppered moth population in the Manchester area was black. Questions 1. What are the varieties of colour in the peppered moth species? 2. Which moth is camouflaged better in the unpolluted wood? 3. What is the advantage to the moth of camouflage? 4. Why did the trees become darker? 5. What happened to the light variety of moths as the trees became darker? 6. What happened to the dark variety of moths as the trees became darker? 7. What happened to the overall appearance of the moth species? 8. What do we call this change?

title: Trisomy monosomy jigsaw
subject: Science
searchText: Trisomy 18 and 13 What are trisomies ? The term trisomy is used to describe the presence of three chromosomes, rather than the usual pair of chromosomes. For example, if a baby is born with three #21 chromosomes, rather than the usual pair, the baby would be said to have "trisomy 21." Trisomy 21 is also known as Down syndrome. Other examples of trisomy include trisomy 18 and trisomy 13. Again, trisomy 18 or trisomy 13 simply means there are three copies of the #18 chromosome (or of the #13 chromosome) present in each cell of the body, rather than the usual pair. What are trisomy 18 and trisomy 13? Trisomy 18 and trisomy 13 are genetic disorders that include a combination of birth defects. This includes severe intellectual disability, as well as health problems involving nearly every organ system in the body. Unfortunately, most babies born with trisomy 18 or 13 die by age 1. It is important to note that some babies with trisomy 18 or 13 do survive the first year of life. Therefore, these disorders are not universally fatal. In the absence of any immediate life-threatening problems, accurate predictions of life expectancy are difficult to make. There are a few reports of babies with trisomy 18 or 13 surviving to their teens, however, this is unusual. Trisomy 18 is also called "Edwards syndrome," named after the physician who first described the disorder. Trisomy 13 is called " Patau syndrome," in honor of the physician who first described it. What causes trisomy 18 and trisomy 13? Usually, each egg and sperm cell contains 23 chromosomes (half the normal number i body cells). The union of these cells creates 23 matched pairs, or 46 total chromosomes at the time of fertilization. In this manner, a person receives exactly half of their genetic material from each biological parent. Sometimes, an error occurs when an egg or sperm cell is forming, causing it to have an extra chromosome #18 or #13 inside. If this egg or sperm cell contributes that extra chromosome 18 to the embryo, then trisomy 18 results. If this egg or sperm cell contributes that extra chromosome 13 to the embryo, then trisomy 13 results. The extra chromosome 18 or 13 can come from either the mother or father. The features of trisomy 18 and trisomy 13 result from having this extra copy of chromosome 18 or 13 in each of the body's cells. Occasionally, the extra chromosome 18 or 13 is attached to another chromosome in the egg or sperm; this is called a translocation. This is the only form of trisomy 18 or 13 that can be inherited from a parent. Sometimes, a parent can carry a "balanced" rearrangement, where chromosome 18 or 13 is attached to another chromosome. However, since the parent does not have any extra or missing chromosome material, they are said to have a "balanced translocation" and they are usually normal and healthy. Rarely, mosaic trisomy 18 or 13 may occur when the error in cell division occurs after fertilization. These affected persons have some cells with an extra chromosome 18 or 13 and others with the normal number. What types of problems do children with trisomy 18 typically have? Babies with trisomy 18 appear thin and frail. They fail to thrive and have problems feeding. Trisomy 18 causes a small head size, with the back of the head (occiput) prominent. Ears are usually low-set on the head. The mouth and jaw are unusually small, and there is a shortened sternum (breastbone). At birth, these babies are small for their age, even when delivered full-term, and have a weak cry. Their response to sound is decreased and there is often a history of infrequent fetal activity during the pregnancy. Most babies with trisomy 18 have heart defects. They clench their fists in a characteristic manner and fully extending their fingers is difficult. Joint contractures—where the arms and legs are in a bent position, rather than relaxed—are usually present. The feet may be referred to as "rocker bottom," due to their curved shape. Babies with trisomy 18 may also have spina bifida, eye problems, cleft lip and palate, and hearing loss. It is also common to see feeding problems, slow growth, seizures, high blood pressure, kidney problems, and scoliosis (curvature of the spine). In males, the testes sometimes fail to descend into the scrotum. Most babies with trisomy 18 have problems that affect all parts of the body in some way. The majority of children with trisomy 18 will have most, but not all, of the health problems mentioned here. Heart problems, feeding difficulties, and an increased susceptibility to infection are factors which, most often, contribute to the death of these children. What types of problems do children with trisomy 13 typically have?﻿ Babies with trisomy 13 often have a low birthweight, even when born full-term. They have a small head, with a sloping forehead. Usually, there are major structural problems with the brain that are diagnosed shortly after birth. Often, the front of the brain does not divide properly, resulting in a condition called holoprosencephaly . This can cause changes in the development of the baby's face, where the eyes are close set, or the nose or nostrils are underdeveloped. Cleft lip and cleft palate are common in babies with trisomy 13. Eye problems are common and the ears are low-set and unusual in shape. Sometimes, babies with trisomy 13 can have scalp abnormalities (cutis aplasia) which resemble ulcers. They can also have birthmarks that are purplish-red in color ; the color is due to tiny blood vessels close to the skin (hemangiomas). Many babies with trisomy 13 have extra fingers and toes (polydactyly). The feet may have prominent heels. In many cases, there are other health problems present at birth. These include heart defects, kidney problems, and/or an omphalocele (a condition in which some of the abdominal organs protrude through an opening in the abdominal muscles in the area of the umbilical cord). In males, the testes sometimes fail to descend into the scrotum. Females may have an abnormally shaped uterus, called a bicornuate uterus. How are trisomy 18 and trisomy 13 diagnosed? Since trisomy 18 and trisomy 13 each have a unique group of characteristics, a physician may be able to determine whether a baby has trisomy 18 or 13 simply by physical examination. To confirm the physical findings, a small blood sample can be taken and the chromosomes can be analyzed to determine the presence of an extra #18 or #13 chromosome. Chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomy 18 and 13 can be diagnosed before birth by analyzing cells in the amniotic fluid or from the placenta. Fetal ultrasound during pregnancy can also give information about the possibility of trisomy 18 or 13. Ultrasound is not 100 percent accurate, since some babies with trisomy 18 and 13 may look the same on ultrasound as those without the syndrome. A chromosome analysis, whether performed on a blood sample, cells from the amniotic fluid, or placenta, is very accurate . What is the risk for parents of a child with trisomy 18 or trisomy 13 having another child with trisomy 18 or 13? In general, for women under 35 years of age, the chance of having another baby with trisomy 18 or 13 depends on several factors. The risk to having a baby with trisomy 18 or 13 does increase slightly with each added year of maternal age. After birth, the physician usually takes a blood sample from a baby suspected of having trisomy 18 or 13, to perform a chromosomal analysis (called a karyotype). This confirms the physical findings of trisomy 18 or 13 and determines the underlying chromosomal abnormality. This information is important in determining the risk in future pregnancies. (Translocation and mosaic trisomy 18 and 13 have different recurrence risks for future pregnancies). The physician may refer parents to a genetic physician or genetic counselor who can explain the results of chromosomal tests in detail. This includes what the recurrence risks may be in another pregnancy and what tests are available to diagnose chromosome problems before a baby is born. Can trisomy 18 or trisomy 13 be cured or prevented? There is no cure for trisomy 18 or trisomy 13. We are not certain how to prevent the chromosomal error that causes trisomy 18 and trisomy 13. To date, there is no scientific evidence that a parent could have done anything to cause or prevent the birth of their baby with trisomy 18 or 13. What else should I know about trisomy 18 and trisomy 13? Because many babies born with trisomy 18 and trisomy 13 may not live beyond the first few days or weeks of life, it is possible that parents may have to face the fact that the baby may never go home from the hospital. Many times, parents are frightened and overwhelmed by all of the information associated with trisomy 18 and 13. Decisions surrounding the care of an infant with trisomy 18 and 13 are difficult and personal. There are many resources available to parents to help them during this time, including early intervention services, hospice care, social workers, the hospital chaplain or clergyman, and genetic counselors . Families who have or have had a baby with trisomy 18 or trisomy 13 are particularly helpful and supportive since they have experienced many of the same questions and emotions. Down syndrome is a genetic condition. It is not an illness or a disease. Our bodies are made up of millions of cells. In each cell there are 46 chromosomes. The DNA in our chromosomes determines how we develop. Down syndrome is caused when there is an extra chromosome. People with Down syndrome have 47 chromosomes in their cells instead of 46. They have an extra chromosome 21, which is why Down syndrome is also sometimes known as trisomy 21. Although we know how Down syndrome occurs, we do not yet know why it happens. Down syndrome occurs at conception, across all ethnic and social groups and to parents of all ages. It is nobody's fault. There is no cure and it does not go away. Down syndrome is the most common chromosome disorder that we know of. One of every 700-900 babies born worldwide will have Down syndrome, although this number is lower in Australia - see Down syndrome population statistics . Down syndrome is not a new condition. People with Down syndrome have been recorded throughout history. People with Down syndrome have: some characteristic physical features some health and development challenges some level of intellectual disability. Because no two people are alike, each of these things will vary from one person to another. A test for Down syndrome can be carried out before a baby is born. Down syndrome is usually recognised at birth and is confirmed by a blood test. It was named after Dr John Langdon Down who first described it. What does it mean to have Down syndrome? Back to top Most of the young people growing up with Down syndrome today will lead quite ordinary lives in the community. Some people with Down syndrome may not need much help to lead an ordinary life, while others may require a lot of support. Having an intellectual disability HYPERLINK "https://www.downsyndrome.org.au/what_is_down_syndrome.html" \l "top" Back to top Down syndrome is the most common cause of intellectual disability that we know of. Everyone who has Down syndrome will have some level of intellectual disability. There will be some delay in development and some level of learning difficulty. Because everyone is unique, the level of delay will be different for each person. When a baby is born, there is no way to tell what level of intellectual disability the child may have. Nor can we predict the way in which this may affect a person's life. However, we do know that having Down syndrome will not be the most important influence on how that person develops and lives their life. Instead, what happens after birth will be much more important and family, environmental, cultural and social factors will shape their life, just like everyone else. Variation and identical twins
Task – version A

Read the description of a pair of identical twins.


 Mateo and Felipe are identical twins. Mateo is five minutes older than his
 brother. Today is their 30th birthday.
 'Feliz cumpleaños, big brother.' Felipe can speak fluently in both Spanish and
 English. Mateo only speaks English but with a strong Scottish accent which
 sometimes confuses his brother.
 When they were very young, family circumstances forced the boys apart.
 Mateo went to live with his father, a football coach, in Edinburgh, Scotland,
 whilst Felipe remained with his grand-parents on the family olive farm in
 Andalucia, Spain.
 Both young men have dark brown eyes and black hair. Mateo's hair reaches
 his shoulders and Felipe's is very short. They have a wide gap between their
 two front teeth.
 When he was a toddler, Felipe used to roll up his tongue and poke it out at his
 grand-mother's parrot, Loro, which he did not like. Mateo broke his leg when
 he was eight and learnt from the doctor that his blood group was O+. In
 Andalucia, when Felipe was told about the accident he decided to send his
 brother a keyring carved in the shape of a bull. Whilst wrapping the present,
 he noticed his fingerprints on the sticky tape and wondered for a moment, if
 they were identical to Mateo's.
 When he was seventeen years old, Mateo applied to do sports science at
 university. He was amazed to learn that Felipe had chosen to do the same
 course in the same city! They decided to share a flat with two friends. At first,
 their friends had no problem telling the twins apart as Felipe had very dark
 skin whilst Mateo's face was pale. Felipe was also one centimetre taller than
 his brother.
 The friends soon decided to join a gym. They were very competitive! It was
 discovered that Felipe had a greater grip-strength than his twin and could
 work out for longer on the rowing machine. But Mateo always beat his brother
 on the squash court.
 Today, they both support Manchester United and like to wear beanies when
 it's cold. Mateo won't admit, even to his twin, that he is afraid of birds. Felipe
 regularly plays the guitar and their grand-parents describe him as 'the
 musical one'. Mateo doesn't play any instruments but he does sing opera and
 Ed Sheeran songs very loudly in the shower!


When you first see identical twins, they can be hard to tell apart. This is
because much about the human body is controlled by genes and identical
twins have identical genes.

As well as (usually) having the same birthday, they also share the same
physical features, such as eye colour.

But, as you have read, Mateo and Felipe are not exactly the same. How people

                                                     Variation and identical twins
live and their environment, will alter the effect of their genes.

Instructions

Have 5 different colours ready (they don't have to be identical to those listed
below). Choose pens or pencils which make a thin line. These will help you
draw around the words you select so you can still read them easily.

Pink – circle all the physical features the twins have. Now draw a table with
two columns, one for Mateo and the other for Felipe. Record all their physical
features.

Green – In your table, circle the physical features which are different in both
boys.

1. Why do Mateo and Felipe have some features which are exactly the same?
2. Can you explain why some of their features are different?
    Brown - circle the coincidences.
    Orange – circle the other skills and attributes they have between them.
    Draw a second table with two columns and list all the orange-circled words.
    Blue - In both tables, circle any physical features and skills which can be
    easily measured.
3. Are any of these blue-circled words 'measured' in words or letters
   (qualitatively)?
4. Using numbers will give you quantitative measurements which can be
   easily compared. What units would you use to measure the other blue-
   circled features and skills?
5. Look at your second table. What skills and attributes do you think the twins
   share and what is your evidence for your conclusion?
6. Which features or skills do you judge to have an equal genetic and
   environmental influence? Explain why you think this.


For further research or home-learning:

    a. Can Mateo also roll his tongue? Explain your thoughts.
    b. What blood group is Felipe? Outline your evidence.
    c. Are their fingerprints identical? Why do you think this?

Discussion points

1. Why do Mateo and Felipe have some features which are exactly the same?
    These features are controlled by their genes and their genes are identical.

2. Can you explain why some of their features are different?
    These have been affected by their environment: hair can be cut; skin tone
    is affected by exposure to sunlight and Mateo lives in Scotland whilst Felipe
    spent his childhood in Spain; grip-strength depends on practice – Felipe has
    lived on a farm and may have helped out, making his grip stronger. This
    may also have given him greater endurance. Mateo may be better at
    squash because this indoor sport is one which can be done regularly in a
    colder, wetter climate.
3. Are any of these blue-circled words 'measured' in words or letters
   (qualitatively)?
    Eye colour; hair colour; tongue roll; blood group; fingerprints; skin colour

4. Using numbers will give you quantitative measurements which can be
   easily compared. What units would you use to measure the other blue-
   circled features and skills?
    Hair length – cm; gap between teeth – mm; height – m and cm; grip-
    strength – Kg, N or mmHg (often with a dynamometer); work-out – hours,
    mins, sec; squash – no unit as such just number of winning games.

5. Look at your second table. What skills and attributes do you think the twins
   share and what is your evidence for your conclusion?
    Share sporting ability as they can beat each other, although in different
    sports possibly due to their different exposure to physical activity when
    young; also father is a football coach, so they will have inherited and share
    some of his genes. Both like football but why the same team? Is this simply
    a coincidence?
    May both have a fear of birds – Felipe 'did not like' the parrot; Mateo doesn't
    admit his fear of birds.
    Both may be equally musical as one plays guitar and other sings opera with
    confidence.

6. Which features or skills do you judge to have an equal genetic and
   environmental influence? Explain why you think this.
    Language – humans genetically predisposed to communicate with
    language.
    Type of language and accent – result of environment.
    Musicality – genes may complement each other to bring about a strong
    musical potential.
    Instrument and skill – heavily dependent on environment.
    Sporting ability – as above.

dating
1   A carbon containing compound produced by a living thing.

    from the Sun) changing nitrogen atoms into carbon-14 atoms.

3   The radioactive carbon dioxide is absorbed by plants in photosynthesis
    and made into sugar and later into other organic compounds in the plant.

    part of the animal’s body tissues.

7   Rock cannot be dated using carbon-14 dating unless it contains material
    that was originally part of a living organism (such as coal). Few rocks are

A neutralisation reaction occurs when an acid reacts with a metal hydroxide or

title: Acid Rain
subject: Science
searchText:
Acid Rain
What is Acid Rain?

Acid rain is a result of air pollution. When any type of fuel is burnt, lots of different
chemicals are produced. The smoke that comes from a fire, or the fumes that come out
of a car exhaust don't just contain the sooty grey particles that you can see - they also
contain lots of invisible gases that can be even more harmful to our environment.

Power stations, factories and cars all burn fuels and therefore produce polluting gases.
Some of these gases (especially nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide) react with the
tiny droplets of water in clouds to form sulphuric and nitric acids. The rain from these
clouds then falls as very weak acid - which is why it is known as "acid rain".

Rain is always slightly acidic because it mixes with naturally occurring oxides in the air.
Unpolluted rain would have a pH value of between 5 and 6. When the air becomes
more polluted with nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide the acidity can increase to a pH
value of 4. Some rain has even been recorded as being pH 2.

Vinegar has a pH value of 2.2 and lemon juice has a value of pH2.3. Even the strongest
recorded acid rain is only about as acidic as lemon juice or vinegar and we know that
these don't harm us - so why do we worry about acid rain?

The Effects of Acid Rain

Acid rain can be carried great distances in the atmosphere, not just between countries
but also from continent to continent. The acid can also take the form of snow, mists
and dry dusts. The rain sometimes falls many miles from the source of pollution but
wherever it falls it can have a serious effect on soil, trees, buildings and water.

Forests all over the world are dying, fish are dying. In Scandinavia there are dead lakes,
which are crystal clear and contain no living creatures or plant life. Many of Britain's
freshwater fish are threatened; there have been reports of deformed fish being
hatched. This leads to fish-eating birds and animals being affected also. Is acid rain
responsible for all this? Scientists have been doing a lot of research into how acid rain
affects the environment.

Forests

It is thought that acid rain can cause trees to grow more slowly or even to die but
scientists have found that it is not the only cause. The same amount of acid rain seems
to have more effect in some areas than it does in others.

As acid rain falls on a forest it trickles through the leaves of the trees and runs down
into the soil below. Some of it finds its way into streams and then on into rivers and
lakes. Some types of soil can help to neutralise the acid - they have what is called a
"buffering capacity".

Other soils are already slightly acidic and these are particularly susceptible to the
effects of acid rain.



Acid rain can effect trees in several different ways, it may:
 • dissolve and wash away the nutrients and minerals in the soil
which help the trees to grow.

• cause the release of harmful substances such as aluminium into the soil.

• wear away the waxy protective coating of leaves, damaging them
and preventing them from being able to photosynthesise properly.

A combination of these effects weakens the trees which means that they can be more
easily attacked by diseases and insects or injured by bad weather. It is not just trees
that are affected by acid rain, other plants may also suffer.

Lakes and Rivers

It is in aquatic habitats that the effects of acid rain are most obvious. Acid rain runs off
the land and ends up in streams, lakes and marshes - the rain also falls directly on
these areas.

As the acidity of a lake increases, the water becomes clearer and the numbers of fish
and other water animals decline. Some species of plant and animal are better able to
survive in acidic water than others. Freshwater shrimps, snails, mussels are the most
quickly affected by acidification followed by fish such as minnows, salmon and roach.
The roe and fry (eggs and young) of the fish are the worst affected, the acidity of the
water can cause deformity in young fish and can prevent eggs from hatching properly.

The acidity of the water does not just affect species directly, it also causes toxic
substances like aluminium to be released into the water from the soil, harming fish and
other aquatic animals.

Lakes, rivers and marshes each have their own fragile ecosystem with many different
species of plants and animals all depending on one another to survive. If a species of
fish disappears, the animals which feed on it will gradually disappear too. If the extinct
fish used to feed on a particular species of large insect, that insect population will start
to grow, this in turn will affect the smaller insects or plankton on which the larger insect
feeds.

Buildings

Every type of material will become eroded sooner or later by the effects of the climate.
Water, wind, ice and snow all help in the erosion process but unfortunately acid rain
can help to make this natural process even quicker. Statues

title: Acids and Bases
subject: Science
searchText:
An acid is classed as a substance that produces H+ ions
when it is dissolved in water.

Some acids just split into separate ions for example
Hydrochloric (HCl) and Hydrofluoric (HF) acids.

HCl(aq) → H+(aq) + Cl-(aq)


Other acids are made from the reaction of a non-metal oxide
with water when it dissolves. Some of these are carbon dioxide
(CO2), nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and sulphur trioxide (SO3).

SO3(g) + H2O(l) → H2SO4(aq) ↔ 2H+(aq) + SO4-2(aq)

The double headed arrow (which should be two arrows on top
of each other) shows that the reaction goes both ways.


A base is a substance that produces hydroxide ions (OH-
-
 ) when it is dissolved in water.

Metal hydroxides will separate into ions in water.

NaOH(aq) → Na+(aq) + OH-(aq)


Other bases react with water to produce the hydroxide ions

Metal oxides
CaO(s) + H2O(l) → Ca(OH)2(aq) → Ca2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq)

Metal carbonates
CaCO3(s) + H2O(l) ↔ Ca2+(aq) + OH-(aq) + HCO3-(aq)

Metal hydrogencarbonates
NaHCO3(s) + H2O(l) ↔ Na+(aq) + OH-(aq) + H2CO3(aq)

Ammonia
NH3(g) + H2O(l) ↔ NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq)
 None of the exercises ask you to show how the hydroxide ions
are formed, however it is good to be aware of what happens as
you will use it later.

Exercise 37: Acids and Bases
This is just asking you to either name or write the formula of
the compound and then classify it as an acid or a base.

If you use the examples you should be ok with this part.



Reactions of Acids and Bases

Acids and bases react in predictable ways. For example, an
acid and a hydroxide will always combine to form water and an
ionic salt. The ionic salt is formed from the left over reactants.

There are four common types of acid/base reactions.

1. Acid + Hydroxide → Water + Salt
Eg. Hydrochloric acid + Sodium hydroxide → Water + Sodium
chloride
     HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → H2O(l) + NaCl(aq)

2. Acid + Oxide → Water + Salt
Eg. Nitric acid + Calcium oxide → Water + Calcium nitrate
     2HNO3(aq) + CaO(s) → H2O(l) + Ca(NO3)2(aq)

3. Acid + Carbonate → Water + Carbon dioxide + Salt
Eg. Hydrochloric acid + Calcium carbonate → Water + Carbon
    dioxide + Calcium chloride
     HCl(aq) + CaCO3(s) → H2O(l) + CO2(g) + CaCl2(aq)

4. Acid + Hydrogencarbonate → Water + Carbon dioxide
   + Salt
Eg. Nitric acid + Sodium hydrogen carbonate → Water +
    Carbon dioxide + sodium nitrate
     HNO3(aq) + NaHCO3 → H2O(l) + CO2(g) + NaNO3
 Another important reaction of acids which is not covered in this
section is the reaction of acids with metals

Acid + Metal → Hydrogen gas + Salt
Eg. Hydrochloric acid + Magnesium → Hydrogen gas +
Magnesium chloride
    2HCl(aq) + Mg(s) → H2(g) + MgCl2(aq)

Exercise 38: Neutralisation
For this exercise, you need to use the general reactions to
predict what will be formed in the reaction.

For the first one, you are adding acid to a metal hydroxide,
which always produces water and a salt. You need to finish the
word equation first, write the symbol equation, and then
balance your symbol equation.

Sulphuric acid + Potassium hydroxide → Water + Potassium
sulphate

H2SO4(aq) + KOH(aq) → H2O(l) + K2SO4(aq)

Then balance

H2SO4(aq) + 2 KOH(aq) → 2 H2O(l) + K2SO4(aq)

or bases are called ________________.

wide range of pH’s. It can be used to determine the pH of a
solution reasonably accurately. Which colours of universal
indicator show: acidic solutions?
                                      basic solutions?
                                      neutral solutions?

Aim: To test a range of household products to determine
whether they are acids or bases.

Equipment: A range of household substances
       Universal indicator and colour chart
       A depression tile
       Safety glasses

Procedure:
  1. Place a small amount of the substance to be tested in a
     dimple on the tile.
  2. Add 3 drops of universal indicator to the substance.
  3. Record the colour of the indicator.
  4. Use the colour chart to determine the pH of the substance.
  5. Classify each substance as an acid, a base or neutral.

 Substance Tested         Colour of         pH      Acid/Base/
                          Indicator                  Neutral

   acids you tested are strong and which are weak?




2. Strong bases have a pH of between 12 and 14. Which of the
   bases you tested are strong and which are weak?




3. Which products are neutral?

4. Sally was cleaning her oven and she got some oven cleaner
   on her arm. She noticed it started to burn and itch. On the
   oven cleaner bottle it said the cleaner was a base. Which
   household product do you think would help stop the burning
   and why?

Title: Discovering Acids and Bases
WHAT ARE ACIDS AND BASES?
Acids and bases are two kinds of special chemicals. Almost all liquids
are either acids or bases, which is determined by the type of ions in
them. An acid has many hydrogen ions, and splits apart in water to
release these hydrogen ions. On the contrary, bases have hydroxide
ions that combine with hydrogen ions. Scientists us a pH scale to
determine whether a liquid is an acid or a base. PH refers to hydrogen
ion concentration, which is measured by a scale. The scale goes from
0-14, where liquids having a pH level of 0-7 are acids, and 7-14 are
bases. Any substance with a pH level of 7 is considered neutral.

IMPORTANT QUESTIONS:
What substances are acids/bases?
How are all acids/bases similar?

similar, and discovered bases are similar. We will use our discoveries
to explore and understand how pH levels of substances are affected
when diluted.

Chapter 5                                    Chemical
reactions
               Ionic compounds and
EXTRA WORKSHEET 2:

precipitation reactions
Ionic compounds form crystal lattices of cations and anions. Below in Table 1
is a list of some common cations and anions that make up ionic compounds.

Table 1

        Positive ions (cations)                                 Negative ions (anions)
    Chemical name               Symbol                      Chemical name                        Symbol
Hydrogen ion            H+                            Fluoride                             F–
Lithium ion             Li+                           Chloride                             Cl–
Sodium ion              Na+                           Bromide                              Br–
Potassium ion           K+                            Iodide                               I–
Copper(I) ion           Cu+                           Hydroxide                            OH–
Calcium ion             Ca2+                          Nitrate                              NO3–
Magnesium ion           Mg2+                          Oxide                                O2–
Barium ion              Ba2+                          Sulfide                              S2–
Copper(II) ion          Cu2+                          Sulfate                              SO42–
Iron(II) ion            Fe2+                          Carbonate                            CO32–
Iron(III) ion           Fe3+                          Nitride                              N3–
Aluminium ion           Al3+                          Phosphate                            PO43–


Naming ionic compounds
Naming ionic compounds is relatively simple. The naming conventions follow
just two rules:

1    The chemical name is made up of the name of the cation followed by the
     name of the anion.
     Example: an ionic compound made up of potassium cations and fluoride
     anions is known as potassium fluoride.


2    Ions from the same atom but with a different charge are distinguished by
     roman numerals that show the charge of the ion. These roman numerals
     are included in the chemical name.




            Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                 ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1         Page 1
     Example: Iron atoms form two ions – iron(II), Fe2+ and iron(III), Fe3+. These
    both form oxides known as iron(II) oxide and iron(III) oxide.


Questions

    following ionic compounds:

    a   MgCl2

    _____________________________________________________________

    _____________________________________________________________

    d   CuCO3
    _____________________________________________________________

    _____________________________________________________________

    _____________________________________________________________

    g   Ca3(PO4)2
    _____________________________________________________________

2   Write the chemical formulas for the following ionic compounds:

    a   lithium carbonate __________________________________________


    b   aluminium bromide _________________________________________


    c   copper(II) nitrate ___________________________________________


    d   sodium chloride ___________________________________________


    e   calcium iodide _____________________________________________


           Copyright © Pearson Australia 2012 (a division of Pearson Australia Group Pty Ltd)
                                ISBN 978 1 4425 2366 1         Page 2
     f      ammonium hydroxide _______________________________________


    g      lithium nitride _____________________________________________


Predicting precipitation reactions
Some ionic compounds are soluble in water (dissolve) and some ionic
compounds are insoluble in water (do not dissolve). This means that when
two aqueous solutions of soluble ionic compounds are mixed, the ions may
exchange to form an insoluble compound. When this occurs, the insoluble
compound comes out of solution as a solid.

This type of chemical reaction is known as a precipitation reaction and the
insoluble solid is known as the precipitate. Scientists can predict if mixing two
solutions will result in a precipitate by using solubility rules.

Some solubility rules are shown in Table 2. These rules tell you which
combinations of anions and cations are soluble and which combinations are
insoluble.

searchText:
Making Salts
 Aim: to make and name salts by neutralisation reaction.

Equipment:
                                                        Safety Information
• Sodium hydroxide solution
                                                        Acid – corrosive to skin and eyes
• Beaker
                                                        Wear goggles, clean spills
• 50 cm3 measuring cylinder                             immediately.

• Hydrochloric acid                                     Glassware – risk of cuts if broken.

• Dropping pipette                                      Apply pressure to wounds and inform teacher
                                                        immediately.
• Stirring rod or capillary tube
                                                        Bunsen burner – risk of burns.
• Universal indicator paper
                                                        Place under cold running water for ten
• Evaporating basin
                                                        minutes. Inform teacher.
• Bunsen burner

• Gauze

• Tripod

• Heat proof mat




Method (series circuit):
Step 1: You must wear goggles at all times. Measure 25cm3 of sodium hydroxide solution into a beaker.

Step 2: Drop by drop, add hydrochloric acid to the sodium hydroxide.

Step 3: After every few drops, take a small sample on the stirring rod or capillary tube and test the pH.
Keep adding acid until you have obtained a neutral pH result (pH 7 – green).

Step 4: Once you have a neutral solution, pour it into an evaporating basin.

Step 5: Using a tripod, mat, gauze and Bunsen burner set-up as shown above, heat the solution, until
about 1/3 remains. This is a saturated solution.

Step 6: Once the equipment is cool, move the evaporating basin to a warm place in the room, and leave
to evaporate completely overnight.


                                                Page 1 of 2
                                                                                    Making Salts

Questions
 1. What is meant by neutralisation?

 2. What is a saturated solution?

 3. What is the name of the salt produced in the reaction?

 4. Write a word equation for the neutralisation reaction in your investigation.

 5. Name the salt produced in these reaction:
    a. Hydrochloric acid and potassium hydroxide
    b. Sulphuric acid and calcium carbonate
    c. Nitric acid and calcium hydroxide




                                                Page 2 of 2
 Answers
1. What is meant by neutralisation?
   An acid and a alkali react together and produce a salt and water with neutral pH.

2. What is a saturated solution?
   A saturated solution cannot dissolve anymore solute. In this example no more salt can be
   dissolved.

3. What is the name of the salt produced in the reaction?
   Sodium chloride

4. Write a word equation for the neutralisation reaction in your investigation.
   hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide  sodium chloride + water

5. Name the salt produced in these reaction:
   a. Hydrochloric acid and potassium hydroxide
   Potassium chloride
   b. Sulphuric acid and calcium carbonate
   Calcium sulphate
   c. Nitric acid and calcium hydroxide
   Calcium nitrate

acid in them. Record which metal you add to each tube.

Step 6: Observe any reactions and make a note of your observations in your

searchText: ﻿Precipitation Reactions Sometimes it is necessary for chemists to identify the presence of ions in solution for example testing water samples. When identifying unknown positive ions and negative ions we can use precipitation reactions in order to determine what ions are in solution. When an ionic solid dissolves in water we call this an aqueous solution. Some ions in aqueous solutions react to form insoluble precipitates. This is due to the chemical properties of the new ionic compound which affect its solubility in water. Some salts produced from these reactions give bright coloured precipitates that are characteristic of those ions. These solids form due to strong ionic bonds between positively and negatively charged ions that make the salt insoluble in water. A chemical reaction can be thought of in terms of reactants and products. We add reactants together to get products: REACTANTS ➔ PRODUCTS To understand what happens in a chemical reaction between two ionic solutions, all you need to recognise is that the ions simply swap partners. For example: a b c d a d c b Lead Nitrate + Potassium Iodide ➔ Lead Iodide (solid) + Potassium Nitrate This is true for all precipitation reactions. Materials Required Dropper bottles containing solutions of: Silver Nitrate, Barium Chloride, Sodium Hydroxide, Sodium Chloride, Potassium Bromide, Potassium Iodide, Copper Nitrate, Iron(II) Sulfide, Iron (III) Chloride, Lead Nitrate and Zinc Sulfate. 8 test tubes Test tube rack What to do? • Mix ten drops of each solution in separate test tubes. • What compound forms the solid precipitate (look at solubility rules)? • Record your observations for each reaction in the table provided. Results Table Reactants Name of Ionic Solid Formed Observations AgNO3 + NaCl Silver Chloride Eg A white precipitate forms when the two solutions are mixed. This indicates a chemical change has occurred. AgNO3 + KBr AgNO3 + KI NaOH + FeS NaOH + FeCl3 NaOH + CuNO3 Pb(NO3)2 + KI BaCl2 + ZnSO4 Solubility Rules We know which compound is the solid due to the ions solubility in water (this is due to the chemical properties of these ions). • All ionic compounds that contain lithium, sodium or potassium are soluble in water. • All ionic compounds that contain nitrate ions are soluble in water. • All metal hydroxides are insoluble in water (except LiOH, NaOH and KOH). • Chloride, fluoride and iodide form precipitates with silver and lead ions. • Barium ions form solids with sulfate ions. What to do? • Write word equations for each reaction. • Make sure you indicate which compound forms the solid. • Use the solubility rules to help you determine this. title: Reaction of zinc with iodine
subject: Science
searchText: ﻿Reaction of zinc with iodine This experiment involves the synthesis of a metal salt by direct reaction of a metal and a non-metal. Zinc powder is added to a solution of iodine in ethanol. An exothermic reaction occurs, forming zinc iodide, which can be obtained by evaporating the solvent. Zn + I2 → ZnI2 This experiment illustrates the difference between metallic and non-metallic elements and their reaction to form a compound with new properties. Materials Apparatus and chemicals Eye protection Each group (or demonstration) requires: 3 x Test-tubes and bungs Test-tube rack Measuring cylinder (10 mL) Electric kettle Small filter funnel Filter paper Pasteur pipette Thermometer (0–100 oC) Spatula Watchglass Weighing boat or suitable container for zinc powder Chemicals Solid iodine (Harmful, Dangerous for the Environment), about 0.5 g Zinc powder (Highly Flammable. Contact with water can also release a flammable gas, dangerous for the environment), about 0.5 g Ethanol (Highly Flammable) about 5 mL Procedure SAFETY: Wear eye protection a Measure out 5 mL of ethanol using a measuring cylinder. Place a thermometer in the ethanol and record the temperature. b Add the ethanol to 0.5 g of powdered iodine in a test-tube. Stir carefully, using the thermometer, to dissolve the iodine. The solution should be dark brown. Note the temperature. c When all the iodine has dissolved, slowly add the zinc powder using a spatula and stir the mixture with the thermometer. The temperature should rise, indicating an exothermic reaction. d When the reaction is finished, the color of the iodine should have faded and excess zinc will be left. If not, add further small amounts of zinc powder and stir until the brown color due to iodine has gone. e Filter the solution into another test-tube. f Using a pipette, transfer a few drops of the filtrate on to a watch glass and allow the solvent to evaporate. This can be sped up by placing the watch glass on a beaker containing some hot water. Zinc iodide will be left as a white solid. What’s going on? In this reaction a metal and non metal are being reacted together to form a new substance with different properties. The new substance that is formed is called an ionic substance. This is because in this reaction the two elements are going through a chemical change where they are being transformed from neutral atoms to form positive and negative ions. The zinc metal is losing two electrons to form Zn2+ and the iodine molecules are gaining electrons to form two I- ions. As you will see the physical appearance of the two reactants will change with the formation of the new products, along with their chemical properties. Observations • Note the physical appearance of each substance • Note what occurs during the reaction • Note the appearance of the new substance Questions 1. How do you know a reaction has occurred? 2. What do you think exothermic means? 3. How have the physical and chemical properties of each reactant changed? 4. What is an ion? * This experiment is an assessment item and is to be handed in as a written up lab report, containing an aim, method, procedure, observations, discussion and conclusion. searchText: Neutralisation Reactions: Reactions of acids and hydroxides Background A neutralisation reaction is when an acid reacts with a base, in this case a hydroxide. This reaction produces water and a salt. Neutralisation reactions are very common. Every time we brush our teeth, the toothpaste, which contains a base, neutralises the acids left on our teeth by bacteria. Indigestion, which is caused by too much acid in the stomach, can be relieved by taking an antacid, which are bases in liquid or tablet form. The general reaction equation for an acid combining with a hydroxide is: acid + hydroxide → water + salt When hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide, it produces water and sodium chloride. HCl + NaOH → H 2 O + NaCl Aim : To investigate the neutralisation of a hydroxide with an acid. Equipment : Test tubes x 7 Test tube rack Universal indicator Distilled water Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) Potassium hydroxide (KOH) Hydrochloric acid (HCl) Sulphuric acid (H 2 SO 4 ) Nitric acid (HNO 3 ) Safety glasses Lab coat Method : Put one cm of distilled water in a test tube and add one drop of universal indicator. What colour is the indicator in distilled water? This is the colour you are aiming for. Put approximately 12 drops of sodium hydroxide in a test tube. Add one drop of universal indicator. Record the colour in the results table. One drop at a time, add the hydrochloric acid until you notice a colour change. Record the colour in the results table. Record how many drops of acid you added in the results table. Repeat the process for all combinations of hydroxide and acid. Results : Results for Sodium hydroxide No. of Drops of NaOH Initial colour of indicator Final colour of indicator No. of drops of acid added HCl H 2 SO 4 HNO 3 Results for Potassium hydroxide No. of Drops of KOH Initial colour of indicator Final colour of indicator No. of drops of acid added HCl H 2 SO 4 HNO 3 Questions: At what point was the solution neutral? Explain why. Bees can give you a very nasty sting. The painful sting is caused by the methanoic (formic) acid they inject. What can be done to relieve the sting? Explain why vinegar would not relieve a bee sting. Write a word equation for each of the reactions you conducted in your experiment. Sodium hydroxide + Hydrochloric acid → Neutralisation Reactions: R eactions of acids and carbonates Background The reaction between an acid and a carbonate is a neutralisation reaction. These reactions produce water and a salt, as well as a third product, carbon dioxide. The general reaction equation fo r an acid combining with a carbonate is: acid + carbonat e → water + salt + carbon dioxide When hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium carbonate, it produces water, sodium chloride and carbon dioxide. HCl + Na 2 CO 3 → H 2 O + NaCl + CO 2 You can test for carbon dioxide using limewater. The limewater goes from clear to milky if carbon dioxide is present, due to the formation of a calcium carbonate precipitate. Aim : To investigate the reaction of metal carbonates with an acid. Equipment : Test tubes Test tube rack Test tube stoppers 100 mL beaker Limewater Pipette 10 mL measuring cylinder Samples of various metal carbonates Acids (hydrochloric and nitric) Safety glasses Lab coat Method : Pour 25 mL of limewater into the beaker. Be careful not to shake the limewater bottle. Into a test tube, put a pea sized sample of sodium carbonate. Measure 3 mL of hydrochloric acid in the measuring cylinder. Pour the acid into the test tube and quickly stopper it. Once the reaction has finished, using the pipette, add a small amount of limewater to the test tube by dribbling it down the side of the test tube. Record your observations in the results table. Repeat the experiment with other combinations of acids and carbonates. Record all your tests and observations in the results table. Results : Carbonate Acid Observation of reaction Observation of limewater test Sodium carbonate (Na 2 CO 3 ) Hydrochloric (HCl) Questions: Write a word equation for each of the reactions you conducted in your experiment. The first one has been started for you. Sodium carbonate + Hydrochloric acid → For each of your word equations, write a formula equation underneath. Reaction of Metals with Acids Background The reaction between an acid and a metal is not a neutralisation reaction because metals are not bases and the reaction does not produce water. Instead, this type of reaction produces hydrogen gas and a salt. Some metals, like sodium, react violently while some are unreactive, or inert. The general reaction equation fo r an acid combining with a metal is: acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas When hydrochloric acid reacts with magnesium metal, it produces magnesium chloride and hydrogen gas. HCl + Mg → MgCl 2 + H 2 The test for hydrogen gas is the ‘pop’ test. The gas produced can be collected in an inverted test tube. When a lit match is held near the mouth of the test tube, a popping sound can be heard as the hydrogen reacts with oxygen in the air to form water. Aim : To investigate the reaction of metals with an acid. Equipment : Test tubes Test tube rack Samples of various metals Hydrochloric acid Sulphuric acid Acetic acid (vinegar) Matches Safety glasses Lab coat Method : Pour 2 cm of hydrochloric acid into a test tube. Add a small piece of magnesium to the acid. If there is a noticeable reaction, hold a second test tube inverted over the reaction tube. This will collect the gases produced in the reaction. Hold a lit match to the mouth of the test tube you collected the gas in. If hydrogen has been produced, you should hear a small popping sound. Record your observations in the table. Repeat the magnesium reaction with sulphuric and acetic acid. Try other combinations of acids and metals. Record all your tests and observations. Which of the metals you tested was the least reactive? Write a word equation for six of the reactions you conducted in your experiment. The first one has been started for you. searchText: Types of Reactions Chemical reactions can be categorized into a variety of types. Five common types that we will study are synthesis , decomposition , combustion , single replacement and double replacement . Be familiar enough with the description of each type so that you are able to classify a reaction if given a chemical equation or verbal description. 3980878 228479 Synthesis: Synthesis reactions involve the formation of more complex compounds (many atoms) from simpler compounds and/or elements. The most common synthesis reaction involves the formation of a compound from its elements. Examples: H 2 ( g) + O 2 (g) → 2 H 2 O (g) H 2 ( g) + N 2 (g) → 2 NH 3 (g) General: A + B → AB Synthesis reactions are also referred to as combination, for mation, and addition reactions. 3115945 204470 Decomposition: Decomposition reactions involve the breaking down of more complex compounds (larger, more atoms) into simpler compounds and/or elements. These reactions can often be thought of as being the opposite of synthesis reactions. Decomposition reactions often require heating in order to occur. Examples: 2 H 2 O (l) → 2 H 2 ( g) + O 2 (g) 2 KClO 3 ( s) → 2 KCl (s) + 3 O 2 (g) General: AB → A + B Combustion: Combustion reactions involve the reaction of a substance with oxygen gas (O 2 ). It is often referred to as burning. The products of the reaction are oxides of the elements in the reactants. Hydrocarbon combustion leads to the formation of carbon dioxide gas and water vapor . Examples: 2 Mg ( s) + O 2 (g) → 2 MgO (s) CH 4 ( g) + 2 O 2 (g) → CO 2 (g) + 2 H 2 O (g) General: AB + O 2 (g) → A x O y + B w O z Some combustion reactions are also synthesis reactions. For instance, the combustion of magnesium leads to t he formation of magnesium oxide. Single Replacement: 3308350 6350 Single replacement reactions involve the reaction of an element with an ionic compound. The single element replaces one of the ions in the compound. If the lone element is a metal, then it will replace the positive ion in the compound. If the lone element is a nonmetal , then it will replace the negative ion. Examples: 2 Al ( s) + 3 CuCl 2 ( aq ) → 3 Cu (s) + 2 AlCl 3 ( aq ) 2 NaCl ( s) + F 2 (g) → Cl 2 (g) + 2 NaF (s) General: A + BC → AC + B ( if A is a metal) A + BC → BA + C (if A is a nonmetal ) Single replacement reactions are also referred to as single displacement reactions. 3175000 68580 0 0 Double Replacement: Double replacement reactions involve the reaction of two ionic compounds to form two different ionic compounds. The positive ion in one compound replaces the positive ion in the other compound. Examples: 2KI ( aq ) + Pb (NO 3 ) 2 ( aq ) → PbI 2 (s) + 2 KNO 3 ( aq ) HCl ( aq ) + NaOH ( aq ) → NaCl ( aq ) + H 2 O (l) General: AB + C D → AD + BC Double replacement reactions are also referred to as double displacement reactions, and less commonly as metathesis reactions. Many double replacement reactions involve the formation of a precipitate. The two reactants and one of the products are aqueous solutions of ionic salts and the other product is an ionic salt that is not soluble in water. It is seen as a precipitating solid. This is sometimes termed a precipitation reaction . Some double replacement reactions involve the reaction of an acid with a base; these are a special case of double replacement reactions known as acid-base neutralization reactions . searchText: ﻿THE REACTIVITY OF SOME METALS Activity Series Aim: To test the chemical properties of some metals and arrange them in order of their chemical activity. Materials: Aluminium, magnesium, copper, iron, lead, tin, silver and zinc Steel wool 6 test tubes and rack Zinc sulphate solution (saturated) Copper sulphate solution (saturated) Dilute hydrochloric acid Procedure: 1. Place 5ml of zinc sulfate solution in each test tube. 2. Add a metal sample to each and leave it for 3 to 5 minutes. 3. Record any reactions that occur. A reaction may be indicated simply by a dark deposit on the metal. If the metal remains shiny, you can infer there was no reaction. 4. Wash and clean the samples. Then repeat the steps 1 to 3 using copper sulfate and hydrochloric acid. Again recording your results. Results: Hydrochloric Acid Zinc Sulfate Solution Copper Sulfate Solution Aluminium Copper Iron Lead Magnesium Tin Silver Zinc Questions and Conclusions: Look carefully at your data table and answer these questions. 1. (c) One solution only? (d) No none of the solutions? 3. Try to put the metals in order from most reactive to least reactive. 4. Suppose you want to make a metal tank to hold copper sulfate solution.                                                                    Examiner’s
Name: Donald
                                                                     notes

1. Name the element that is always involved in oxidation
reactions
                                                             (1)
     Oxygen

2. What type of chemical reaction is represented by this

         fuel + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
equation?

                                                             (1)
     Burning

3. Explain how rust is formed.
                                                             (2)
       Rust is made when iron gets wet and oxygen gets to
       it. Rust is called iron oxide (the iron oxide was iron
       but oxygen has got to it).

4. Define the term ‘displacement’ by using an example
                                                            (3)
       Displacement is when a less reactive metal takes the
       place of a more reactive metal. For example,
       magnesium might take the place of a different metal
       – it kicks out the other metal because its more or less
       reactive than the one being kicked out displaced.

5. Propane is a fuel. Write an equation for the combustion
of propane.
                                                          (2)
      Propane + oxygen = carbon dioxide + water

6. Describe how magnesium oxide and carbon dioxide
could be obtained from magnesium carbonate.
                                                           (3)
       Magnesium carbonate could be put in a test tube and
       heated. It would then become magnesium oxide and
       carbon dioxide gas. You could use a Bunsen burner
       to heat the test tube but you should be careful not to
       get burnt.

7. Complete the word equations.
                                                             (4)

8. Write word equations for these reactions:
    a) The thermal decomposition of lithium carbonate
       Copper carbonate → Copper oxide + Carbon dioxide
    b) The oxidation of magnesium
       Magnesium + Oxygen
    c) The combustion of kerosene
       Kerosene  Carbon dioxide + Water
    d) The reaction between copper and iron chloride
       Copper + Iron chloride  Iron + Copper chloride
       Copper + Iron chloride  Copper chloride + Iron
                                                                                          (8)

9. Use examples to explain the term ‘thermal
decomposition’.
                                                                                          (6)
       Thermal means heat, so thermal decomption means
       chopping things up (decomption) using heat.
       Compounds can be broken up into elements using
       thermal decomposition. For example, sodium
       carbonate can be heated and it’ll become sodium and
       carbon dioxide.

Teaching notes
This ‘peer-assessment’ task is designed to be used by students after they have
studied types of chemical reactions. It should be used to consolidate learning.

Students of secondary age are notoriously critical. They take delight in noticing
Donald’s errors, misconceptions and lack of exam technique. Sometimes
however, Donald surprises the students with a great answer!

To stimulate discussion, Donald’s work has been most successfully used in pair
or small group work, followed by targeted whole class questioning.




The following marks and comments are expected from students:

     1.       Donald would score 1 mark.

     Donald has correctly recalled that oxidation involves oxygen (being added
     to a substance).



     2.       Donald would likely score 0 marks.

     To gain the mark, Donald needs to use the term ‘combustion’ which is the
     type of reaction where oxygen combines with another substance (fuel) to
     produce heat and light.



     3.       Donald would likely score 1 mark.

     Donald has recognised the need for oxygen and linked this to the idea of

     would best be represented by an equation (iron + oxygen → iron oxide)
     iron becoming iron oxide. However, the actual formation of the iron oxide

     and this would get Donald the second mark – simply saying ‘oxygen has
     got to it’ isn’t quite enough.



     4.       Donald is confused and would score 0 marks.

     Donald should have said that a more reactive metal takes the place of a
     less reactive metal (he said the opposite) for the first mark. Magnesium is
     a good example to use, but he needs to say that it would ‘kick out /
     displace’ a less reactive metal and give an example (he said more or less).

© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2014        23322                             Page 4 of 8
                                   Types of chemical reaction assessment activity
     The third mark could be obtained by illustrating the idea of displacement
     fully by using an equation.




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2014        23322                           Page 5 of 8
                                   Types of chemical reaction assessment activity
     5.       Donald would likely score just 1 mark.

     Unfortunately, Donald has made the common error of using an ‘equal’ sign
     instead of an arrow in the middle of the equation. The reactants do not
     equal the products, they simply react together to make them.




     6.       Donald would likely score 2 marks (at most).

     One mark will be scored for the word ‘heat’ or ‘heating’ and he may be
     lucky to get another mark for a procedural comment such as using a test
     tube or a Bunsen burner. However, Donald should have stated that the

     illustrate the process using an equation (magnesium carbonate →
     type of reaction that needs to occur is thermal decomposition or he could

     magnesium oxide + carbon dioxide).




     7.       Donald has done quite well and would score 3 marks.

     Donald’s first three equations are perfect.

     He has got confused in the last equation – potassium as a more reactive
     metal displaces silver, leaving potassium chloride, not potassium silver
     (which could not be a compound – it is two metals).



     8.    Donald seems much less confident writing whole word equations.
     He would probably score just 3 marks out of a possible 8.

     The first equation asked for the thermal decomposition of lithium
     carbonate, not copper carbonate so it should be:

                    lithium carbonate  lithium oxide + carbon dioxide

     The second equation gets 1 mark for the reactants, but Donald has not
     given the product. It should be:

                          magnesium + oxygen  magnesium oxide

     Donald gets 1 mark for the products. However, he has forgotten that
     combustion involves oxygen combining with the fuel and so it should be:


© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2014         23322                            Page 6 of 8
                                    Types of chemical reaction assessment activity
                        kerosene + oxygen  carbon dioxide + water




© www.teachitscience.co.uk 2014         23322                           Page 7 of 8
                                     Types of chemical reaction assessment activity
     Donald has correctly written the reactants, so he can have 1 mark for this.
     However, he has forgotten that displacement will only occur if the metal is
     more reactive than the one in the compound. In this case, copper is less
     reactive than iron and so there is no reaction. It could be written in one of
     these ways:

                       copper + iron chloride  copper + iron chloride

                             copper + iron chloride  no reaction




     9.       Donald would likely score 2 marks.

     In 6-mark questions at GCSE, responses are marked in bands of 1-2, 3-4,
     5-6. In each band, literacy is also considered. The same idea can be used
     at KS3 to develop understanding of this way of marking.

     Donald does make a fairly good explanation of what thermal
     decomposition means (breaking down using heat) although breaking down
     would be preferable to chopping up.

     However, to get 3-4 marks, he would need to give a correct example,
     which he has not done. Sodium carbonate can indeed undergo thermal
     decomposition, but it would become sodium oxide and carbon dioxide.

     To get 5-6 marks, the example should be given clearly as a word equation
     (or even a symbol equation) and it should perhaps be noted that there is
     one reactant, yet two products.

     Students should also note his incorrect spelling of the word
     ‘decomposition’. This is particularly silly because the word is in the
     question. He would still get 2 marks though as this band does not require
     accurate spelling.

     Overall, Donald would score about thirteen marks. He needs to improve
     his ability to write word equations and his understanding of scientific
     terminology (e.g. combustion, thermal decomposition) in order to improve.
     He needs to review the definition of displacement and use a reactivity
     series to work out whether elements will displace each other.

- Black holes—page 1

Name:

Skills: interpreting, applying, analysing, evaluating

Black holes are incredibly dense, far denser than the closely packed neutrons that make up neutron stars.
Whatever form the matter inside a black hole takes, there cannot be atoms as we understand them. The
mass of a black hole is thus very large for its size. For example, a black hole with the same mass as the Earth
would be less than two centimetres across! All that mass creates a fiercely strong gravitational field in the
space around a black hole.

The strength of any gravitational field decreases in what is known as an “inverse square’ relationship.
Thus, ifyou double your distance ftom the centre of a black hole, the gravitational field strength decreases
to a quarter. This means that the gravitational field near a small black hole weakens very rapidly with
distance. This is different from our experience in Earth’s gravitational field. For us, a change of several
metres, or even several kilometres, does not create a noticeable change in the gravitational field. That is
because our distance from the centre of the Earth is over 6000 kilometres.

Only the mass of a body, and the distance from its centre, affect the strength of its gravitational field. The
radius of the Earth is about 6370 km, and its mass is about 6 x 10” tonnes. The table below shows how the
gravitational field strength changes with distance near the Earth’s surface, and near a black hole having the
same mass as the Earth.

Apparent brightness is a measure of the brightness of stars as they appear to us on Barth. Just because
a star appears brighter than another when viewed from Earth, it doesn’t mean itis actually brighter, as its
brightness may be due to it being much closer to us. To compare how bright stars actually are, we need to
compare their brightness if viewed from the same distance. This may be done theoretically, and we then use
the term ‘absolute brightness’. The lower the value, the brighter the star, When the scale was first used, the

have had to be assigned negative values.

searchText: Doppler effect The Doppler effect , named after physicist Christian Doppler who proposed it in 1842, is the change in frequency of a wave for an observer moving relative to the source of the wave. It is commonly heard when a vehicle sounding a siren or horn approaches, passes, and recedes from an observer. The received frequency is higher (compared to the emitted frequency) during the approach, it is identical at the instant of passing by, and it is lower during the recession (as it moves away) Light and the Doppler effect The Doppler effect for electromagnetic waves su ch as light is of great use in A stronomy and results in either a so-called “ redshift ” , as things move a way from the observer or a blue shift as they move towards the observer. This colour change is used to help investigate the movement of galaxies and their stars. Since most galaxies are moving away from each other this is supporting evidence for the Big Bang theory.

searchText: 21/09/2017 CERES: Hubble's Classification System Hubble’s Classification Scheme Go back to Lesson. Edwin Hubble developed a galaxy classification scheme consisting of four types: elliptical, spiral, barred spiral, and irregular. Three of these types are represented in the "tuning fork" diagram below. Elliptical Galaxies An elliptical galaxy shows no spiral structure and can vary from almost round (what Hubble called E0) to almost cigar shaped (called E7). This classification is based on our perspective from Earth and not on the actual shape. Spiral Galaxies As their name implies, spiral galaxies have outstretched, curving arms suggestive of a whirlpool or pinwheel. Hubble distinguished different sub- classes according to the tightness of the arms and the size of the nucleus. He called these Sa, Sb, and Sc. In terms of the arms, Sa is the tightest wound while Sc is the most open. In terms of the nucleus, Sa has the largest while Sc has the smallest. The galaxies that appear to have a spiral disc but no visible arms are called S0. Barred Spirals Barred spirals show the same spiral structure as normal spirals, and also a prominent bar through the nucleus. The spiral arms emerge from the end of the bar. The sub-classifications are the same as for normal spirals. Irregulars Certain galaxies lack either an obvious spiral structure or nuclear bulge, appearing instead as a random collection of stars with no obvious order. They are distinguished from ellipticals by their lack of symmetry. http://btc.montana.edu/ceres/html/Galaxy/galhubble.html 1/1

searchText: Stars initially form from clouds of dust and gas……………… The force of gravity makes the dust particles come spiraling in together. As they do, gravitational energy is converted into heat energy and the temperature rises……………… When the temperature gets high enough, hydrogen nuclei undergo nuclear fusion to form helium nuclei and give out massive amoun ts of heat and light. A star is born…………… The star immediately enters a long stable period where the heat created by the nuclear fusion provides an outward pressure to balance the force of gravity pulling everything inwards. In this stable period it ’ s called a MAIN SEQUENCE STAR…….. Eventually the hydrogen begins to run out and the star then swells into a RED GIANT. It becomes red because the surface cools………… A small star like our Sun will then begin to cool and contract into a WHITE DWARF and then finally as the light fades completely it becomes a BLACK DWARF……………………….. Big stars start to glow brightly again as they undergo more fusion and expand and contract several times forming heavier elements in various nuclear reactions. Eventually they explode in a SUPERNOVA…………… The exploding supernova throws the outer layers of dust and gas into space leaving a very dense core called a NEUTRON STAR. If the star is big enough this will become a BLACK HOLE…………... The dust and gas thrown off by the supernova will form into SECOND GENERATION STARS like our Sun……………….

What do you think a star is made of? _________________________________________________________________ ___________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Stars are gaseous objects in space that give off light and heat. They are made mainly of hydrogen and helium, with traces of heavier elements such as boron, carbon and nitrogen. For example, our sun contains about 80% hydrogen and 19% helium, while the remaining 1% is made up of the heavier elements. Compared with the size of the Earth, the sizes of stars are enormous. searchText: Types of Nebulae Nebula are clouds of gas and dust in space. There are five main types of nebulae: * Reflection Nebulae * Emission Nebulae * Dark Nebulae * Planetary Nebulae * Supernova remnant Type of Nebulae Description of Nebulae Example Reflection Nebulae The dust and gas of this type of nebula does not emit its own light. Instead, it reflects light from nearby stars and/or galaxies The Iris nebulae Emission Nebulae These nebula make their own light. Energy from a nearby star heats up the gas and dust in the nebul a. The gas and dust gets energized and start s to release light. The Eagle nebula Dark Nebulae These nebula are dense and block out the light from stars and other nebula behind them. searchText: Where Did the Universe Come From? Steady State Model . This is the old explanation. This says that the universe is infini te in size and has always existed the way it is today. Infinite means never ending. Big Bang Theory . This is a newer idea. It states that at one time in the past all of the matter in the universe was in one place. It then exploded (Big Bang) and all the matter started to spread out forming the universe. A man called Hubble worked out the Big Bang Theory. By studying light he noticed that the Galaxies in the universe were spreading out. He thought if they are all spreading out they must have all started in one place. Distance in Space In space because the distances are so far apart we have to use special units of measure. Light year. This is the distance light travels in one year. It is equal to 9.5 trillion km (9500000000000km). Try these Light Years (ly) To go from light year to Km multiply by 9500000000000. To go from Km to light years divide by 9500000000000 Km 1 9500000000000 2 28500000000000 0.05 Parse c. This is an even bigger unit of measure for distance. One parsec is close to 3 light years. Sometimes Mega parsecs are used.

searchText: Where Does a Star get its Energy From? The sun is a star. The stars you see in the night sky are suns. Our sun is just one of innumerable other suns. In a star 2 hydrogen atoms are joined together to make one helium atom. This happens over and over again, with many hydrogen atoms. When two atoms are fused together to make another element it is called nuclear fusion. When this fusion occurs a lot of energy is released. This is how a star gets its energy. The reason this can happen is because the sun is huge and has a lot of gravity. Gravity is the force of attraction between all matter. It is the gravity that causes enough pressure to “ squash ” (fuses) the hydrogen atoms together. In space we find Nebula. Nebulae are clouds of dust and gas. Slowly the dust and gas comes tog ether due to gravity. Eventually the cloud becomes very dense with a lot of gravity. This gravity gives enough pressure to cause the fusion. title: First law-questions
subject: Science
searchText:
Unit: Force & Motion
Topic: Newton’s First Law - Questions
Answer all questions on a separate sheet of paper.

1.        Does the law of inertia pertain to moving objects, objects at rest or both?

                                                               both

2.        If you were in a spaceship and fired a cannonball into frictionless space, how much force would have to be exerted
          on the ball to keep it moving once it has left the spaceship?

                                                               None

3.        An elephant and a mouse both have the same weight - zero - in “gravitation-free” space. If they were moving toward
          you with the same speed, would they bump into you with the same effect? EXPLAIN!

 NO! The larger mass of the elephant means it has a larger inertia. This means it will be more difficult to change its
                                    state of motion and will therefore “run” you over.

4.        In the cabin of a jetliner that cruises at 600 km/h, a pillow drops from an overhead rack. Does a passenger walking
          up the aisle have to worry about the pillow slamming into her and knocking her over? Explain.

                NO. Since both are in the “same” relative motion, the pillow will simply fall to the floor.

5.        Many automobile passengers have suffered neck injuries when struck by cars from behind. How does Newton's law
          of inertia apply here? How do headrests help to guard against this type of injury?

When hit from behind, the car accelerates forward as does the body since it is pushed by the seat. The head however,
             unless there is a headrest, tries to “stay put.” This results in the head “snapping back”.

6.        Suppose you place a ball in the middle of a wagon, and then accelerate the wagon forward. Describe the motion of
          the ball relative to the ground?

                                                 The ball maintains its position.
          - Describe its motion relative to the wagon?

                            The ball rolls to the back of the wagon.

7.        If an elephant were chasing you, its enormous mass would be most threatening. But if
          you zigzagged, its mass would be to your advantage. Why?

 Its large mass means it has large inertia resulting in the elephant having a difficult time
                                  changing its direction.

8.        Two closed containers look the same, but one is packed with lead and the other with a few feathers. How could you
          determine which has more mass if you and the containers were orbiting in a weightless condition in outer space?

                                                           Shake them.

9.        If suddenly the force of gravity of the sun stopped acting on the planets, in what kind of path would the planets
          move?

                                                          Straight lines.

10.       A helium balloon is held by its string in a car with the windows rolled up. The car, initially at rest, accelerates
          forward. Which direction does the balloon move? Explain.

     Forward. A helium balloon floats to the top of the atmosphere. As the car accelerates forward, the air in the car
              “hangs back” due to its inertia, causing the balloon to “rise” to the “top” of the atmosphere.

 FORCES

   Forces are pushes or pulls.
   A force has a size and a direction, shown by an arrow.
   Symbol F
   Unit newton (N)
   Net Force is the combined effect of all forces on an object.
   Forces in the same direction add together.
   Forces in opposite directions subtract.
   Weight force is force due to gravity.    F=mxg          g = 10 m.s-2    m = mass
   Friction force opposes motion of object. Often causes heat.

    F=mxa


F is net force on object in newtons
m is mass of object in kilograms
a is acceleration on object in metres/sec/sec (m.s-2)

Calculate the acceleration of the above car if its mass is 1000 kg and net force acting is 250 N.
a = F/m       a = 250/1000         a = 0.25 m.s-2



WORK AND POWER
Work
 Work is the amount of energy transferred when an object is moved over a distance.
 Work is only done when a force moves the object.

  W work
W is = F xenergy

 F is the force moving the object, in newtons

Examples:

     Calculate the work done by the person.
     W=Fxd                   W = 800 x 2 = 1600 J
     The toy car has gained 1600 J of Kinetic Energy
2.   A weight lifter lifts a 50 kg box from ground to a height of 2m. What is the work done by
     the weightlifter?
     The 50 kg box needs a force of 500N to lift it against gravity (F = m x g     F = 50 x 10)
     W=Fxd                   W = 500 x 2 = 1000N




        The box has gained 1000N of Gravitational Potential Energy

Energy transfers above assume no energy lost to friction.


Power

    Power is the rate that work is done.
    Symbol P
    Unit watt (W)
    1 watt means 1 joule of energy transferred (work done) each second.

    P=W/t
