searchText:
Forces

Force can cause an object to change its velocity or shape.
Forces push, pull, tug, heave, squeeze, stretch, twist or press.
Forces can change:
             The shape of an object
             The movement of an object
             The speed of an object
             The direction of an object
Not all forces can be seen but the effects can be measured. Forces can
either be contact forces, where the force needs to be in contact with the object                      experiencing
the force OR non-contact forces that will act on an object from a distance without touching it.

Units of Force, Motion and Energy in Science

 Quantity                                      What is it measured in?        Symbol       Equipment used


 Force (including weight)                      Newton                         N            Spring balance

 Mass                                          kilograms                      kg           scales



 Velocity / speed                              metres per second              ms-1         Ticker timer

 Acceleration                                  metres per second per second   ms-2         Ticker timer
 (including gravitational acceleration)

 Energy (including Work)                       Joules                         J




Contact and non-contact forces




Pushes, pulls, friction and tension are contact forces. The object that causes the force touches the object it acts
upon. Non-contact forces such as electrostatic forces, magnetic forces and gravitational forces act without
contact between the object.
113 | P a g e       GZ Science Resources
 Gravity is a force, which acts between bodies even though they are not in contact

Objects create a gravitational field around them. Gravity gives objects of mass in the field a weight force.
    the bigger the object; the stronger the field
    the further away from the object, the less gravitational pull
Any other object within the field is pulled to the center of the mass:
       >accelerating
       >feeling weight
When gravitational force is acting on an object then we can say the object has weight force




Thrust force

Thrust (or applied force) requires some parts of an object (whether gas, liquid or solid) being pushed forcefully
from itself (rocket fuel from a rocket, for example). Once the rocket has left, the "thrust" is no longer present. It
also requires reaction (actual touching) of the thrust medium against the object.

Acceleration is the state of an object, due to a force applied. It is dependent on the force, and on the mass of
an object, but is not a force itself. Friction force opposes an object that is experiencing thrust force. Thrust and
friction are “paired forces” that act in opposite directions on an object.



Friction often provides opposing force acting on moving bodies


                                                   Friction is a force that opposes motion. If an object has
                                                   no motion, then there is no friction.

                                                   When friction occurs, and one surface moves against
                                                   another, the movement causes Kinetic energy to be
                                                   changed into heat energy.

                                                   Smooth surfaces create less friction than rough surfaces.
                                                   Friction that occurs between air or water and a solid body
                                                   is called resistance.

                                                   If friction and thrust forces are equal and opposite, then
                                                   they are said to be balanced.



114 | P a g e     GZ Science Resources
 Support forces

Support forces are equal and opposite to an object experiencing weight
if the forces are balanced. Support force in air is called lift and in water is
called buoyancy.

Buoyancy is an upward support force caused by a fluid that opposes the
weight (gravitational force) of an object in the fluid, usually water. Once
the object remains at a set depth then the support force and weight force
are balanced.




Balanced and unbalanced forces




                                                                           If pairs of forces acting on an
                                                                           object are equal and opposite,
                                                                           they are said to be balanced.

                                                                           relative magnitude of the force.

searchText: ﻿Kinetic Energy and Potential Energy Kinetic Energy Kinetic Energy is associated with the motion of an object. It depends on the mass and velocity of the object. A bullet travelling towards a target, a javelin moving through the air and a person running all have kinetic energy. An object’s Kinetic Energy (KE) can be calculated using the formula Kinetic Energy(J) = ½ mass( kg) x velocity 2(m/s) KE = ½ mv2 Example Calculate the KE of a football which has a mass of 0.4 kg travelling at 5m/s Formula Working Answer/ Units Potential Energy Energy can be stored in a variety of ways such as in food, as stored energy for our body, in petrol as stored energy for a car, in water turning the turbines to create electrical energy or a skier at the top of a mountain has stored energy which becomes kinetic energy (for movement) An object’s Potential Energy (PE) can be calculated using the formula Potential Energy(J) = mass (kg) x gravity(9.8m/s/s) x height(m) PE = mgh Example Calculate the PE of a tennis ball which has a mass of 0.05 kg hit to a height of 8m Formula Working Answer/ Units Kinetic energy and potential energy are related. Imagine a high board diver plunging straight down into the water. At the moment immediately before she leaves the board, her potential energy will be at a maximum. At this stage the diver is stationary and has zero kinetic energy but her position, high above the pool means her potential energy is high. When the diver leaves the board her KE increases until the instant prior to entry to the water when KE is at a maximum. At this point, PE is at a minimum since her height is now reduced to zero. searchText: ﻿Use physics to describe the operation of technological devices, and to solve problems Introduction: Forces and Motion – Year 11 information in 1 easy lesson (plus year 12 work!) Speed & Velocity • The rate at which a body moves from one location to another is usually described as either speed (s) or velocity (v) Average velocity (ms-1) = Distance covered (m) Time taken (s) d v t • if it took 4 hours to travel from Dunedin to Christchurch which is 360km, what is the average speed? • Egs: • What is the speed of a car in kmh-1 if it covers 15km in 30 minutes? • Find the speed of a runner in ms-1 if she covers 1000m in 7 minutes. Converting Units kmh-1 is converted to ms-1 by…… x 1000 (m in km)  3600 (s in hr) ms-1 is converted to kmh-1 by ….. x 3600 1000 Egs: • A cricket ball is bowled at 134km per hour. • Convert 134 kmh-1 to ms-1 (37.22) • If the batsman is 18 m from the bowler when the ball is released, how long has he to prepare this stroke? (about 0.5 s) • Stephen fancied himself as a tennis player. He asked Peter to time his serves from the serve line to the netting fence (30m) • Find the speed of the serve in metres per second if the measured time was 1.2s. (25) • Convert this speed to kmh-1 Distance-Time Graphs d stop constant speed Acceleration • An object changing its speed is accelerating – positively or negatively (decelerating) Acceleration (ms-2) = final velocity – initial velocity (Δv) Time taken (s) v a t • Eg: Calculate acceleration of a trolley which changes from 2ms-1 to 5ms-1 in 2 seconds. Velocity-Time graphs v constant speed accn t Activity: Optional Year 11 Pathfinder: p38-9 no’s 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10,11 Vectors and Scalars • A scalar is a physical quantity that has size (magnitude) but no direction. Egs include distance, speed and temperature • A vector is a physical quantity that has both size and direction. Egs include displacement, velocity and force • A vector can be represented by an arrow. The length represents the magnitude and the arrow represents the direction. • Vectors can be added graphically by placing the tail of the second vector on the head of the first. The vector drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the second vector is the resultant. It is identified by a double arrow. Eg Tom walks 6m in an easterly direction followed by 8m in a northerly direction. Find: a) the total distance Tom has travelled b) the shortest distance from the starting point. Solution: a) The total distance is 6+8 = 14m b) The shortest distance is calculated using a vector diagram and pythagoras’ theorem which states that for a right angled triangle, the hypotenuse squared equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. So: √62 + 82 = √ 36 + 64 = √100 = 10m Let’s Get Moving- Checking Motion understanding! 1. Complete the table. Name Symbol(s) Metric unit Some other units comment Time s minute, ______ How ________ an even takes to occur d m cm, ____ How _______ something has travelled Speed v ______ or _____ mms-1, ______ Distance covered during one unit of _______ v ms-1 ______, kmh-1 Speed in a particular ____________ Acceleration ms-2 Kmh-1s-1, ______ Rate of change of ___________ 2. Use the formula triangles to complete the equations. v = a = Δd= Δv= Δt = Δt = 3. Complete the table Distance Travelled Time taken Speed 100m 20s 5s 12cms-1 2.5km 125ms-1 1500km 100kmh-1 15min 80kmh-1 186km 3h Initial speed Final speed Change in speed Time taken Acceleration 5ms-1 17 ms-1 4s 0kmh-1 72kmh-1 24s 15 ms-1 -50 ms-1 10s 35kmh-1 15kmh-1 5kmh-1s-1 35 ms-1 55 ms-1 11s 180kmh-1 4s -15kmh-1s-1 4. What does a negative acceleration tell you? 5. Convert these measurements to the new units. Show your working. a) 1km = m b) 1675m = km c) 1h = s d) 720s = h e) 72kmh-1 = ms-1 f) 5 ms-1 = kmh-1 Forces – Checking what you know • Forces push, pull, tug, heave, squeeze, stretch, twist or press. • Forces change: the shape of an object the movement of an object the speed of an object • Some forces act by contact which needs to touch an object to produce an effect, eg pushing by hand, ocean waves crashing on rocks, tiny forces holding a soap film together eg thrust, support, friction (drag) • Some forces do not need contact, and can act at a distance. These are non contact or field forces eg magnetic, gravitational and electrostatic Direction and Strength of Forces • Forces can act upwards, downwards, sideways, or any direction at all. • Arrows are used to show direction of forces • Strength of force is shown by the thickness or length of an arrow. Measuring Forces • Meters that measure forces usually have springs in them. The bigger the force the more the spring is squashed or stretched. • Spring balance or forcemeter or newtonmeter are often used in schools. • A spring is stretched by the pulling force and squashed by the pushing force. • The amount of force has a unit called a newton (N) • Notice that 1kg = 10N. What would 2kg be? 0.5kg? 100kg? Balanced and Unbalanced Forces • The forces acting on an object determine how that object will move. If we push on some object and the object doesn’t move, then the force we exert must be balanced by another force. • An unbalanced force will produce acceleration Newton’s First Law of Motion If the forces acting on an object are balanced, then the object will either stay still or keep moving at the same speed in the same direction. Thus a force is needed to make something speed up or slow down or change direction. Eg. In a car crash, a large force acts on the car and quickly stops the car. However, the driver will keep on moving with the same speed in the same direction until a force slows him or her down. The force is hopefully provided by a seatbelt or airbag. Without either, the driver may continue moving right through the windscreen and out of the car. Newton’s Second Law of Motion If there are unbalanced forces acting upon an object, then the object will accelerate in the direction that the net force acts. The size of the acceleration depends upon the mass of the object and size of the force. This is illustrated by the relationship F=m.a In sport, acceleration can be improved by better force from muscular contraction or reducing the weight of the object to be moved. Eg for javelin, shotput etc you can improve strength and for running you can reduce weight. Laboratory: Tug of War Acceleration due to Gravity • A free falling object has an acceleration of 9.8ms-2 (more commonly rounded to 10ms-2). This means that each second its speed will increase by 10ms-2 until it reaches terminal velocity Laboratory: Determining acceleration due to gravity Tug-O-War What to do: • Have one person hold the trolley still in the middle of the bench • By varying the sizes of m1 and m2 set up each force arrangement shown in the table below • When each arrangement is ready, record F1 and F2 then let the trolley go and observe the motion. NB: Catch the trolley before it crashes or else! Results: Arrangement F1(N) F2 (N) Net force (N) Observation with respect to acceleration F1 >>>>>F2 F1 > F2 F1 = F2 F1 < F2 F1 <<<< F2 Conclusion: Write a statement which summarises your findings. Determining the Acceleration of Gravity Materials: strong thread, large metal washers, retort stand, metre ruler, stopwatch Principles and Method: • When a body accelerates, its velocity changes over time. For eg; if you drop a ball from the top of a tree, gravity pulls on the ball and causes it to move faster and faster toward the ground. If a body has an acceleration of 9.8ms­­-2, this means that after one second, the body has a velocity of 9.8ms-1‑, after 2 seconds, a velocity of 19.6ms-1 and so on. • Gravity is a force that causes the pendulum to accelerate and swing back and forth. We will use a pendulum to find the magnitude of the acceleration of gravity because the pendulum executes simple harmonic motion. T= 2Π T= the period of the pendulum, l is the length of the pendulum, and g is the acceleration of gravity. There is no mass in the formula indicating the period (time) is independent of mass. • Pull the pendulum back 10-15º and release. Measure the time required for the pendulum to swing 10 times, and divide by 10 to find the average T. Substitute this value and the measured length of the pendulum (from retort stand to washer) into the following equation and solve for g: g= • Record your results in the table below. Repeat with 3 different lengths of pendulum, and calculate an average value of g. The accepted value for the acceleration is 9.8ms­­-2. What experimental errors might you have made? • Calculate the relative error of your values of g using the following formula: Relative error= (observed – accepted) * 100% = ( your g – 9.8) * 100% = Accepted 9.8 Length of pendulum (m) TRIAL- period T (s) Average calculated acceleration of gravity g (ms-2) Average Relative error % 1 2 3 Mass and Weight • Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kg. The mass of an objects is the same regardless of where it is located in the universe. • The weight of an object is the force of gravity that acts on the object. The weight of an object depends on where it is located in the universe. • Weight is measured in newtons (N) because it is a force. • Weight can be calculated from Fw = m.g where g is the acceleration due to gravity and on earth, is accepted as 10Nkg-1. • The weight of an object on the moon is 1/6 that on Earth because the gravitational field strength is less. Worksheets • Some ‘quick’ problems • ESA book (y11) • 12 physics pathfinder exercises. Equilibrium • When the resultant force on an object is zero, the object is in equilibrium. • In this case, the object is either not moving (static equilibrium) or it is moving in a straight line at constant speed (dynamic equilibrium). Some ‘Quick’ Problems 1. The diagram shows the forces being applied to a 160kg bicycle and rider. a) what is the direction and size of the nett force acting on the bike and rider? b) Calculate the acceleration of the bike and rider. Give the correct unit with your answer. 2. A motorbike with its rider has an acceleration of 10ms-2. The nett force exerted by the engine is 5800N. Calculate the combined mass of bike and the rider. 3. How would the acceleration of a dragster be affected if the following changes were applied? a) the mass of the dragster remains constant but…… i) the engine is tuned up to give twice the force ii) the engine is de-tuned to give half the force b) the engine force remains constant but….. i) the mass of the dragster is doubled ii) the mass of the dragster is halved. Torque -Optional reading from pp167-9 for Torque. • Forces are often used to rotate or turn objects – this turning effect is called a torque or moment. • The turning of a door handle, using a spanner to tighten a nut and the force applied to the pedal of a bicycle are examples of torques. • The torque is always stated relative to a point called the pivot. • To describe a torque, the size of the force and the perpendicular distance between the line of action of the force and the pivot must be known. • Torque is calculated as: T = F. d⊥ Where F = Force and d⊥ = perpendicular distance between line of action at force and pivot • The SI unit for torque is the Newton-metre, Nm. The direction of the torque is usually stated as being clockwise or anticlockwise Balanced Ruler • A suspended ruler was balanced by moving a mass-stack to a position where the ruler no longer turns. • The weight F of the mass-stack produces a clockwise torque Tc = Fd1 where d1 is the distance of the point of suspension of the mass stack from the pivot. • The weight Fg of the ruler acts through its centre of gravity. • The weight Fg of the ruler produces an anit-clockwise torque TA = Fgd2 where d2 is the distance of the centre of gravity of the ruler from the pivot. • The balanced suspended ruler is said to be in rotational equilibrium as it obeys the principle of turning moments Principle of Turning Moments For an object in

searchText: ﻿QUESTION ONE: Bike Riding Sam and Trevor live in Christchurch. Because the city area where they live is flat, the two boys ride their bikes everywhere rather than spend money on bus tickets. (a) Sam has to ride 2.4km to school and it normally takes him about 6 minutes. Calculate Sam’s average speed in ms-1 riding to school. (b) Sam learns in Science that while he is riding there are four main forces acting on him. These are: friction, thrust, gravity and reaction forces. (i) On the diagram below draw in four labeled arrows to represent these four forces. (ii) Describe a situation in which the two forces acting in the vertical direction would not be equal and opposite. Also comment on what would happen in this situation you have described. (c) Trevor complains to Sam that he seems to have to do more work riding his bike than Sam does. Ignoring their fitness levels, suggest two reasons why Trevor may in fact be correct. (d) (i) Sam decides to calculate his maximum acceleration from a standing start. His speedometer tells him he had reached a speed of 20ms­1 after 3.6s. Showing the equation you use and the working involved, prove that his acceleration was 5.6ms-2. (ii) The combined mass of Sam and his bike is 70kg. Assuming that Sam’s maximum acceleration is 5.6 ms-2, calculate the maximum force he uses to accelerate. Use the equation F = m x a. (iii) Trevor does the same calculation as Sam and finds that his maximum accelerating force is 340N. If Trevor applies this force steadily over a distance of 25m, calculate his power output if it took him 10s to travel the 25m. QUESTION TWO: Bungy Jumping Sam decides to do the bungy jump while visiting Skipper’s Canyon with his friend Trevor. The drop is around 100m from a bridge above the canyon. Complete the statements below to compile a summary of this unit. The missing words can be found in
the word list below.
 1. Speed is a measure of the …………… at which an object moves over a distance.
 2. …………… speed can be calculated by dividing the distance travelled by the time taken.
 3. …………… is a measure of the rate of change in position. In order to describe the velocity fully,
    the …………… of the change in position must be stated.
 4. The …………… speed of an object is its speed at a particular instant of time.
 5. The …………… of an object moving in a straight line is a measure of the rate at which it changes
    speed.
 6. The average acceleration of an object can be calculated by …………… the change in its speed by
    the time taken for the change.
 7. The force of gravitational attraction to a large object such as a planet is called …………… .
 8. An object will remain at rest, or will not change its speed or direction, unless it is acted upon by an
    outside, …………… force.
 9. The acceleration of an object depends on the mass of the object and the …………… force acting
    on it.
10. When an object applies a force to a second object, the second object applies an …………… and
    …………… force to the first object.

title: Motion energy 2009
subject: Science
searchText: ﻿ Motion energy is correctly termed kinetic energy (you may remember this from last year). It is the energy something posesses if it has movement, for example a bullet has a lot of kinetic energy because it is moving very fast. This kind of energy is of great interest to athletes as it is how they will win their race! Stability is also an important aspect of sport, whether you are a javelin thrower, a gymnast or a sprinter you will want to maximise stability in a variety of positions. 1. CENTRE OF MASS The centre of mass of a sportsperson is the single point through which the whole mass of the body can be seen to act. The postion of the centre of mass can affect the balance of an athlete. Examples of the effect of the centre of mass include; gymnasts whose centre of mass is off centre at inappropriate times can lose their balance; divers with the same problem will have trouble executing a high scoring dive. Weightlifters stand with their feet apart to lower their centre of mass and give them greater stability (ASTA, 2000). ACTIVITY 1: Determining the Centre of Mass Materials: 1 Plumb-bob 1 sheet of shapes to cut out scissors, glue, poster paper The centre of mass can be determined using a plumb-bob, which consists of a piece of thread with a mass on one end. Method: 1. Cut out the model. 2. Push a pin into any point on the model and tie the plumb-bob to the pin. 3. Trace the vertical line on the model formed by the hanging thread. 4. Push the pin into another point on the model and again trace the vertical line formed by the hanging thread. 5. The point where these two lines intersect is the centre of mass. Mark it with a big X 6. Now cut out the remainder of the figures, find their centre of mass. 7. Place them in correct order to show the changes in the centre of mass of an athlete performing the long jump. 8. Glue to the paper provided and write an appropriate heading to explain your series of figures. 2. FORCES Forces are a very important part of our every day life. While we may not want to execute a triple cartwheel with a round off on our way to school we want to be able to get off the bus safely and manage walking up and down stairs and getting around in general. We experience many different forces nearly all of the time. A force is a push or a pull which one object applies to another object. The unit of force is the Newton (N). In each of these situations give an everyday example of a; force that get objects moving. Example…………………………. force that stops moving objects . Example…………………………. force that changes the direction in which an object is moving. Example…………………………. force that stretches an object. Example…………………………. force that might squash, bend, twist or turn objects. Example…………………………. force that prevents movement of objects by balancing other forces acting on the same object. Example…………………………. Some forces act at a distance e.g. gravity (weight), electric forces, magnetic forces. Some forces act on contact e.g. impact (collision) forces, elastic forces, friction, muscular forces.  Some important forces that we will look at are WEIGHT and FRICTION. Mass is the amount of matter in an object (and has the unit of kg). Weight is a measure of the force of gravity on an object (and has the unit of N). Thus, mass of an object remains constant no matter where the object is. However, the weight of an object varies, depending on the force of gravity being exerted on the object. Weight and mass are related according to the equation weight = mass x "g" where "g" is the force of gravity. If weight has the unit of N and mass the unit of kg then "g" will have the unit of N/kg (Newtons per kilogram). On earth "g" has the value of approximately 9.8 Nkg. Examples 1. a) What is the weight of an apple which has a mass of 0.25 kg? b) What is the weight of a 500 g object? 2. Gravity is 2 N/kg on the moon. a) What would be the weight of a 6 kg object on the moon? If an object is resting ("sitting") on a table, the object exerts a force on the table. This force Fw is equal to the weight of the object. Examples 1. A book of weight 10 N is resting on a table. What force does the book exert on the table? 2. A box of mass 40 kg is placed on the floor. What force does the box exert on the floor? ACTIVITY 2: Mass and Weight. Aim: Investigating the difference between mass and weight in the Earth’s gravitational field. Equipment: 5.0 N spring balance a set of slotted 50 g masses retort stand bosshead and clamp Method: 1. Pull down the hook until it reads 1 N. Then pull down to 2 N, you will get a feel for how strong a 1 and 2 newton force is. 2. Hang the spring balalnce from a rod fixed to a retort stand and adjust the pointer so that is reads zero. 3. Attach a 50 g mass to the hook of the spring balance and recod its weight in newtons in the table below. 4. Add the masses one at a time, until you have a total mass of 400 g. Record the mass in kilograms nad weight in newtons as you go. Mass (g) Mass (kg) Weight (N) 5. Use your results to complete a copy of the graph below. 6. Draw a line through the points you have plotted and continue your line to where you think it should be if you measured the weight of a mass of 500 g. ( This process is called extrapolation.) Questions: 1. The gravitational force field on the moon is less than that on earth. Would your items have a different mass on the moon? Explain. 2. Would your items have a different weight on the moon? Explain. 3. If your items were weighed in a gravitational field that had a strength of 11.5 N/kg then calculate the weight of one of your items in that situation. Friction is a force which arises whenever one object moves, or tries to move, over another. Friction always acts in the direction opposite to the direction of the motion. Factors that affect friction are - the nature of the two surfaces in contact - lubrication between the two surfaces - the size of the force pushing the two surfaces together. Example For each of the following situations, in which would the force of friction between the two surfaces be the greater? a) a box sliding over a carpet; or the same box sliding over a polished wood floor. b) a car with bald tyres moving on a road; or the same car with new tyres moving on the same road. c) a box being pushed over a floor; or a box on rollers being pushed over the same floor. ACTIVITY 3: Measuring the force of friction. Aim: To examine the force of friction of different surfaces. Materials: A block of wood A spring balance String Method: 1. Attach the force measurer to the block of wood as shown in the above diagram. 2. Pull the block smoothly over the bench at a constant speed. Measure and record the force required to keep the block moving at a constant speed. Make sure you repeat each trial at least three times. 3. Repeat this for two other different surfaces. SURFACE TYPE TRIAL 1 TRIAL 2 TRIAL 3 FRICTIONAL FORCE (N) (AVEREAGE) Questions: 1. Would the addition of extra mass to the wooden block increase or decrease the sliding frictional force? Would it depend on whether you put the additional block on top or beside the first one? Explain what you think. If you have time, test your ideas. 2. Name a sport in which friction is a problem. Explain. 3. What reduces the friction between the iceskates and the ice? PROBLEM SHEET 1 - Forces 1. i) Give two examples of situations in which contact forces are acting. ii) Give two examples of situations in which forces are acting at a distance. 2. Draw a brick being pulled along by a rope in the space below. i) What force is slowing up the brick? ii) How could you make the brick slide along more easily? 3. i) An astronaut weighs 750 N on earth. What is his mass? ii) If gravity on the moon is 2 N/kg, what is his weight on the moon? iii) What is his mass on the moon? 4. A body has a mass of 10 kg. What is its weight in Newtons? 5. i) What would be the weight of a 1000 g mass on the moon if gravity is 2 N/kg? ii) What would it weigh on earth? iii) What would its mass be on earth? 6. i) What would be the weight of a 500 g object be on the moon where gravity is 2 N/kg? ii) What would the object weigh on the earth? iii) What would the mass of the object be on earth? ANSWERS. 1. i) when two cars collide, when a box is pushed by a person ii) when two magnets are brought close together, when a charged comb is placed near some dry hair. 2. i) friction ii) lubricate the surface, smooth the surface, put the block on rollers 3. i) m = = 76.5 kg ii) Fw = m x g = 76.5 x 2 = 153 N iii) mass = 76.5 kg 4. Fw = 10 x 9.8 = 98 N 5. i) mass = 1 kg Fw = m x g = 1 x 2 = 2 N ii) Fw = m x g = 1 x 9.8 = 9.8 N iii) Mass = 1 kg 6. i) mass = 0.5 kg Fw = m x g = 0.5 x 2 = 1 N ii) Fw = m x g = 0.5 x 9.8 = 4.9 N iii) mass = 0.5 kg 3. SPEED Speed is the rate of change of distance of a body. The average speed is the distance moved per unit time, Speed(av) = distance time Speed is a scalar quantity as it does not require any direction to be named. The unit of speed is determined by using the formula, that is, dividing the units of length (m) by units of time (s), (or m/s ) ( or km/h) Example 1: A girl can run 600 metres in 2 minutes. What is her average speed in metres per second? Distance = 600m Average speed = distance Time = 2 min = 120s time Average speed = ? = 600 120 = 5m/s Answer: The girl's average speed is 5m/s PROBLEM SHEET 2- Speed 1 A toy car travels 5 metres in 4 seconds, calculate its average speed. 2 What is the average speed of a car which travels 250m in 15 s? 3 By how much is a car exceeding a 60 kilometres per hour speed limit if it travels 120 kilometres in 1.5 hours? 4 Calculate the average speed in metres per second of a rifle bullet which travels one kilometre in 0.5 seconds. 5 What is the average speed of a sprinter who runs 100m in 12.5 s ? 6 A body travels 36m in 4s. What is its average speed? 7 Determine the average speed (in kmh-1) of a plane which flies a distance of 720 km in 1.5 hours. Answers: 1) 1.25m/s; 2) 16.7m/s 3) 20km/h; 4) 2000m/s 5) 8m/s 6) 9m/s 7) 480km/h Measuring Speed This policewoman is using a laser to detect the speed of on coming cars. Why is it important to measure the speed of cars? In what other situations in measuring speed important? Ticker timers are useful tools when measuring speed in a classroom situation. Ticker timers produce dots on a strip of paper at very precise intervals, which allows you to measure the speed of the object that has produced the dots. The ticker timer produces 50 dots per second. (50 Hz or 50 cycles per second is the frequency of AC electricity). Which means 5 dots in every 0.1 second. This precision allows you to calculate the distance travelled in 0.1 seconds. Since, speed is equal to distance divided by time, then you can calculate the speed from a ticker timer tape. What is the speed of this above sample in m.s-1? searchText: Motion Graphs Describing the motion of an object is occasionally hard to do with words. Sometimes graphs help make motion easier to picture, and therefore understand. Remember: Motion is a change in position measure by diastanece and time. Spoeed tells us the rate at which an object moves. Velocity tells the speed and direction of a moving object. Acceleration tells us the rate speed or duirection changes. Distance-Time Graphs Plotting distance against time can tell you a lot about motion. Let’s look at the axes: Time is always plotted along the bottom on the X-axis . The further to the right on the axis, the longer the time from the start. Distance is plotted up the left had side of the graph on the Y-axis . The higher up the graph, the further the distance from the starting point. 438150 142875 If an object is not moving, a horizontal line is shown on a distance-time graph. 504825 116840 Time is increasing to the right but the distance does not change. The object is not moving so we say it is at rest. If an object is moving at a constant speed, it means it has the same increase in distance in a given time. Time is increasing to the right, and the distance is increasing constantly with time. The object moves at a constant speed. Constant speed is shown by straight lines on a graph. 419100 128905 Let’s look at two moving objects: Both of the lines on the graph show that each object moved the same distance, but the object shown by the steeper dashed line gets there before the other one. 476250 114935 In this case, a steeper line shows the same distance travelled but in a shorter time. Both lines are straight, so b o th speeds are constant. Graphs that show acceleration look different from those that show constant speed. 409575 155575 The line on this graph is curving upwards. This shows an increase in speed since the line is getting steeper. In a given time, the distance the object moves is getting larger, it is accelerating. Summary: A distance-time graph tells us how far an object has moved with time. The steeper the graph, the faster the motion. A horizontal line means the object is not changing its position. If it is not moving, we say it is at rest. A downward sloping line means the object is returning to the start. 857250 29845 Examine the graphs below. searchText: Newton’s Laws of Motion Name _________________________ Newton’s first Law of Motion states: A body will continue in its state of motion unless acted upon by an external force. This means, if a body is at rest, it will remain ________________. If a body is travelling at constant velocity, it will continue ___________________________________. This property of a body to stay in its state of motion is called its inertia . This law explains why a magician can whip a tablecloth out from underneath plates and glasses. You can try this using a beaker, a coin and a piece of card. Question 1. Explain why seatbelts help prevent injuries to passengers when a car stops suddenly in a collision. Question 2. People can get whiplash (neck injury) if the car they are seated in is hit from behind while they are stopped at a traffic light. Explain why, using Newton’s first law. Question 3. Why is it difficult for a charging elephant to change direction? Newton’s second law of motion describes that a body’s acceleration is proportional to the net force acting on it. This means that a large force will produce a _______________ acceleration, while a small force will produce a ________________ acceleration. The mass of the body is also important. Force = mass x acceleration or F = m.a Force is measured in ______________ which has the symbol N. T o calculate force in Newtons, mass must be in kilograms (kg) and acceleration must be in m/s/s (ms -2 ). If an object has a large mass, it will need a _________ ___________ to accelerate it. Eg., it needs more force to push a car than to push a bicycle. Question 4. Describe what would happen to a wheelbarrow’s acceleration if two people are pushing it instead of one. Question 5. If the acceleration caused by gravity is equal to 9.8 ms -2 , calculate the force exerted on a falling basketball with a mass of 0.62 kg. We know that acceleration can be calculated using the equation a= v-u t So if F = m x a , we can combine the 2 equations to make F=m (v-u) t or Ft=m(v-u) This equation helps us to understand many applications of Newton’s laws – in collisions and in sports. In a car collision, what this equation means is that if the car stops in a short amount of time, the force acting on the car and its passengers will be high. That is, if time is small, force will be ___________. This is why many of the road safety devices focus on letting passengers take more time to stop. Crumple zones in cars ensure that the passenger seats keep travelling for a bit longer once the front of the car has hit an obstruction like a wall . Since the car’s change in velocity is the same in a collision whether it stops suddenly or not, a l onger time to stop means that the force acting on the passengers is _________, and this reduces the amount of injury. Question 6. Fences and signposts on the side of the roads are designed so that they give way if they are hit by a vehicle. Explain how this is safer for drivers than the old rigid steel posts and fences. Question 7 . Why are dashboards in cars padded? (You need to mention force and time in your answer.) Question 8. When a cricketer catches a ball, he will move his hands towards his body in the direction that the ball is travelling. Explain how this allows the cricketer to catch the ball without hurting his hands. The second application of this equation is to do with sport. Often sportspeople want to hit or kick or throw a ball faster and further. However, the amount of force they can exert is limited by their strength. If the force is allowed to act on the ball for longer, it will cause a larger change in velocity. This is why tennis players and footballers follow through, keeping the racquet or foot in contact with the ball for a fraction of a second longer. Ft=m(v-u) If time, t is increased then the ball’s change in velocity will be increased. Question 9 . Explain why most golfers swing the club in a continuous swing, even after the ball has been hit. Question 10. Many of the top tennis players have their racquets strung with fairly loose strings. How does this enable them to hit a ball at close to 200 kmh -1 ? Newton’s third law of motion states ‘For every force there is an equal and opposite force’. Eg 1. As you are sitting on your chair, gravity is pulling you downwards. You don’t fall to the ground because the chair exerts an equal and opposite force upwards on you. Eg 2. When we walk, we push back on the ground, and the ground exerts an equal force in the opposite direction, pushing you forward. This process is assisted by friction. If you try to walk on slippery ice, it is difficult to push backward on the ground, so you don’t travel forward as easily. Eg 3. When a rocket launches, it pushes burning fuel down out of the rear of the rocket. The fuel pushes with an equal and opposite force up on the rocket. Draw a diagram showing this. Question 11. Use Newton’s third law to explain how a swimmer moves through the water. Question 12. When someone fires a rifle, it recoils into the shooter’s shoulder. Explain this using Newton’s law. Choose one of Newton’s laws to fill out the table below, then explain your choice. Sometimes there are more than one correct answer. Your justification is important. Situation Newton’s law Why did you choose this law? We bend our knees when we land after jump ing off a table so we don’t hurt ourselves A rower pulls the oar through the water to propel the boat People standing in a bus tend to fall forward when the bus stops A basketballer jumps up to the ring It takes a long time to stop an ocean liner A baseball pitcher follows through with her hand when she throws the ball If we are catching an egg, we need to move our hands towards our body so the egg doesn’t crack Year 10 Physical science assignment Forces in sport Choose a sport or other activity (dance, fishing, racing, etc) and research the forces involved in this sport. You could discuss which forces are helpful in this sport, and which forces are unhelpful. Often friction needs to be reduced in a sport as it causes drag . Discuss how Newton’s laws of motion apply in this sport. Your presen tation should be approximately 3 pages long. This includes the diagrams that you will provide to illustrate your understandings. You will be given some time in class to conduct your research. Due date ___________

searchText: ﻿NEWTON’S SECOND LAW OF MOTION What does this mean? What variables govern the acceleration of the following bodies? NEWTON’S SECOND LAW can be stated as: a = _F_ m where a = acceleration in msֿ² F = total force on the object (Newtons) m= mass of the object (kg) Can also be stated as F = m a Example: A space shuttle has a mass of 2.2 million kilograms, of which 86% is the mass of fuel, most of which is burnt during the launch. There are two forces acting on the space shuttle; downward pull of gravity, at 22 million Newtons, and the upward thrust resulting from the burning of fuel which is about 29 million Newtons. The forces acting on the space shuttle are not balanced. The total force acting on the space shuttle is 7 million Newtons upwards. Newton’s second law of motion can be used to estimate the acceleration of the space shuttle at blast off: a = _F_ m = 7 000 000 N upwards 2 200 000 kg = 3.2 msֿ² The space shuttle is gaining speed at the rate of only 3.2 msֿ² or 11.5 km/h each second. Small acceleration at blast off is not a problem because as the fuel is burnt, the mass of the space shuttle gets smaller. As this happens the acceleration gradually increases, and the space shuttle gains more speed quickly. Practice Exercises 1. What force will accelerate an 18 kg object at 3 msֿ²? 2. Find the mass of a block if a 65 Newton force accelerates it at 2.5 msֿ². 3. An 8000 N force acts on a 125 kg vehicle. What acceleration is produced? 4. A 150 kg motorcycle is retarded at 2.5 msֿ². Magicians often pull a table cloth from under a table set with china. Use Newton’s first law to explain how this is possible. In reality, the china will probably still move slightly in the direction of the table cloth. Explain why this happens. Rockets in space keep moving without needing engines to do so. Use your knowledge of the composition of space to e xplain why this happens. Even when a person is not wearing a seatbelt, thei r lower body is less likely to be influenced by inertia than their head. Identify which force slows the lower body but is unable to act on the upper body and head. A car on ice is almost impossible to stop. Use the concept of inertia to explain why. What is the force that is required to regain control? Propose a reason why truc k cabins need to be rigid and able to withstand a heavy blow from the rear. Seatbelts can leave bad bruising and cracked ribs in a car accident. Explain why they do this. Your friend is arguing that this is a good reason not to wear a seatbelt. What reason would you give you friend to convince them to wear a seatbelt? Are passengers in the rear of a car safe when not wearing seatbelts? Explain why or why not. What is Newton’s second law of motion? Use your knowledge of how to use a speed triangle to draw a triangle for the force equation. Describe what happens to the acceleration when the same force pushes larger and larger masses. Describe what happens to the acceleration of an object if the force pushing it is increased. Force Accel - eration Mass Calculate the force, in Newtons (N), being applied if: A 5 kg box accelerates at 4.1 m/s 2 . A 1.3 tonne car accelerates at 2 m/s 2 . A 400 g ball accelerates at 4 m/s 2 . searchText: Speed and Acceleration using a Ticker Timer coil magnet ticker tape power input ( a.c .) vibrating bar carbon paper disc A ticker timer is a piece of equipment which can be used to measure speed and acceleration. The ticker timer has a bar which vibrates at a known frequency of 50 times per second. A piece of ticker tape is passed under the bar and a carbon paper disc is threaded between the bar and the ticker tape. There is a small nodule at the end of the bar which produces a dot each time it hits the tape. The time between each dot is 1/50 th of a second, or 0.02 seconds. By measuring the distance between 6 dots (5 spaces) and dividing by the time taken (0.02 x 5 = 0.1 sec) the average speed can be calculated. Look at the ticker tape below. Use the following method to calculate the speed the tape was moving. Draw a line through a dot near the left. Draw a second line through the fifth dot after that. Measure the distance between the dots in cm. Calculate the speed in cm per second by dividing by 0.1 seconds (the time it takes to make 5 dots) Try the two examples below To calculate acceleration using a ticker timer, you must calculate the average speed of multiple intervals on your ticker tape. Look at the ticker tape below. Speed = Change in speed = Calculate the acceleration of this ticker tape by Putting a line through the first dot. Put a line through every fifth dot after that. Use the method on the previous page to find the average speed between the first two lines. Repeat the process for the other 3 intervals to get the average speed for each interval. Find the change in speed between each interval. The acceleration is the change in speed divided by the time between the intervals, in this case 0.1 seconds. Try to find the acceleration of the ticker tapes below using the method above.

searchText: Speed and Velocity Practice Problems Distance Speed Time Speed If a car travels 500m in 4 0 seconds how fast is it going in m/s ? A cyclist travels 6 0km in 2 hours . What is his speed in km/h? Tim drives 400m to the shops in 20 seconds. Calculate the average speed of the car in m/s. If the speed limit in the area is 70km/h, was Tim speeding? ÷3.6 speed in speed in km/h m/s ×3.6 The pitcher’s mound in baseball is 85 m from the plate. It takes 4 seconds for a pitch to reach the plate. How fast is the pitch? A train travels 510m in a time of 17 seconds. Calculate the average speed of the train in m/s. Calculate the average speed of the train in km/h. A plane travels 3 95,000 meters in 9000 seconds. What was its speed in m/s ? How fast is it travelling in km/h? Barry walks to Scott’s house, a distance of 600m in 5 minutes, but Scott is not home. Barry then walks to John’s house, 300m away and it takes him 3 minutes. What speed , in m/s, was Barry walking at on his way to Scott’s house? What was Barry’s speed , in m/s, between Scott and John’s house? What was Barry’s average speed , in m/s, for the whole journey? Time How long does it take for a car travelling at 15m/s to go 600m? How long wi ll it take for a bug to travel 9 meters across the floor if it is travelling at 1.5 m/s? A bus is travelling at 20 m/s. How long does it take for the bus to travel 72km? (Hint: change the speed to km/h) A bullet travels at 850 m/s . How long will it take the bullet to go 1 km? (Hint: change the distance into m) Sarah swims backstroke at an average speed of 8 m/s. How long will it take her to complete a 200 m race? How long would it take for the sound of thunder to travel 1, 500 m if the speed of sound is 340 m/s? A train travels in a straight line from one station to the next at 40km/h and then returns at 60km/h. If the two stations are 5km apart, how long is the train’s journey? Distance A model car travels at 2.5m/s for 5 seconds. How far does the car travel? A train is moving at 10m/s. How far does it travel in 5 seconds? The fastest train in the world moves at 500 km/h. How far will it go in 3 hours ? Mike rides his motorcycle at an average speed of 20 m/s for 500 seconds. How far did he ride in metres? How many kilometres did he ride? A snail can move approximately 0.3 m/min. How many metres can the snail cover in 15 minutes? Distance Speed Time A person in a kayak paddles down a river at an avera ge speed of 10 km/h. After 3 hours, how far has she travelled? A plane flies east at 250km/h for 3 hours and then south at 200km/h for 1 hour. How far did the plane travel in the first part of the flight? How far did the plane travel in the second part of the flight? What is the total distance travelled? What is the average speed of the plane for the whole journey? Velocity (Optional) A plane flies 420km due north in 2 hour s . Find the average velocity of the plane in km/h. A boat sails 1.2km due east for a time of 5 minutes. Find the average velocity of the boat in m/s. An aeroplane flies due north with an average velocity of 85m/s for 20s. Calculate the displacement of the aeroplane. A truck travels along a straight road with a constant velocity of 30m/s. After 15 seconds, how far has the truck travelled? Beth rides her horse 3km east and then 4km north. The trip takes her 30 minutes. What is the total distance Beth travelled? What is her average speed in km/h? What is Beth’s displacement? What is her average velocity? Amanda drives her car 35km north and then 75km south in a time of 2 hours. What is her average speed in km/h? What is her displacement? What is her average velocity in km/h? CHALLENGE PROBLEM 1 Bill and Amy want to ride their bikes from their house to school which is 14.4 kilometers away. It takes Amy 40 minutes to arrive at school. Bill arrives 20 minutes after Amy. How much faster (in meters/second) is Amy’s average speed for the entire trip? 5717540 165735 CHALLENGE PROBLEM 2 ÷3.6 speed in speed in km/h m/s ×3.6 Do you remember the fable of the tortoise and the hare? The giant tortoise can reach a speed of about 7.5cm/s. A hare can run as fast as 20m/s. If their race was 1km long, how long was the hare asleep if the race resulted in a tie?

title: The Science of Airbags
subject: Science
searchText: 1586865 4348480 Name: Class: Mark: /10 % 40000 20000 Name: Class: Mark: /10 % 3714750 371475 0 0 YEAR 10 SCIENCE ARC TRANSITION ASSESSMENT SIX THE SCIENCE OF AIRBAGS -2771775 2382520 0 0 PART ONE: Air Bag Study Guide Research airbags and complete the following questions. 1. What is the intended purpose of an air bag? 2. W hat is a major concern with air bags? 3. What is being done to make air bags safer? 4. W hat are three rules for drivers of cars with passenger-side air bags? 1. 2. 3. 5. What gas fills up the air bag? 6. Explain how an air bag works. 7. How long does it take for the air bag to inflate? PART TWO: It's a Crash Test, Dummy The engineers who design air bags are able to determine the exact quantity of chemicals needed to inflate the air bag to the proper volume, and in the correct amount of time. If the air bag is under inflated or inflates too quickly, the passenger will still be injured by the steering wheel. If the air bag over inflates or inflates too slowly, the passenger will hit the inflating airbag and be injured. It is critical to get just the right amount of gas in the air bag. During th is exploration, you will attempt to find the amount of sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) required to react with 25 ml of acetic acid (vinegar) so that the bag is inflated, with no appreciable quantity of either reactant left. This will allow you to develop some idea of a limiting reactant. (Depending on the atmospheric pressure, the amount of baking soda required to fully inflate the bag should be between 1.5 and 3.0 grams.) In this reaction, acetic acid combines with sodium bicarbonate to form water, carbon dioxide, and sodium acetate. The chemical equation for this reaction is: HC 2 H 3 O 2 + NaHCO 3 ---> H 2 O + CO 2 + NaC 2 H 3 O 2 The carbon dioxide is the gas that fills the bag, and the sodium acetate will be dissolved in the water. It is important to realize that this is not exactly how an air bag works, but is a good analogy that allows you to simulate the inflation of a protective device in the classroom. Be prepared for some messes with the egg drop test. It is recommended that a plastic sheet be placed under the "drop zone" to assist in cleaning up. It is important to find a container for the egg drop that is the right size; three-pound butter tubs or small shoe boxes work well. Also be sure to wash your hands well after handling raw eggs. It’s a Crash Test, Dummy Introduction In a real automobile safety restraint system, the air bag is a large plastic bag of about 65.0 L which fills with nitrogen as soon as a sensor tells it that the car’s forward momentum has been drastically lowered. The nitrogen is produced by the rapid decomposition of sodium azide (NaN3), which produces nitrogen gas (N2). In this lab, we will create our own air bag technology utilizing sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) and acetic acid (vinegar). Your task is to find the correct amounts of sodium bicarbonate and acetic acid to use to create the right amount of gas (carbon dioxide) to fill the bag. If done correctly, your bag should fill up, but not pop open. There also should not be any sodium bicarbonate or acetic acid left in the bag. Part 1 Procedure : Before starting, look at the data table in which you will record the amount of acid, the amount of sodium bicarbonate, a description of how the bag inflated, and whether there was acetic acid or sodium bicarbonate left over. 1. To keep it simple, you are always going to have the same amount of acetic acid in the bag: 25 ml. Add 25 ml of acid to the bag. 2. Then measure 0.5 grams of sodium bicarbonate and record it in the data table. Place the sodium bicarbonate in a small piece of tissue. 3. Drop the sodium bicarbonate wrapped in tissue into the bag. Flatten the bag to remove the air and seal the bag as quickly as possible. As soon as the acetic acid soaks through the tissue, the chemicals will begin to react and bubble; the gas that is produced is carbon dioxide (CO 2 ). The bag should begin to inflate. 4. When the bubbling stops, mix the ingredients around to be sure that the reaction is complete. 5. Then test how inflated the bag is by pinching it. Write a description in the data table. 6. If all of the sodium bicarbonate seems to be gone, open the bag and add a small amount of sodium bicarbonate to see if more bubbles form. If they do, then there was still some acetic acid left in the bag. If not, then all of the acetic acid reacted. Make a note in the data table if there was acetic acid left in the bag. 7. Repeat this process by increasing the amount of sodium bicarbonate by 0.5 grams until all of the acetic acid is used up, indicated by the presence of sodium bicarbonate in the bag (because there was no acetic acid left to react with it). DATA TABLE Part 2 Now you will put this knowledge to the test: a crash test. You will design and build a “vehicle” for your crash test dummy, a raw egg. The goal here is to build your vehicle so that it will protect the egg from breaking, even when dropped from a height of 2 meters. The only materials you can use are: a container for the egg (e.g., a small cardboard box or large butter tub) two plastic bags acetic acid sodium bicarbonate tape a graduated cylinder a balance a meter stick Procedure : Follow the steps below using the ratio of sodium bicarbonate to acetic acid that inflated the bag, with no acetic acid or sodium bicarbonate left over. (You wouldn’t want acid in your air bag, would you?) 1. Inflate one or both bags, whichever you think would work best. 2. Place the inflated bag(s) and the egg in the container. 3. Drop from 2 meters. 4. Check your passenger. Did it survive the crash? Analysis and Conclusions : 1. How much sodium bicarbonate had been added when there appeared to be no acetic acid or sodium bicarbonate left after the reaction? 2. Did this amount of sodium bicarbonate (when there was no acetic acid or sodium bicarbonate left) inflate the bag fully? If not, how could you change the amounts of sodium bicarbonate and acetic acid so that the bag is full, but with no reactants left over? 3. What are reactants? Use question #2 to help you form a definition for “reactants.” 4. Draw a picture of the vehicle you used. 5. What was the result of your crash test? 6. What changes would you make to your vehicle to further protect your passenger? 7. How is this experiment similar to an air bag in a car? How is it different? 8. How does figuring out the correct ratio of reactants help manufacturers of real air bags.

title: Velocity
subject: Science
searchText: Velocity Speed is the distance and object travels in a set amount of time. Velocity and speed are very similar ideas, but velocity is a vector , and speed is not. Suppose we knew that someone was driving at thirty-five kilometres an hour (35 km/hr), but the direction wasn't given. How would you draw an arrow to represent a vector? You can't know how to draw the vector if you only have one value (either amount or direction). In this example, you were never told about the direction. Physicists would say that the speed is thirty-five kilometres an hour (35 km/hr), but the velocity is unknown. On the other hand, if you're moving at 35 km/hr in a northern direction, then you would have an arrow pointing north with a length of 35. Physicists would say that the velocity is 35 km/hr north. Velocity is the rate of motion in a specific direction . I'm going that-a-way at 30 kilometers per hour. My velocity is 30 kilometers per hour that-a-way. Average speed is described as a measure of distance divided by time. Velocity can be constant, or it can change (acceleration). Speed with a direction is velocity . Remember vectors? You will use a lot of vectors when you work with velocity. Our real world example of navigation on the ocean used velocity for every vector. Velocity is a vector measurement because it has an amount and a direction. Speed is only an amount (a scalar). Speed doesn't tell the whole story to a physicist. Think of it another way. If I tell you I'm driving north and ask you how long until we get to the city. You can't know the answer since you don't know my speed. You need both values. Acceleration is the rate at which an objec t changes its speed or velocity . Suppose you are riding your bike. You start out going very slowly, hardly pedalling at all. Now you begin to pedal as hard as you can, to speed up - you are accelerating. Now that you are going at a normal speed, you stop pedalling so hard, and just pedal normally. You're still going, but you're not getting any faster, just going along at your normal speed. You're not accelerating anymore. If you stop pedalling now, friction will work on your bike tires (and you'll have friction from the air , too), and you'll soon start to go slower. That's negative acceleration, or deceleration. You're still going, but you are slowing down. One important cause of acceleration is gravity . Suppose you dive off a cliff or a high diving board. You will start off falling slowly, but as gravity pulls on you, you will speed up (accelerate) until you are going very fast. The acceleration of Earth's gravity will speed you up at about 9.8 meters per second per second (9.8 m/s 2 , or 9.8 meters per second squared ). That means that for every second you fall, you'll be going 9.8 meters/second faster. Standing on the cliff before you jump, you're going zero meters/second. One second after you jump, you'll be going 9.8 meters/second. Two seconds after you jump, you'll be going 19.6 meters/second. Three seconds after you jump, you'll be going 29.4 meters/second. Key words Word Meaning Average speed The distance an object travels in a set amount of ___________. Velocity Acceleration What causes acceleration on a bicycle? What causes deceleration (negative acceleration) on a slowing bicycle? What causes the acceleration of a falling ball? What causes deceleration (negative acceleration) on a slowing ball ? searchText:
Year 10 Energy and Change 2009



                            YEAR 10 ENERGY AND CHANGE 2009


MOTION

Everything in the universe is in a state of motion. The earth itself is filled with moving things. The earth
spins on its axis. The planets of our solar system orbit the sun. Our solar system moves through space as
part of the Milky Way Galaxy. The stars and galaxies move away from each other. It might seem
impossible to find a simple way to describe and understand the motions of all these objects. However, this
is just what physicists have done.


WHAT CAUSES MOTION ? (photos from Nardelli et al, 2004)
You are already familiar with the idea that forces are a push, pull, twist or stretch which can produce a
change in the shape, speed or direction of an object. Objects move because they have unbalanced forces on
them. Usually there is more than one force acting on an object, so the movement is a result of the combined
effect of those forces.

Arrows are often used to represent forces with the direction of the arrow showing which way the forces are
operating. The length of the arrow is used to show the size of the force i.e. the longer the arrow the bigger
the force.




                                    ▼
The arrows describing these forces on the kayaker are even in length which means that the forces are the
same size. These forces are acting in opposite directions, which means the force of the kayakers mass
(called his weight) is pushing against the force of the water which is pushing up. These forces are balanced
so he doesn’t move up or down.




  1
 Year 10 Energy and Change 2009



The lateral arrows are uneven in length which means the forces are uneven. The forward force is produced
by the kayaker pushing his paddle in the water and this is greater than the force of drag (or friction) in the
water so the kayaker moves forward in the water.
Everyday you experience forces on your body which push and pull you in a range of directions. These
forces include that of the air pushing on you; which is surprisingly high; some 100 000 N for every square
metre of body size (the average human body is approx. 0.8 m2). We call this air pressure and it is a
measure of the force exerted per square metre of body area. As the force of gravity is pulling the air
particles towards the earth’s surface then the air pressure is greatest closest to the surface and decreases as
you rise through the atmosphere. Air pressure at the surface varies depending upon the air temperature and
movements.




Similarly water particles push against your body exerting a considerable force when you are immersed
underwater. The deeper you go the more water particles pushing down on your body so the greater the
force. In fact for even 10 m of depth there is another 100 000 N pushing in on your body.

There are other forces acting on your body under the water too including the force of the diver’s mass
(weight) and the force of the water pushing up on the diver (buoyancy). The following diagram shows some
of these forces. When a diver has these forces all perfectly balanced it is called neutral buoyancy.

  2
 Year 10 Energy and Change 2009




ANOTHER APPLICATION OF FORCES IN SPORT : SURFING
Read the following passage which describes how Layne Beachley uses forces to her advantage when surfing.




  3
 Year 10 Energy and Change 2009



                                                              Surfing is like skating downhill while being
                                                              pulled uphill. The force of gravity pulls the
                                                              surfer down the wave while the drag pulls the
                                                              surfer back up the wave. Surfing is a fine
                                                              balance between the forces of gravity, buoyancy
                                                              and drag. The force of friction prevents the
                                                              surfer from slipping off the surf board. Rubbing
                                                              wax on to the deck of the board gives it a rough
                                                              surface which in turn increases the force of
                                                              friction. Friction is a force acting in the opposite
                                                              direction to that in which the object is moving.

                                                              QUESTIONS:
                                                              1.Think about another sporting example where
                                                              friction is useful. Describe the situation and
                                                              explain how friction plays a role.

               In science, graphs are used to visually display data gained through experimentation. There are a number of
               different types of graphs, and it is important that you choose the right one to display your data.
               Although software is available for creating graphs, drawing your own graphs is a useful skill to develop.

               Line graph
               A line graph is used to display data that is continuous. That is, each point is related to the one before and the
               one after. Examples of continuous data are length, weight and temperature. For example, suppose that you
               measured the temperature in a beaker of water while it is being heated over a Bunsen burner for a period of
               10 minutes. The data you collected is shown in the following table.

               When drawing a line graph, you need to use the following steps.

                1 Draw two axes at right angles to each other.

                2 Make sure the axes are long enough to show all of the information, with an arrow on the end of each.

searchText:
Biology – keyword save or scrap?
Teaching notes

This resource is designed to help pupils learn to answer extended response
questions effectively.


Students have the word list in front of them plus various coloured pencils.


Use the PPT to reveal the three clues one at a time. After each clue is revealed,
students decide which words to 'save or scrap', before showing the next clue.
Then show students the exam question.


They are then asked to underline certain words using different colours. At this
point go over some of their ideas to iron out any misconceptions such as bile
breaking down fat molecules.


When this is done students use prompts to help them plan an answer the
question. A simple mark scheme is revealed and students write an answer to
the question.


As an alternative to using the PPT the clues, instructions and mark scheme
could be printed on paper and handed out to the students at the appropriate
time.

                                                                    Biology – keyword save or scrap?
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------



Clue 1

The question is about living things.


-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------



Clue 2

The question concerns a process carried out by humans and other
animals.


-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------



Clue 3

The process is digestion.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------



The question

'Describe how different parts of the digestive system help break down dietary
fats so they can be absorbed.'


Instructions

       Underline the substances involved in the digestion of fats in blue

       Underline the places where these substances are produced in green

       Underline the products of fat digestion in red

       Highlight where these products are absorbed in yellow

       Circle words which are connected to the effect of bile on fats

       Add an 'F' to words which are connected to another function of bile

Planning your answer

Now you are ready to plan your answer the question

Use the prompts below to help you....

       substances involved in fat digestion
       their function
       where they are produced
       the products
       where the products are absorbed

Are there any other words remaining in your 'save or scrap' list
which are relevant? Plan how you will use these.


-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------



Writing your answer

Use the mark scheme to help you write an answer to the question.

Mark scheme

Level 1
1 – 2 marks: The answer includes one of the prompts i.e. one
substance OR it's function OR where produced OR the products OR
the site of absorption.

Level 2
3 – 4 marks: A simple description naming the enzyme OR bile and
including its function and at least one other prompt i.e. where
produced; the products; where absorbed

Level 3
5 – 6 marks: A detailed description which includes the enzyme AND
bile AND all of the prompts OR three prompts AND a description of
mechanical digestion.

Investigating the Causes of Rusting
Aim: To investigate factors which affect rusting.

Equipment:
• Safety goggles
                                                         Safety Information
• 4 test tubes                                           Calcium chloride - causes irritation to skin, eyes
• Small beaker                                           and respiratory organs. Harmful if inhaled or
                                                         swallowed.
• Stirring rod
                                                         Wear goggles at all times.
• Test tube rack
                                                         Glassware – risk of cuts if broken.
• Rubber bung for test tube
                                                         Apply pressure to wounds and inform
• Cotton wool                                            teacher immediately.
• Forceps

• Marker pen

• 4 iron nails

• Anhydrous calcium chloride granules

• Vegetable oil

• Dropping pipette

• Deionised water

• Boiled deionised water

• Table salt

Method:
Step 1: Label the tests tube 1, 2, 3 and 4

Step 2: In test tube 1, fill ¼ of the test tube with deionised water and add a nail

Step 3: In test tube 2, fill ¼ of the test tube with boiled deionised water and add a nail. Carefully drop
some oil onto the water – with the pipette – to create an air tight layer

Step 4: Mix salt into some deionised water in the beaker, and stir with the rod until dissolved

Step 5: In test tube 3, fill ¼ of the test tube with the salt solution you just made, and add a nail

Step 6: In test tube 4, add about 2 cm depth of calcium chloride granules and add a nail. Seal the test
tube with the rubber bung

Step 7: Leave the nails for 3 days

Step 8: Record your observations into a suitable table

                                                 Page 1 of 2
                                                                            Investigating the Causes of Rusting




 Test tube conditions:
 Test tube 1 – water and air

 Test tube 2 – water, no air (removed during boiling process / sealed by oil layer)

 Test tube 3 – water, air and salt

 Test tube 4 – no water, air (calcium chloride absorbs the water, bung prevents moisture from air)


Questions:
 1. Use the information from the box above to make a clear table of the conditions of each test tube.

 2. Describe what your results have shown.

 3. Explain your results using your understanding of the oxidation reaction which causes rusting.

 4. Was your investigation accurate? How can you improve it?




                                                Page 2 of 2
                                                                            Investigating the Causes of Rusting


Answers:
 1. Use the information from the box above to make a clear table of the conditions of each test tube.

        Test Tube                    Air                      Water                         Salt

            1                         Y                         Y                            N

            2                         N                         Y                            N

            3                         Y                         Y                            Y

            4                         Y                         N                            N



 2. Describe what your results have shown.
    The results show that rusting occurs in the presence of water and air (test tubes 1 and 3). It
    should also show that salt increases the rate of rusting.

 3. Explain your results using your understanding of the oxidation reaction which causes rusting.
    The oxidation reaction of iron requires oxygen, which is in the air, and dissolved in the water.
    Although water was present in test tube 2, it had been boiled so any dissolved oxygen had been
    removed. Test tube 4 did not show any rusting because only air was present.

 4. Was your investigation accurate? How can you improve it?
    The accuracy of the measurements of the different chemicals used was not very accurate. Rather
    than measuring by cm depth it would be more accurate to measure the mass in g, using a top pan
    balance. Measuring the liquids as ¼ filled test tubes was also not accurate and could be improved
    by measuring in millilitres using a measuring cylinder.

Investigating the Effects of Exercise
Aim: To describe how the body changes during exercising.

Equipment:
• A partner to work with

• A blood pressure monitor                                Safety Information
                                                          Exercise – possible injury
• A timer
                                                          Do not exercise more than you feel comfortable
                                                          with. Any sickness or dizziness inform the
                                                          teacher immediately.

                                                          Only exercise in a clear space.



Method:
Step 1: Decide who will be the ‘coach’ and who will be the ‘exerciser’

Step 2: Exerciser – find your pulse, either on your neck or wrist, and count
the number of ‘beats’ you can feel in 15 seconds. Multiply this by 4 to get
the BPM. Record your resting pulse rate

Step 3: Measure the exerciser’s blood pressure using an automatic monitor
and record the results

Step 4: Whilst resting, observe the amount of redness and sweat on the
exerciser’s face, as well as their breathing pattern. Record these observations

Step 5: Exerciser – perform some moderate exercise e.g. 50 jumping jacks or
jogging on the spot for 2 minutes

Step 6: Repeat steps 2 to 4 and record your measurements after exercise

Step 7: Swap roles and repeat for the other person



Questions:
 1. Describe how your pulse rate changed after exercising.

 2. Describe how your blood pressure changed after exercising.

 3. Describe how your appearance (redness and sweating), and your breathing changed
    after exercising.

 4. Explain why you think you saw the changes you observed.

                                                                         Investigating the Effects of Exercise
Answers:

 1. Describe how your pulse rate changed after exercising.
    The pulse rate has increased.

 2. Describe how your blood pressure changed after exercising.
    The blood pressure has increased.

 3. Describe how your appearance (redness and sweating), and your breathing changed
    after exercising.
    The face will have become more red than before. There may be visible sweating. The breathing
    will have become deeper and more rapid.

 4. Explain why you think you saw the changes you observed.
    When the body is exercising there is a demand for more energy; and therefore more oxygen to
    release the energy.
    The pulse rate increases as the heart works faster to pump more blood, carrying oxygen, to the
    cells.
    The blood pressure increases as the heart is pumping faster and harder, so the blood is being
    moved at a higher pressure.
    The blood vessels move towards the surface, and sweating begins in order to transfer excess heat
    energy from the body (by evaporation of sweat).
    Breathing becomes deeper and more rapid in order to get more oxygen into the body, and to
    remove the increased production of carbon dioxide.
